Sports.title: Joshua Buatsi vs Willy Hutchinson 2 Live Results: Round-by-Round Updates
Sports.content:
Welterweight Jack Rafferty (28-0-1, 18 KOs) defeated Hovhannes Martirosyan (20-2, 12 KOs) by a 12-round unanimous decision to claim the vacant IBO title. The judges scored it 116-111, 116-111 and 114-113 after a hard-fought contest that saw both men land heavy punches.

Martirosyan boxed effectively off the back foot and enjoyed lengthy spells of success, while Rafferty kept pressing and throwing in volume. Rafferty scored a disputed knockdown in the 12th, with the incident drawing questions over whether a push had sent Martirosyan through the ropes.

That call proved crucial on the closest card, where Rafferty finished just one point ahead. Martirosyan’s late fade allowed Rafferty to finish strongly, but the unbeaten favorite had to work through a much tougher fight than the two wider scores suggested.

Bradley Rea (23-2, 12 KOs) knocked out Ezra Taylor (13-2, 9 KOs) in the second round to retain his WBA Inter-Continental light heavyweight title. The scheduled 10-round contest ended abruptly as Rea punished Taylor’s decision to trade early.

Taylor was dropped and appeared unsteady, raising questions about whether the referee should have ended the fight sooner. Rea finished the job with a heavy knockout, handing Taylor his second consecutive defeat. Taylor’s own punching power offered little protection once Rea had him hurt.

Coming off a stoppage win over Liam Cameron, Rea delivered another decisive finish to strengthen his position in the division.

Gully Powar (14-1-1, 1 KO) captured the vacant British featherweight title with a unanimous technical decision over Zak Miller (17-2, 3 KOs). The judges scored it 96-95, 97-94 and 96-94 after the scheduled 12-round contest was halted in the 10th.

Severe swelling on Miller’s forehead from accidental head clashes prompted the doctor to stop the fight and send it to the scorecards. Powar’s persistent pressure and punch volume helped him edge a competitive contest, with both fighters landing quality shots.

Miller remained willing to fight, but the swelling prevented him from getting the final two rounds to overturn Powar’s lead. Powar secured the Lonsdale Belt at his second attempt after drawing with Rhys Edwards in his previous British title challenge.

Middleweight Stephen Clarke (11-0, 2 KOs) defeated Harley Collison (3-10-2) by an eight-round points decision. Referee Steve Gray scored it 80-72, awarding Clarke every round. The Liverpool prospect controlled the contest and took a clear victory over the experienced Southampton fighter.

Collison completed the distance, giving the 25-year-old Clarke eight rounds of work. A former national amateur champion, Clarke is trained by Stephen “Swifty” Smith and managed by Paul Smith. This was another step in his professional education, although stronger opposition will provide a better measure of his progress.

Junior middleweight John Joe Carrigan (5-0, 5 KOs) stopped Cheikh Diop (6-2) in the fourth round to maintain his perfect knockout run. The 19-year-old southpaw secured the finish against an opponent who had previously lost only by decision.

Diop entered with more professional experience but became the fifth fighter unable to go the distance with Carrigan. The Carlisle teenager turned professional in late 2025 after winning gold at the Under-19 World Championships.

He trains in Hartlepool and has carried his amateur success into a promising start with Queensberry Promotions. The official time of the stoppage was not immediately available.

Tony Yoka (16-3, 12 KOs) defeated Kostiantyn Dovbyshchenko (10-21-1, 7 KOs) by a six-round points decision in their heavyweight bout. The reported score was 59-55 for the Frenchman.

Yoka controlled the contest, although the Ukrainian veteran took him the distance. Dovbyshchenko has also gone the rounds with Moses Itauma, making this a predictable opportunity for Yoka to get some work.

The 2016 Olympic gold medalist is rebuilding after consecutive defeats to Martin Bakole, Carlos Takam and Ryad Merhy. This victory kept that process moving, but beating an opponent with Dovbyshchenko’s record offers little evidence of how Yoka would fare against contenders.

Javokhir Ummataliev (3-0, 1 KO) defeated Atacayte Santana (4-4-2, 1 KO) by a six-round points decision in super middleweight action. The referee scored it 60-54, giving the Uzbek all six rounds. Ummataliev controlled the contest and secured a clear win in his third professional appearance.

Santana completed the distance after entering as a clear underdog. The 21-year-old Ummataliev arrived in the professional ranks with a strong amateur background, including a 2025 World Championship gold medal. After stopping Damian Drabik in two rounds in his previous outing, he gained more rounds of professional experience against Santana.

Super middleweight prospect Alex Arthur Jr. (6-0, 1 KO) defeated Jose Aguirre (2-32, 1 KO) by a six-round points decision. Referee Steve Gray scored the contest 60-54, awarding Arthur every round.

The 24-year-old Scot controlled the fight and finished with a clear victory over the experienced Costa Rican. Aguirre completed the distance, giving Arthur six rounds of work in his sixth professional outing.

Arthur is the son of former WBO super featherweight champion Alex Arthur. The win provided more experience, although Aguirre’s lengthy losing streak limits what it tells us about the unbeaten prospect.

Tumi Phillips (7-1, 1 KO) defeated Angelo Dragone (10-17-1) by decision in their super lightweight bout. The referee scored it 40-37 for Phillips.

Phillips controlled the contest and was a clear winner at the finish. The younger fighter produced a solid showing against an opponent with considerably more professional experience.

Dragone heard the final bell after suffering a stoppage defeat in his previous outing. No knockdowns were reported, with Phillips taking the victory without any major drama. The official score was not immediately available.

Sports.title: Da’Mazion Vanhouter Floors Ivan Balaz Three Times In TKO Win
Sports.content:
Da’Mazion Vanhouter (14-0, 11 KOs) overwhelmed Ivan Balaz (9-2, 7 KOs) with three first-round knockdowns, using a destructive body attack to secure a TKO victory on Saturday at the Copper Box Arena in London. The scheduled eight-round heavyweight contest lasted less than two minutes before the referee stopped it following the third knockdown.

Balaz had previously dropped Johnny Fisher, but he never established that kind of threat against Vanhouter. The 21-year-old American attacked early and repeatedly put him on the floor, turning a potentially dangerous opening round into a brief, one-sided fight.

Much of Vanhouter’s damage came downstairs. His body punching gave Balaz more to defend than shots aimed at the head, and the repeated knockdowns left the Slovak without enough time to recover or build an attack of his own. By the third trip to the canvas, there was little reason to continue.

The result extended Vanhouter’s stoppage streak to eight and followed his recent victories over Raphael Murphy and Raphael Akpejiori. His British debut provided another example of his early finishing power, although the speed of the victory limited what could be learned about his ability over longer fights.

Balaz’s previous performance against Fisher gave this matchup some interest. An opponent who has already hurt a bigger-name heavyweight presents an obvious risk if a prospect leaves himself open while chasing a knockout. Vanhouter removed that risk quickly by making Balaz defend from the outset.

The body attack was the most encouraging part of the performance. Young heavyweight punchers can become too focused on landing one spectacular shot upstairs, especially when opponents begin retreating or covering up. Attacking the torso gives them a larger target and can punish a defensive guard that protects the chin while leaving the ribs and midsection exposed.

Against Balaz, Vanhouter’s approach produced immediate results. The knockdowns arrived too quickly for the fight to settle into anything resembling a competitive contest. Balaz needed an opportunity to interrupt the American’s offense, but he could not create one before the referee intervened.

Vanhouter’s physical progression also makes him an unusual heavyweight prospect. Having begun his professional career near 154 pounds, he has developed into a fighter weighing more than 230. That change makes future opposition particularly relevant: stronger heavyweights who can absorb his opening attack will provide a better indication of how his power and conditioning hold up together.

Those questions remain for later fights. Balaz could not take Vanhouter beyond the opening round, much less force him to adjust after several rounds of resistance.

For this outing, Vanhouter completed the job emphatically. Three knockdowns and a sustained attack to the body gave him another early stoppage, keeping his unbeaten record intact and providing a clear reason to increase the difficulty of his next test.

Vanhouter is already drawing inevitable comparisons to Moses Itauma. Same age bracket, identical trail of early bodies, and the usual promoter machinery hyping him as the next heavyweight savior. The difference is Itauma actually stepped up, and Filip Hrgovic quickly proved what happens when an explosive kid runs into a granite chin that doesn’t fold in two minutes.

That is why nobody should get carried away by Vanhouter’s demolition of Ivan Balaz. Smashing an overmatched target to the ribs is easy work. Dropping a guy three times inside two minutes tells you zero about how Vanhouter reacts when somebody takes his best shot, walks through the fire, and makes him fight backward. Beating up a hurt fighter is a world away from surviving a dogfight.

If Vanhouter is going to become what his backers claim, he needs opponents who come to fight, not collect a check. Racking up highlight-reel knockouts against soft touches looks great on social media, but Itauma learned the hard way what happens when you skip the learning curve. Vanhouter handled business, but until he finds someone willing to fire back, we have no idea how good he actually is.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma Wants Hrgovic Revenge, Warren Requires Top-10 Test
Sports.content:
Moses Itauma wants another shot at Filip Hrgovic, but Frank Warren says he must reestablish himself first. The promoter is targeting a top-10 heavyweight for Itauma’s comeback, although the opponent’s style will reveal far more than a ranking number about how effectively that fight prepares him for revenge.

Warren hopes to announce Itauma’s return next week. Hrgovic also has mandatory business to complete against Frank Sanchez, leaving Itauma with a rebuilding job while the title picture plays out.

“Well, that’s what he’d like. He asked for that immediately, and it’d be a big event. There’s no doubt about it,” Warren told BoxNation regarding an Itauma-Hrgovic rematch. “Sold out last time. I’m sure if we put it on again, it was so exciting a fight, it would sell out again. But first of all, he’s got to reestablish himself, and Filip’s got to get rid of his mandatory against Sanchez.”

Asked what level of opponent he wanted for Itauma’s return, Warren answered: “Top 10.”

That sets a high bar on paper, yet it reveals little about the specific technical hurdles Itauma will need to clear. A top-10 ranking covers vastly different tactical challenges. Pairing him with someone like Bakhodir Jalolov would force Itauma to solve height, reach, and distance management against a towering southpaw who dictates range behind a long jab. That offers a valuable puzzle, but it represents a different examination from the physical pressure that broke him down against Hrgovic.

A veteran like Joseph Parker represents the opposite stylistic end. Parker possesses the durability to absorb clean contact, the veteran craft to work on the inside, and the sustained output to test whether Itauma can defend while moving. Backing up in straight lines leaves a fighter vulnerable to being marched into the ropes. An opponent with Parker’s engine would compel Itauma to pivot off the centerline, escape off the back foot, and reset ring position rather than settling into a simple linear retreat.

A useful return bout must also address what happens at the end of his combinations. Against an opponent who fires back through incoming punches, Itauma cannot afford to admire his work with his chin exposed or his guard down. A fighter who punches between exchanges will compel him to roll, tuck his chin, or slip out of range the moment his offense concludes.

Pacing remains just as central to his development. Itauma built his reputation on early knockouts, but burning through his reserves trying to blast out a durable contender carries obvious hazards. A test against someone capable of taking solid contact would force Itauma to establish his jab, vary his punch selection, and bank rounds without exhausting himself in search of a single finish.

Warren does not need to throw him into another firefight to achieve those ends. Another loss would derail the rematch entirely. The trick is finding an opponent who makes Itauma solve the specific stylistic puzzles Hrgovic presented while still offering a clear route to a confidence-building win.

Sanchez could alter that landscape before Itauma gets his second chance. Warren noted that Sanchez previously stepped aside to permit the initial bout and now holds mandatory status. Should Sanchez take the belt, avenging the loss to Hrgovic and pursuing the world title will point in different directions.

Queensberry would then have to weigh whether a grudge match carries enough commercial appeal without the hardware on the line. For Itauma, the immediate priority remains narrower: overcome an opponent who asks enough difficult questions to make a second meeting with Hrgovic truly winnable.

Putting Itauma right back in with Hrgovic after a single confidence builder is a classic promotional trap, and history shows that rush rarely ends well for a young fighter.

At 21, Itauma suffered the exact kind of loss that leaves scar tissue. Being carried out on a stretcher after emptying his entire gas tank through eight rounds reveals a deficit you cannot patch up in one training camp. Hrgovic did not just beat him on points; he broke him physically and mentally by weaponizing his granite chin, size, and steady, chopping output.

Hrgovic’s pre-fight psychological read proved spot on: he openly predicted that Itauma had never faced real adversity, had never felt what happens when his best shots fail to stop a man, and would drown in deep water. Itauma swept early rounds, but by round eight, he had completely redlined trying to force a finish.

Once Hrgovic survived the storm, Itauma had zero tactical fallback. Going back into the ring with a 6’6″ puncher who now knows he can absorb everything Itauma throws and outlast him is handing Hrgovic the psychological blueprint on a silver platter.

One tune-up does not solve that kind of problem. A single soft touch or showcase fight lets a fighter look explosive again, but it teaches him nothing about pacing in rounds nine through twelve, managing energy against someone who refuses to go down, or handling heavy incoming shots when fatigued.

If Warren matches him with a hand-picked opponent who folds inside four rounds, Itauma steps right back into a Hrgovic rematch with the same structural flaws that got him stopped in August.

Itauma needs two or three genuine developmental bouts against durable, grinding heavyweights who make him work every minute of ten or twelve rounds without handing him an early exit. He has plenty of time on his side. Rushing him into an immediate rematch to salvage a narrative risks cutting a potentially elite career short before it even gets off the ground.

Sports.title: Bill Haney Opens Rematch Door, Norman Jr Must Deliver
Sports.content:
Brian Norman Jr. has a long road ahead if he wants a second crack at Devin Haney, and taking out Abel Ramos on December 19 is merely step one. With Haney eyeing massive paydays elsewhere, Norman must string together dominant wins to convince the public that a return bout would play out any differently.

“Handle your business, and you might get what you’re looking for again,” said Bill Haney on social media, aiming the message squarely at Brian Norman Sr.

Norman (29-1, 23 KOs) meets Ramos (29-6-3, 22 KOs) in a 10-round co-feature at Chase Center in San Francisco. Haney headlines against IBF champion Liam Paro, targeting another belt to sit alongside the WBO strap he lifted from Norman last November on DAZN PPV.

Bill left plenty of wiggle room. Even a destructive win over Ramos does not guarantee a return date, especially if Haney handles Paro and targets full unification. Norman likely needs multiple statement victories to build real commercial appeal.

Ramos alone will not create that demand. The real opening is the platform: fighting directly in front of Haney’s crowd and proving that the glaring flaws from the first encounter have been corrected.

Norman looked gun-shy after eating an early flash knockdown he never saw coming. He spent round after round letting Haney flick the jab at will from distance, failing to make the fight ugly or cut the ring. By the time Norman showed genuine urgency in the championship rounds, the scorecards were long gone.

The blueprint for a return requires relentless, disciplined pressure from the opening bell. Norman cannot surrender minutes watching Haney reset behind the jab and dictate the terms of engagement. He has to march inside behind hard combinations, force Haney into sustained defensive shells, and stay alert to incoming counters.

Norman must also solve the clinching problem. Haney repeatedly tied him up inside to stall offensive rhythm before sliding back out to safety. Norman was far too passive in those moments, content to wait for the referee to separate them.

David Haye understood how to make fighters pay for holding. Instead of waiting around, Haye would free an arm and unload rapid, clubbing headshots over the top to force guys to let go. Norman needs that exact type of spite: cracking Haney with fast, cuffing punches around the guard the second he reaches in, continuing to fire until the referee breaks them up.

That approach might not stop the holding completely, but it punishes the tactic. Tying up a fighter who continues to batter the body burns far more stamina than holding someone who politely stands still. Norman has to turn every clinch into an exhausting chore.

Ramos provides a live test for that engine. He dropped Mario Barrios in their spirited draw and handed Tahmir Smalls his first career defeat. Norman bounced back by halting Josh Wagner, but Ramos will force him to stay sharp under fire.

A win over Ramos will not erase questions about how Norman handles the jab and grab. Stringing together stoppages over seasoned contenders is his only route to forcing Haney back into the ring.

The fathers can talk all they want. Norman has to show in the ring that he can make Haney fight instead of coasting.

Sports.title: Chris Billam-Smith vs Chev Clarke Live: Round-by-Round Updates From Zuffa Boxing 12
Sports.content:
Heavyweight Da’Mazion Vanhouter (14-0, 11 KOs) dropped Ivan Balaz (9-2, 7 KOs) three times en route to a first-round TKO in their scheduled eight-round bout. Vanhouter attacked the body with heavy punches, giving Balaz little opportunity to establish his own offense.

All three knockdowns came inside the opening two minutes as the unbeaten American overwhelmed his opponent. The referee stopped the contest after the third knockdown, ending a one-sided fight.

Balaz had previously troubled Johnny Fisher, but he could not withstand Vanhouter’s early assault. The 21-year-old recorded his eighth consecutive stoppage, continuing his run of quick finishes.

Light welterweight Kayla Allen (2-0, 1 KO) earned a hard-fought six-round points victory over Julia Igel (5-3, 4 KOs), with the referee scoring it 58-56. Both fighters threw freely from the opening bell, with Allen’s pressure forcing Igel onto the back foot.

Igel stood her ground often enough to land heavy replies, making Allen work throughout her second professional fight. Allen bloodied her opponent and maintained the higher volume, while Igel’s output dipped during spells.

The German southpaw continued firing back, but Allen landed effectively in the later rounds to secure the verdict. After stopping Edina Kiss on her debut, Allen gained valuable rounds against an opponent who tested her beyond the opening attack.

Middleweight Sam Hickey (7-0, 4 KOs) stopped Amaury Massenaux (16-5-1, 4 KOs) in the fifth round of their scheduled eight-round bout. Hickey controlled the action, taking his time to build his attack against the more experienced Belgian.

The Scot maintained steady pressure and inflicted mounting punishment without rushing his work. Massenaux stayed in the contest but could not do enough to disrupt Hickey’s control.

Hickey increased the intensity before the referee stepped in during the fifth to prevent further punishment. The 2022 Commonwealth Games gold medallist passed his latest test with a controlled stoppage victory in his seventh professional outing.

Light heavyweight Umar Dzambekov (15-0, 11 KOs) knocked out Zach Parker (26-3, 18 KOs) with a body shot at 1:47 of the fourth round in their scheduled 10-round bout. Parker had some early success with straight right hands and punches to the body, but Dzambekov repeatedly caught him with his arcing southpaw left.

The unbeaten Austrian’s ability to land that punch gave Parker problems despite the competitive start. Early in the fourth, Parker briefly went down after their legs tangled, with no knockdown scored.

Dzambekov then drove a left hand into the solar plexus, sending Parker to the canvas in pain. Parker could not beat referee Kieran McCann’s count, giving Dzambekov the biggest victory of his career.

Cruiserweight Lucas Roehrig (10-0, 6 KOs) stopped Connal McDonald (5-2, 1 KO) in the seventh round of their scheduled eight-round bout. Roehrig controlled the action with combinations and a sustained body attack, building a lead before forcing the finish.

McDonald struggled to interrupt his offense as Roehrig kept the pressure on. In the seventh, a barrage of unanswered punches drove McDonald to his knees and brought the referee in to stop the contest.

The Scottish Area champion represented a step up for Roehrig, who dealt with the test without needing the scorecards. Trained and managed by George Groves, the 23-year-old earned his sixth stoppage victory.

Featherweight Masood Abdulah (14-1, 8 KOs) scored two knockdowns to defeat Adan Palma (14-2) by an eight-round unanimous decision. The judges scored it 78-72, 77-73 and 76-74.

Abdulah dropped Palma with a short left hook in the opening minute, then used his jab and compact hooks to catch him coming forward. Palma fought his way back into the contest, landing heavy right hands in the fourth round that forced Abdulah to clinch.

A well-timed check left hook sent Palma down again in the sixth, slowing his attack and giving Abdulah more room to dictate the action. Abdulah worked behind his jab and continued finding the left hook over the final two rounds to secure the victory.

Vinnie Kemp (1-0, 1 KO) stopped Liam McElhinney (0-3) with a barrage of body shots at 2:33 of the opening round in their scheduled four-round middleweight bout. Making his professional debut, Kemp charged forward from the opening bell, throwing hard punches and goading McElhinney.

The referee briefly paused the action to warn Kemp about his verbals before allowing the fight to continue. Kemp resumed his attack, stalking McElhinney and driving punches into his midsection.

McElhinney bent forward and covered up against the ropes under the sustained body attack, prompting the referee to wave it off. Kemp’s aggression gave him a quick debut victory, although McElhinney offered little to test him.

Sports.title: Canelo Fought Kovalev, So Why Rule Out Beterbiev?
Sports.content:
Sergio Mora argues that Canelo Alvarez is simply too small for Dmitry Bivol or Artur Beterbiev, but that claim collides with Canelo’s track record. Moving up to light heavyweight did not stop Canelo from taking on Sergey Kovalev, so physical scale alone should not close the book on either matchup.

When Chris Mannix asked what should happen if Bivol gets past Callum Smith, Mora chose a third meeting between Bivol and Beterbiev over a Canelo rematch. He dismissed Canelo’s prospects, pointing to edges that reach beyond the 175-pound limit.

“Bivol’s bigger, he has faster feet, and he has one of the best jabs in boxing that gives Canelo issues. And Beterbiev is just way too big, way too strong, and he has smart footwork as well. Not in and out like Bivol, but it’s smart fundamentally. No, both of those guys are too big for him,” Mora told DAZN Boxing.

The technical points Mora raises hold far more substance than simple scale. Canelo climbed to 175 in November 2019, stopping the 36-year-old Kovalev in the eleventh round to capture the WBO belt. That victory remains a cornerstone of his four-division resume, keeping any future venture at light heavyweight open to legitimate discussion.

If Canelo truly cleaned out 168 and sits on a throne where nobody at super middleweight is worthy, then stepping up to fight Artur Beterbiev is the exact test he should take.

The critics who instantly rule out a Beterbiev clash point to size, power, and danger. Yet those same excuses vanish whenever people praise Canelo for jumping straight to light heavyweight in 2019 to take out Sergey Kovalev. If handling the physical jump to 175 was good enough to claim a belt back then, using size as a shield today doesn’t work. Canelo already established that he will willingly step into the ring against a light heavyweight champion when an opportunity presents itself.

The timing makes the matchup entirely fair game. Beterbiev is past 40, carrying the heavy mileage, wear, and physical toll of a brutal, extended career. When Canelo moved up to dethrone Kovalev, he targeted a 36-year-old champion with clear vulnerabilities. Facing a 41-year-old Beterbiev fits the identical blueprint. If Canelo’s supporters argue that Beterbiev’s age is catching up to him, then Canelo has zero excuses to avoid testing those waters.

Ruling the fight out gives Canelo a convenient pass to linger in safe territory. Instead of entertaining another slow, uneventful outing against Terence Crawford or settling for predictable matchups at super middleweight, Canelo ought to prove his greatness where the stakes are genuine. If he were brave enough to hunt Kovalev at 175, ruling out an aging Beterbiev looks less like caution and more like dodging a fight that would truly test his limits.

Sports.title: Liam Paro Calls Haney’s Knockout Talk A Bluff
Sports.content:
Liam Paro expects Devin Haney to abandon his knockout talk once they fight, leaving the Australian needing to create punching opportunities against an opponent he believes will avoid sustained trading.

Paro would welcome Haney standing with him. His preparations, however, must account for the cautious approach he expects rather than the aggressive one Haney has promised.

“I believe Haney is one of the hardest tasks, just his style. He’s not going to be there to engage. But look, he said that he’s looking for a knockout. I guarantee I’ll beat him in a firefight, but I know he’s not going to do that. He’s a good boxer,” said Paro to the Punch Podcast.

The first problem is getting past Haney’s jab without spending rounds following him. As a southpaw, Paro can contest that punch with his lead right hand, tapping or occupying Haney’s left to disrupt his ability to judge distance. That could help Paro bring his rear left into range without having to rush through a clean jab.

There is a cost to reaching for that control. If Paro becomes preoccupied with Haney’s lead hand, he can leave an opening for the straight right. His hand fighting needs to accompany his footwork, giving him a route to attack rather than becoming an exercise Haney can read.

Paro also needs to distinguish pressure from pursuit. Following Haney around the perimeter would allow the American to choose when to stop, punch, and move again. Short diagonal steps across his route would make Haney change direction or surrender space toward the ropes.

The straight left to the body could help there. Paro does not have to reach Haney’s head with every attack to make his movement less comfortable. Targeting the torso gives him a chance to score beneath the jab and draw a defensive reaction that creates his next opening. Overreaching would leave him vulnerable to a counter or a clinch.

What happens after Haney punches could be just as valuable. Paro needs to position himself to answer before Haney has completed his retreat. A short right hook or a straight left may catch an exit, but only if Paro remains balanced enough to throw immediately. Loading up would let the opportunity disappear.

Paro estimates they have shared close to 100 rounds of sparring. That experience could help him recognize when Haney intends to move, hold, or counter. It also means Haney has substantial knowledge of Paro’s approach. Familiarity becomes an advantage only if Paro can disguise what he does next.

His first-round knockout of Brock Jarvis demonstrates the danger when he lands cleanly. It does less to explain how he will manufacture that opening against Haney.

Paro’s clearest route is to make brief encounters productive: interfere with the jab, close space without reaching, and score before Haney gets clear. If he can do that consistently, he can win rounds without needing Haney to accept the firefight he expects him to refuse.

Sports.title: Melikuziev Crushes Sharipov To Keep Munguia Fight On Track
Sports.content:
Bektemir Melikuziev cleared his final obstacle before an expected world-title shot, knocking out Karomatullo Sharipov in the second round Friday night at Nikki Beach Resort in Dubai. The WBA mandatory challenger finished his overmatched opponent quickly, keeping his pursuit of super middleweight champion Jaime Munguia on course.

Uzbekistan’s Melikuziev (18-1, 12 KOs) needed less than two rounds to finish Tajikistan’s Sharipov (4-4-1, 3 KOs) in the main event of MUKA Boxing’s “Fury by the Sea” card. The scheduled four-round bout marked Melikuziev’s return after more than eight months out of the ring.

The decisive moment came late in the second round. Melikuziev landed a heavy shot that sent Sharipov flat onto his back, bringing the fight to an end. There was no recovery from the knockdown, and the 30-year-old southpaw had completed the immediate task in front of him.

Melikuziev pressed forward in the available second-round footage, finding opportunities to land clean power punches despite brief clinches and return fire. Sharipov could not keep the more experienced contender from getting into punching range, and the difference in their power became decisive before the round ended.

It was the result Melikuziev needed from a fight with limited competitive upside. Sharipov entered with only four professional victories, making this a substantial drop from the opposition the Uzbek contender must beat to become a world champion. A quick knockout met expectations, although it offered little evidence about how Melikuziev will handle a sustained fight against Munguia.

The practical benefit was ending his inactivity. Melikuziev had not fought since stopping Sena Agbeko in seven rounds in February. With his championship opportunity still awaiting a date, Friday’s appearance gave him another training camp and a short spell under fight conditions without committing him to a lengthy contest.

His title claim was already established. The WBA ranks Melikuziev No. 1 at super middleweight and previously ordered Munguia to defend against him. The organization subsequently permitted Munguia to face Nikita Zon on October 31, with the requirement that the winner face Melikuziev next.

Munguia retained his belt by unanimous decision, but his difficult sixth round against Zon gives the mandatory challenger reason for encouragement. Zon hurt the champion badly before Munguia recovered and took control over the second half. Melikuziev’s power makes those defensive openings a concern for Munguia, even allowing for the considerable difference between Friday’s opponent and a reigning champion.

The Ring reported earlier this week that a deal is in place for Munguia to face Melikuziev, although a date and venue have yet to be determined. Friday’s knockout leaves the challenger available to move toward that fight.

For Melikuziev, the title opportunity would represent the biggest step in a rebuilding run that began after Gabriel Rosado knocked him out in 2021. The 2016 Olympic silver medalist later avenged that defeat on points and has now won 11 consecutive fights.

Sharipov was never likely to provide the examination Munguia will. Melikuziev nevertheless did what a leading contender should against this level of opponent: he ended the fight early. The next question is whether he can produce the same damaging offense against a champion capable of surviving trouble and fighting back.

Ghana News.title: ‘Journalists are not enemies of the state’ – Dwumfour urges respect for press freedom
Ghana News.content:
President of the Ghana Journalists Association (GJA), Albert Dwumfour, has called for greater respect for press freedom, insisting that journalists are not enemies of the state amid persistent attacks and harassment of media practitioners.

Speaking at the 30th GJA Media Awards in Accra, he said the Association had recorded more than 50 incidents involving attacks, arrests and harassment of journalists between 2022 and January 2026.

“Journalists are not enemies of the state,” he stated.

Mr Dwumfour said Ghana's progress in international press freedom rankings should not overshadow the challenges journalists continue to face in carrying out their work.

He argued that the true measure of press freedom goes beyond a country's position on an international index to whether journalists can hold powerful institutions accountable without intimidation.

“The true measure of press freedom is not merely where a country ranks internationally, but whether journalists can investigate corruption, question public officials, report on security operations, and hold powerful institutions accountable without intimidation or fear,” he said.

The GJA President called for sustained action to address challenges affecting journalists, including safety concerns, economic insecurity, media independence and professional development.

He said the Association's responsibility was to consolidate the gains made in press freedom while ensuring that persistent threats to journalists were addressed.

“Our responsibility is to consolidate the gains and address persistent challenges,” he stated.

Ghana moved from 52nd in the 2025 World Press Freedom Index to 39th in the 2026 edition, according to figures cited by Mr Dwumfour at the event.

However, the GJA says the reported incidents of attacks and harassment underline the need for continued efforts to protect journalists and safeguard media independence.

Ghana News.title: GJA President warns against complacency despite Ghana’s improved press freedom ranking
Ghana News.content:
President of the Ghana Journalists Association (GJA), Albert Dwumfour, has cautioned against complacency following Ghana’s rise to 39th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index.

He said the improved ranking should not overshadow persistent challenges facing journalists, including safety concerns, economic insecurity, threats to media independence and the need for professional development.

Speaking at the 30th GJA Media Awards in Accra, Mr Dwumfour said Ghana had moved up from 52nd in 2025 and 62nd in 2023, placing fourth in Africa, according to the latest index published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF).

He attributed the improvement to sustained advocacy, institutional commitment and engagement among stakeholders.

“This improvement reflects the importance of sustained advocacy, institutional commitment, and engagement among stakeholders,” he said.

Mr Dwumfour stressed that Ghana’s international ranking should not be the only measure of progress in protecting media freedom.

“The true measure of press freedom is not merely where a country ranks internationally, but whether journalists can investigate corruption, question public officials, report on security operations, and hold powerful institutions accountable without intimidation or fear,” he said.

He urged stakeholders to consolidate the gains while addressing the challenges that continue to affect journalists and media organisations.

“Our responsibility is to consolidate the gains and address persistent challenges including journalist safety, economic insecurity, media independence, and professional development,” he added.

Mr Dwumfour expressed hope that Ghana would improve its position in the next edition of the index, with the ambition of placing among the top three countries.

“Our ambition must be to make Ghana a leading example of press freedom and democratic expression in Africa. We are praying that come next year we will improve on our position and take our ranking position between first and third, God willing,” he said.

The World Press Freedom Index is published annually by Reporters Without Borders and assesses the state of press freedom in 180 countries and territories.

Ghana News.title: Leveraging pension power: How Ghanaian trade unions can turn capital into Worker rights
Ghana News.content:
Globally, organised labour is navigating an unprecedented structural crisis. Membership densities continue to dwindle, undermined by expanding informal economies, shifts in employment relationships like casualisation, and subtle to aggressive corporate anti-union practices. In response, the international labour movement under the guidance of the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC) has continuously urged affiliated unions to innovate, revise, and modernise their organising and recruitment strategies.

Still, while unions in Ghana search for new ways to recruit workers, they often miss one of their most cogent levers: the financial power of public sector workers’ pension funds.

The Financial Goliath Built on Workers’ Sweat

Under Ghana’s National Pensions Act, 2008 (Act 766), mandatory social security contributions equal 18.5% of an employee’s basic salary. While 13.5% goes to the Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT) for Tier-1, 5% is directed into mandatory Tier-2 occupational pension schemes.

Over the past decade, these Tier-2 public sector schemes such as the Health Services Occupational Pension Scheme (HSOPS), the Ghana Education Service Occupational Pension Scheme (GESOPS), and the Public Sector Workers Employees' Pension Scheme (PSWEPS) have grown into financial powerhouses.

Take HSOPS as an example:

Asset Size: Its portfolio commands over GHS 7 billion in assets. Banking Sector Influence: HSOPS holds a substantial 10% equity stake in First Atlantic Bank. Capital Market Impact: Public sector Tier-2 funds provide vital liquidity to the Ghana Stock Exchange (GSE) and government securities.

In short, public sector workers are not just wage earners—they are major institutional investors fueling Ghana's corporate landscape.

18.5% Total Mandatory Social Security (Act 766)

|

+---------------+---------------+

| |

13.5% Tier-1 5% Tier-2

(SSNIT) Occupational Schemes

(e.g., HSOPS, GESOPS)

|

+-----------+-----------+

| |

Equity Stakes Capital Markets

(e.g., 10% First (Ghana Stock Exchange

Atlantic Bank) & Corporate Debt)

The Paradox: Funding the Anti-Union Corporate Machine

Here lies the troubling contradiction: the very capital contributed by unionised public sector workers is frequently channelled into companies that actively suppress trade union rights.

Private commercial banks, service firms, real estate developers, and corporate entities benefiting from pension fund capital investments or credit lines frequently engage in anti-union behaviours:

Discouraging workers from joining union branches. Delaying or refusing to sign Collective Bargaining Agreements (CBAs). Targeting or punishing union leaders within their companies.

Organised labour is effectively financing the growth of corporate entities that actively dismantle worker solidarity. This financial asymmetry must end.

Capital Stewardship: A Strategic Organising Tool

To counter dwindling membership and adapt to modern corporate dynamics, Ghanaian trade unions must introduce Active Capital Stewardship into their core organising strategy:

TRADITIONAL ORGANISING VS. CAPITAL STEWARDSHIP

+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+

| Traditional Strategy | Capital Stewardship Strategy |

+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+

| • Direct workplace recruitment | • Direct workplace recruitment |

| • Worplace petitions | • Pension board ESG policy enforcement|

| • Strikes and demonstrations | • Conditioning capital allocation |

| • Post-facto legal challenges | • Activist proxy voting at AGMs |

+-------------------------------------+-------------------------------------+

Trade Union Trustees Must Assert Control. Public sector pension boards are mandated to include union representation. Union trustees must move beyond passive governance and demand strict Labour-Related ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) Criteria for all fund investments. Conditioning Access to Pension Capital: Public sector funds should establish clear worker-rights standards. Companies seeking equity investments or long-term loans from Tier-2 funds must demonstrate compliance with fundamental international labour standards, respect the right to organise, and maintain signed CBAs. Active Proxy Voting and Direct Engagement: With significant holdings like HSOPS's 10% stake in First Atlantic Bank, union trustees must use their board presence and annual general meeting (AGM) voting power to audit labour relations inside investee entities. "Repent or Deny": The Ultimate Financial Sanction. Anti-union companies benefiting from public sector funds should be given a choice: reform labour relations practices and recognise workers' rights to organise, or face divestment and denial of future worker capital.

Reimagining Recruitment for the Next 15 Years

With 15 years on the front lines of trade union organising, the lesson is clear: workplace organising alone cannot win against modern corporate resistance.

By aligning ITUC’s strategic organising imperatives with the economic leverage of Tier-2 pension funds, Ghanaian trade unions can reshape employer behaviour across the private sector. When anti-union companies realise that hostility toward labour jeopardises their access to billions of cedis in institutional capital, their stance on unionisation will change.

It is time for Ghana's trade union movement to bridge the gap between financial investment and worker organising. Our pension funds must work for us, not against us.

The author is a Principal Industrial Relations Officer at the Ashanti Regional Secretariat of the Health Services Workers Union. He is a Public Policy Analyst/Labour Analyst, Development Practitioner and Non-Executive Board Chairman of the Centre for Social Impact Studies (CeSIS).

Ghana News.title: 2027 Budget review: The ten-billion-dollar question for next Thursday
Ghana News.content:
On Thursday, 12 November, the red dispatch box will return to the floor of Parliament for the reading of the 2027 Budget.

Ahead of that presentation, consider this a diagnostic preview of the government’s flagship economic pitch. To ground it in hard data rather than political rhetoric, I am prefacing this analysis with a sobering twenty-five-year time series calculated by Professor Fred M Dzanku from Bank of Ghana records.

Take a close look at the attached chart before Thursday’s speech begins.

For a quarter-century, Ghana has sung the praises of agriculture at every budget reading and campaign rally. Yet over that exact twenty-five-year span, agriculture’s share of formal commercial bank credit has ranged between 3 per cent and 13 per cent, averaging a meagre 5.7 per cent.

If agriculture received bank credit matching its weight in our economy, that red line on Professor Dzanku’s chart would sit at 100 per cent. We have never once touched 37 per cent.

At the close of 2025, agriculture generated 22.8 per cent of our GDP and employed a third of our workforce. Yet it received just 4.3 per cent of commercial bank loans. Even at our own state-owned Agricultural Development Bank (ADB), less than 30 per cent of the loan book went to agriculture.

The twenty-five-year ledger has exhausted both the topsoil in the middle belt and the old alibis in Accra.

For years, the polite explanation was that high inflation, punitive Treasury bill rates, and unpaid government arrears were crowding out farms and factories. Fix the macroeconomy and pay down state arrears, we were told, and bank credit would naturally flow to producers.

Between March 2025 and October 2026, we ran that exact experiment in real time.

And credit where it is due: the Ministry of Finance, Ghana and the Bank of Ghana delivered on macro stability and arrears.

Inflation dropped to 5.2 per cent. The central bank cut the policy rate in half, from 28 per cent down to 14 per cent. Average commercial lending rates fell below 16 per cent. Even better, after auditing GH¢68 billion in legacy claims, the Finance Minister paid down nearly GH¢13.8 billion of arrears in 2025, programmed another GH¢25 billion for clearance in 2026, brought School Feeding caterer payments up to date, and tightened commitment controls.

Commercial banks responded to that breathing room by pumping nearly GH¢33 billion in fresh credit into the economy, pushing total loans to GH¢128.3 billion by August 2026. Because government cheques were finally clearing, bad loans across the wider banking industry fell from 21.8 per cent in 2024 down to 15.7 per cent.

Yet where did that GH¢33 billion tsunami of new credit actually go?

It went straight to services, short-term commerce, and import trade. While banks were flush with cheaper money, agriculture’s slice of total credit actually shrank further, dropping from 4.3 per cent to 3.1 per cent by August 2026. And while contractor and service defaults fell as government cleared its bills, agriculture was the solitary sector where loan defaults spiked, climbing to a staggering 60.9 per cent.

Clearing macro arrears and cutting interest rates lowered the price of money. It did not change the physics of agricultural risk.

Follow two loan files onto a commercial bank credit committee’s desk, and the divergence makes complete sense.

The first file belongs to an importer bringing containerised frozen poultry or packaged rice through Tema Port. The cash cycle is ninety days. The cargo sits in a bonded warehouse under dual lock. Every shipping manifest and customs entry is digitised. If the borrower stumbles, the bank can liquidate the inventory within a month and recover its principal.

The second file belongs to a maize aggregator in Techiman or an oil palm processor in Kwaebibirem seeking five-year capital. Less than 3 per cent of our farmland is irrigated. When planting-season rainfall fell 25 per cent below normal in 2025, entire harvests were wiped out. Forty per cent of feeder roads turn to mud during harvest. Land titles sit in contested paper registries. And while school feeding caterer payments improved, institutional food suppliers under Free SHS were still chasing GH¢250 million in unpaid bills as recently as October.

No credit officer is going to bet ninety-day customer deposits on a five-year plantation or a three-shift garment factory when six out of every ten agricultural loans are already in default.

We do not starve agriculture and manufacturing because they default. They default because we starve the physical and digital infrastructure that makes them bankable.

Next Thursday, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson will unveil the US$10 billion "New Economy" programme for 2027 to 2030. To fund its seven pillars, led by commercial agriculture, oil palm, pharmaceuticals, and textiles, the government plans to trim our statutory primary fiscal surplus target under the Public Financial Management Act (Act 1136) from 1.5 per cent of GDP down to 0.5 per cent.

Loosening a nineteen-month-old fiscal rule is a serious bet with our hard-won fiscal credibility.

If that fiscal space is spent the old way, handing out seedlings, tractors, and contracts through ministry committees, the money will evaporate just like the flagships before it. Over the last twenty-five years of industrial slogans, manufacturing’s share of bank credit has fallen by more than half, from 25 per cent in 1999 to just 10.5 per cent. Meanwhile, GIRSAL, our agricultural risk-sharing facility, has guaranteed just GH¢300 million a year over six years. That is less than 0.3 per cent of our banking loan book.

If the US$10 billion New Economy is going to bend Professor Dzanku’s curve upward, Thursday’s budget must pass four simple tests:

First, stop direct ministry lending. Channel at least 70 per cent of productive funds through the Development Bank Ghana (DBG) and GIRSAL as first-loss guarantees and irrigation capex, requiring every GH¢1 of public money to crowd in at least GH¢3 of commercial bank credit.

Second, fix the 60.9 per cent default trap at its root. Tie agribusiness support strictly to irrigation, parametric weather insurance, and electronic warehouse receipts on the Ghana Commodity Exchange, while extending the recent discipline in contractor arrears clearance to every downstream food buffer and school supply contract.

Third, power the 24-Hour Economy (Act 1164) before taxing it. A pharmaceutical or garment factory cannot run night shifts on coughing diesel generators. Exempt or defer import duties and upfront VAT on commercial solar inverters, battery storage, and factory tooling at Tema Port.

Fourth, build the invisible digital spine as a true public good, not a tollbooth. Digital Public Infrastructure is missing from the New Economy's seven pillars. Yet, no bank can cheaply price loans for ten thousand smallholders or SMEs without linking the Ghana Card, digital land registries, and GRA e-invoicing into an open credit-scoring rail. That makes the ongoing National Data Exchange (NDX) architecture work under the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations deeply consequential. It must be built to serve citizens and businesses cheaply and efficiently, rather than becoming another revenue-extractive channel where per-query verification fees inflate the cost of credit, business compliance, and state services.

Every budget speech promises a new economy. The beauty of Professor Dzanku’s chart is that the ratio cannot be spun.

Moving agriculture’s credit parity ratio from 14 per cent toward 50 per cent by 2030 will not happen simply because the state loosened its fiscal rule to spend $10 billion. It will happen the day we make a farm in Techiman as bankable on a credit committee's balance sheet as a shipping container at Tema.

Happy Saturday. When the red dispatch box opens on Thursday, what single line item will you be watching?

Sitsofe Mensah

Solutionist | Systems Architect | Tech Policy & Critical Infrastructure.

Ghana News.title: The barcode and the brown notebook
Ghana News.content:
Walk into any of the sprawling red-and-yellow department stores along the Spintex Road or the Tema motorway on a Saturday afternoon. The first thing that strikes you is the quiet.

Nobody is shouting over the price of a blender. Nobody is sizing up your shoes to decide whether to quote you two hundred cedis or three hundred and fifty.

A mother pushes a metal trolley past towering shelves of plastic bins, LED bulbs, and silicone kitchenware. Every item wears a printed barcode. At the till, a young Ghanaian cashier scans the label. The point-of-sale terminal chirps, a thermal receipt rolls out, and the customer steps back into the heat.

Three kilometres away, inside a traditional stall at Makola or Ashaiman, a very different transaction unfolds.

A trader sits behind a wooden counter with a dog-eared brown exercise book and a calculator whose buttons have been rubbed blank by a decade of thumbstrokes. The air is thick with heat and exhaustion. Buying a set of saucepans here takes fifteen minutes of theatrical haggling. The opening price carries a hidden buffer for yesterday's fuel hike, next month's rent, and the trader's fear that the cedi might slip before Tuesday.

For years, many assumed this was strictly an Accra and Tema phenomenon. Not anymore. Drive through Kumasi, Takoradi, Cape Coast, Sunyani, Ho, Koforidua, or Tamale today, and the same unmistakable red-and-yellow signboards are rising along the regional ring roads.

What began as an urban coastal experiment has become a nationwide retail grid.

On 6 November 2026, the Ghana Union of Traders' Associations (GUTA) sounded the alarm: Chinese malls have captured sixty per cent of Ghana's retail market.

Public reaction split instantly along familiar fault lines. To the embattled local merchant, it is an existential invasion demanding state intervention. To the salaried worker stretching a monthly pay cheque across school fees and electricity tariffs, it is simply a report on where their money still buys something.

Leave aside the megaphone politics and the periodic threats to lock up foreign shops. Strip away the emotion, and look at the plumbing of Ghanaian commerce.

We are not watching a war of nationalities. We are watching a collision between two incompatible operating systems: fragmented, high-margin informal trading on one side, and vertically integrated, high-velocity formal retail on the other.

How a Forty Per Cent Price Gap Happens

How does a ceramic dinner set land on a shelf in Sunyani or Ho at forty per cent less in a foreign department store than in a local stall?

Follow the two supply chains backwards to the factory floor.

The typical Ghanaian solo trader operates at the end of a punitive chain. She borrows working capital from a local bank or savings and loans company at thirty-two per cent interest. She buys a return ticket to Guangzhou or Dubai. She pays for a ten-day hotel stay and buys modest stock from a third-tier wholesale middleman.

Because her volume cannot fill a forty-foot container, she pays consolidators for shared container space. At every handoff, a broker takes a cut. By the time the goods clear Tema Port, another layer of cost kicks in. A trader in Tamale or Takoradi either buys secondary stock from an Accra wholesaler or pays punitive haulage fees to truck a few pallets upcountry. Her stock moves slowly in a cramped stall, so she adds a sixty per cent markup just to service her bank loan.

Now trace the ledger of the department store chain down the road.

The operator is rarely an isolated shopkeeper. Usually, the chain is the retail arm of a manufacturing syndicate in Zhejiang or Guangdong. Their working capital comes from China at four per cent interest, or straight from the factory floor in Yiwu as supplier credit. They ship dozens of full forty-foot containers every month into Tema and Takoradi ports. No wholesale brokers. No shared-container fees.

Once the containers clear the port, the chain uses its own fleet to distribute stock directly to its regional branches in Kumasi, Cape Coast, and Sunyani. By bypassing the Accra wholesale middleman altogether, they bring coastal landed prices straight to the regional capitals.

Because they scan thousands of baskets a day across a national network, they do not need a sixty per cent markup on a mop bucket. They price for speed. They take a twelve per cent margin and turn their inventory over four times faster than the stall at Kejetia or Kotokuraba.

When you fund sixty-day inventory with thirty-two per cent commercial debt, you are not running a retail business. You are working for your bank.

The Statutory Mirage

For over a decade, local trade associations treated the repealed GIPC Act, 2013 (Act 865) as a shield, arguing that foreigners had no business selling to consumers. Yet the law never banned foreign large-scale retail. It only reserved petty trading, hawking, and selling inside a traditional market for Ghanaians.

When the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority (GIPA) Act, 2026 (Act 1173) became law in July 2026, the statutory lines became even clearer. Section 32 still reserves market stalls and petty hawking exclusively for Ghanaians. However, Section 31 halved the minimum foreign capital for general trading enterprises from US1,000,000 to US500,000, provided at least seventy-five per cent of the workforce are skilled Ghanaians.

Crucially, as these malls fan out across the regions, Section 36 of Act 1173 now requires foreign enterprises to secure prior written approval from the Authority before opening each new branch location.

By avoiding congested traditional markets and leasing wide plots along regional highways to build standalone, air-conditioned stores with parking lots, foreign chains took the law at its word.

There is an uncomfortable irony here. Both the early spread in Accra and the current expansion into our regional capitals were incubated by Ghanaians. Local landlords and regional skins or stools eagerly lease prime roadside acreage for dollar-denominated rent paid years in advance. Others act as nominal directors to hide beneficial ownership.

Act 1173 finally confronts this complicity. Section 55(1)(a) makes it a crime to let or sublet a market stall or store to a foreigner for reserved trading, carrying a fine of up to 4,000 penalty units. Section 59 criminalises corporate fronting alongside the beneficial ownership rules of the Companies Act, 2019 (Act 992).

Still, paper compliance does not erase customs grievances. Local traders consistently allege that bulk retail syndicates clear containers at Tema Port at effective duty rates indigenous importers cannot match. On this point, the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) and the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry owe the public a forensic customs audit. A fair market cannot tolerate selective valuation at the port.

The Consumer Cushion and the Tax Net

Here lies the quiet policy dilemma nobody wants to say out loud on morning radio. What hurts the traditional market intermediary in the short term has given the Ghanaian household a vital disinflationary cushion, and handed the state a cleaner tax net.

Look at the cost of living outside Accra. For decades, consumers in regional capitals paid a steep "distance penalty" on everyday household goods, buying items that had been marked up first in China, second at Makola, and third at the regional market. As food inflation and utility bills squeezed salaries, the arrival of formal discount malls in regional capitals broke that price monopoly. When a nurse in Ho or a teacher in Sunyani buys school bags, ceiling fans, and plumbing fixtures at thirty per cent below local market prices, their real wage stretches further.

You cannot ask a worker earning four thousand cedis a month to pay a patriotism tax at the market just to keep a four-layer supply chain alive.

Look at tax collection too. For the GRA, chasing Value

Added Tax across forty thousand cash-only tabletop stalls from Techiman to Kasoa is an administrative nightmare. It creates high friction and yields pennies.

A formal retail chain running twenty electronic point-of-sale lanes across fifteen regional branches is different.

Plugging those branches into the GRA's Electronic Invoicing System (E-VAT) captures consumption tax automatically at the till. Add structured Pay-As-You-Earn (PAYE) taxes from hundreds of young Ghanaian cashiers and floor supervisors hired in those regional towns, plus corporate tax and municipal business operating permits, and the fiscal arithmetic is obvious. Formalisation turns retail from a leaky sieve into a verifiable revenue pipe.

Yet we cannot ignore the macroeconomic leak at the end of that pipe.

Neither the GUTA importer nor the foreign department store is an industrialist. Both import finished goods. The difference is where the profit sleeps at night.

When a local merchant in Kumasi or Takoradi makes a hundred thousand cedis in profit, that money stays in our domestic banking system. It builds a house in the region, pays local school fees, and hires local masons.

When a foreign retail chain sweeps its tills across ten regions every evening, its ultimate goal, protected under Section 42 of Act 1173, is to convert those cedis into US dollars and wire dividends home. Worse, as their regional footprint expands, the pressure on the cedi grows. And if the GRA does not strictly police the Transfer Pricing Regulations, 2020 (L.I. 2412), foreign subsidiaries can inflate invoices from their sister factories abroad, shifting taxable profits out of Ghana before corporate tax is ever calculated.

How Ghanaian Enterprises Setup Right, Scale, and Retain Wealth

Protectionism without modernisation is a dead end. We cannot ban barcodes to save the brown notebook.

If we want low consumer prices across all sixteen regions, clean tax collection, and wealth that remains in Ghana, we must stop treating local traders merely as political foot soldiers. We must build the business support services that allow Ghanaian enterprises to structure properly and scale nationally.

Four practical shifts can anchor this transition.

1. Replace Solo Buying with Cooperative Procurement Syndicates

Fifty Ghanaian hardware importers from Accra, Kumasi, and Tamale flying separately to Guangzhou to buy fifty small batches of the same water pump is a triumph of ego over economics. GUTA, backed by the Ghana Enterprises Agency (GEA) and corporate structuring advisors, should establish formal regional and national procurement cooperatives under the Companies Act. When fifty traders pool working capital into a single special-purpose vehicle, they can place consolidated factory orders directly in Asia or across the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). They command factory-gate prices, charter full containers, and distribute directly to regional members without middlemen.

2. Link Formal Bookkeeping to Twelve Per Cent Trade Credit

No merchant can fight four per cent factory credit with thirty-two per cent microfinance debt, especially when shipping cycles take four months. The Development Bank Ghana (DBG) and the Ghana Export-Import Bank should create ring-fenced inventory credit facilities exclusively for registered Ghanaian retail consortia. The condition should be simple: adopt audited accounts, barcode inventory, and full E-VAT integration, and unlock twelve per cent working capital. When compliance lowers the cost of money, traders will formalise willingly.

3. Build Shared Regional Fulfilment and Accounting Infrastructure

Why must every trader rent an overpriced concrete cubicle in a choked city centre? Municipal assemblies, pension funds, and logistics operators can partner to build modern peripheral warehouse-and-retail parks along the ring roads of our regional capitals. Inside these hubs, Ghanaian SMEs should plug into shared, turnkey business support services: cloud bookkeeping, automated GRA tax filing, digital payments, and bulk clearing and haulage fleets. Good corporate structure should be a shared utility, not a luxury.

4. Tie Regional Branch Approvals to Local Manufacturing Quotas

We must use the regulatory leverage of the new GIPA Act, 2026 (Act 1173). Under Section 36, foreign trading enterprises now require explicit written approval from the Authority before opening any new branch in a regional capital. The Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry should tie every regional branch permit to verifiable local shelf-space quotas. Plastic buckets, tissue paper, detergents, cables, agro-processed foods, and mattresses made by Ghanaian factories in Tema, Kumasi, Nsawam, and the regions should claim a mandatory, growing share of those barcode-scanned shelves.

The families pushing trolleys through automatic glass doors in Spintex, Kumasi, Ho, and Tamale are not betraying Ghana. They are voting with their wallets for order, predictability, and respect for their hard-earned cedi.

That is not a funeral notice for indigenous commerce. It is an invitation for Ghanaian business to organise its capital, upgrade its plumbing, and compete at national scale.

Sitsofe Mensah

The author is a Solutionist, Systems Architect, and Technology Associate with IMANI Africa, specialising in Digital Public Infrastructure, data-driven governance, Tech Policy, and Critical Infrastructure.

Ghana News.title: IOTA Leadership Dealership 2026 challenges young people to become solution-driven leaders
Ghana News.content:
Africa’s growing youth population presents a major opportunity for the continent, but persistent unemployment, weak institutional accountability and rapid technological change are raising questions about whether young people are adequately prepared to shape its future.

With millions entering the labour market, speakers at the second Leadership Dealership Conference organised by the IOTA Ministry Groupe have urged young Africans to develop the values, skills and sense of responsibility needed to lead in an increasingly complex world.

The conference brought together speakers from business, technology and faith to examine the character, competence and discipline required for impactful leadership.

For the convenor and President of the IOTA Ministry Group, Apostle Joseph Kwadwo Yeboah, effective leadership begins not with the desire to be in charge but with the willingness to learn from others.

“Nobody was born a leader. Leadership is the consequence of right following,” he said.

Speaking on the theme, The Structure and Function of Impactful Leadership, Apostle Yeboah argued that people must first learn from those who have gone ahead of them before they can effectively lead others.

Drawing on Jesus Christ’s calling of His first disciples in Matthew 4:18–20, he said leadership development requires intentional relationships, guidance and personal commitment.

He identified intention, invention and intervention as three essential elements of impactful leadership.

Intention, he explained, provides direction and vision; invention drives creativity and problem-solving; while intervention requires leaders to take responsibility and act when circumstances demand it.

He also stressed the importance of trust and relationships, arguing that professional competence, communication skills and charisma must be supported by sound moral values.

Apostle Yeboah further challenged participants to translate their faith into practical responsibility, saying spirituality should be reflected in their everyday conduct.

“If there is no deadline, it is not a discipline yet,” he said, emphasising that good intentions must be matched by accountability and action.

Young people urged to take initiative

Chief Executive Officer of Henos Energy, Henry Osei, urged young people to stop waiting for leadership opportunities and instead demonstrate their ability to solve problems.

He said everyone had the potential to lead, but developing that potential required the right environment, guidance and relationships.

“Find a mentor and go where you want to be,” he advised, encouraging participants to seek guidance from people who had already achieved the goals they hoped to accomplish.

Mr Osei recounted forming a small group of promising young men with whom he held brainstorming sessions twice a week. Within five years, he said, members of the group had progressed into leadership positions.

He challenged participants to move beyond simply attending work or church without making meaningful contributions.

For him, leadership is demonstrated through ownership, initiative and the ability to provide solutions rather than merely identify problems.

“Leadership means owning the result,” he said.

AI and automation reshape leadership demands

While mentorship and personal discipline remain important, futurist Kwame AA Opoku said young Africans must also prepare for a future in which technology is changing the nature of work and professional competence.

The founder of the African AI Governance Index, who spoke on Leadership in 2035, said decisions being made today would influence how individuals, institutions and countries navigate the next five to ten years.

He pointed to advances in artificial intelligence, robotics and automation, warning that no profession should assume it is immune to technological disruption.

Citing developments in robotic kitchens, self-driving vehicles, flying taxis and police robots, he illustrated how technology is increasingly taking over tasks traditionally performed by humans.

Mr Opoku also raised ethical concerns about gene editing, artificial wombs and deepfakes, warning that technological advances could create challenges for human identity, trust and the ability to distinguish fact from fabrication.

He expressed concern about the growing use of artificial intelligence for spiritual guidance, saying it raised questions about human judgement, parenting and wisdom.

“This is not an IT problem,” he stressed.

He said Africa faced particular risks if its growing youth population was not matched by sufficient employment opportunities, warning that the resulting pressures could deepen social tensions and instability.

Drawing lessons from unrest in Tunisia, Sudan, Sri Lanka, Kenya and Serbia, he cautioned against development strategies that focused only on immediate needs without accounting for long-term realities.

“If you build for the short term, you build for a world that is already dead,” he said.

Africa must leverage its strengths

Despite the challenges, Mr Opoku said Africa had strengths it could use to navigate the changing technological landscape.

He identified reputation-based markets, a culture of presence, oral intellect and relationships as forms of capital that could become increasingly valuable in a world saturated with artificial content and manufactured identities.

He urged young people to invest in their intellectual development, understand how systems work and recognise their responsibility in shaping the quality of leadership across the continent.

“We don't have a leadership problem. We have a citizens problem,” he said.

The discussions at the conference highlighted the need for young Africans to look beyond the pursuit of positions and focus on developing the capacity to make meaningful contributions to their communities.

The speakers' messages placed emphasis on mentorship, discipline, problem-solving, ethical conduct and an understanding of emerging technologies as important elements of leadership preparation.

Ghana News.title: Medical Superintendents call for stronger emergency care to tackle no-bed syndrome
Ghana News.content:
The Medical Superintendents Group is calling for an expansion of emergency and critical care facilities, alongside improvements in hospital referral systems, to address Ghana's persistent no-bed syndrome.

The group says tackling the problem will require political commitment, sustainable financing and stronger collaboration among healthcare institutions.

Speaking at the 68th Annual General Conference of the Ghana Medical Association (GMA), a representative of the group said hospital managers experienced the challenges associated with the no-bed syndrome firsthand.

“Where we sit, we experience, firsthand, all the challenges associated with the no-bed syndrome,” the representative said.

The group is advocating a stronger National Ambulance Service, improved pre-hospital emergency care and real-time bed management systems to help hospitals respond more effectively to emergencies.

It is also calling for a better distribution of skilled emergency healthcare personnel and effective public-private partnerships to expand access to emergency services.

The representative stressed that individual hospitals and medical practitioners could not resolve the problem without broader institutional and government support.

“The no-bed syndrome, as we know, cannot be addressed by individual hospitals, nor by doctors alone. It requires a strong political commitment,” the representative said.

The group believes the proposed measures would improve emergency response and reduce deaths associated with delays in accessing medical treatment.

It says its ultimate goal is to ensure that no Ghanaian dies because of the lack of a hospital bed, an ambulance or timely emergency care.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
