World.title: Liberia: China Signals Readiness to Expand Agricultural Imports, Eyes Investment in Processing Sector
World.content:
Vice President Jeremiah Koung secures commitment from Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang on market access for Liberian cocoa, coffee and dried chili peppers, while Beijing pledges continued development support and encourages Chinese investment.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

MONROVIA — China has expressed readiness to increase imports of agricultural products from Liberia, including cocoa, coffee beans and dried chili peppers, as the two countries explore ways to expand trade, attract investment and strengthen economic cooperation.



The commitment was conveyed by Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang during bilateral discussions with Liberia’s Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung Sr. in Shanghai on November 5, according to a press release from the Office of the Vice President.

Vice Premier Ding identified the submission and approval of eligible Liberian exporting companies as the next practical step toward accessing the Chinese market. He explained that agricultural products such as dried chili peppers, coffee beans and cocoa from African countries, including Liberia, had been granted access under existing market arrangements.

He encouraged Liberia to submit a list of companies interested in exporting these products to China for the necessary approval procedures, after which successful applicants could begin trading.

The discussions followed Vice President Koung’s participation in the opening of the Ninth China International Import Expo, where he called for greater efforts to translate China’s zero-tariff policy into increased exports, domestic processing and employment opportunities for Liberians.

Ding also expressed China’s willingness to strengthen agricultural trade facilitation with African countries and encouraged Liberia to take advantage of the China International Import Expo and other commercial platforms to connect local producers with Chinese buyers.

Welcoming the opportunity, Vice President Koung identified rubber, cocoa, coffee and other agricultural products as priority areas for expanded trade cooperation.

He emphasized that Liberia wants foreign investment to go beyond the export of raw materials by creating opportunities for domestic processing, skills development and employment.

“Our objective is to create jobs, develop Liberian skills, and retain more value within our economy,” Koung said.

He invited Chinese businesses to explore investment opportunities in Liberia’s special economic zones, particularly in rubber processing, agro-processing and light manufacturing.

In response, Vice Premier Ding said China would encourage more Chinese companies to invest in Liberia and called for continued support to facilitate their operations.

He also identified iron ore mining as an important area of bilateral cooperation, expressing China’s readiness to strengthen policy coordination to ensure that investments generate greater benefits for both countries.

China Outlines Additional Development Support

Beyond trade and investment, the Chinese Vice Premier reaffirmed Beijing’s willingness to support Liberia’s development priorities through ongoing and proposed infrastructure and technical assistance projects.

Ding outlined continued cooperation involving the Congo Town overpass bridges, diagnostic laboratory facilities, agricultural machinery, government vehicles and road-related assistance.

He further disclosed that Chinese working teams would visit Liberia to assess proposed projects involving broadcasting facilities and the renovation of the Capitol Building.

China also pledged to continue providing scholarships and training opportunities for Liberian professionals as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s human resource and technical capacity.

Vice President Koung welcomed the assistance but stressed the importance of incorporating training, maintenance and technical support into development projects to ensure their sustainability.

He also highlighted reliable and affordable electricity as a major national priority, identifying opportunities for cooperation in solar energy, battery storage, hydropower and rural electrification.

Other areas raised by the Liberian delegation included clean water, healthcare delivery, digital connectivity and vocational training.

To move the discussions from commitments to implementation, Koung proposed the designation of focal persons and the identification of a shortlist of priority projects for further engagement between the two governments.

He assured the Chinese delegation that Liberia’s Embassy in Beijing and relevant government institutions were prepared to work with their Chinese counterparts to advance the proposed initiatives.

Liberia Seeks China’s Support at UN Security Council

The discussions also addressed cooperation on international affairs, particularly Liberia’s upcoming presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December.

Vice Premier Ding congratulated Liberia on its forthcoming presidency and expressed China’s readiness to maintain close communication and cooperation with Monrovia.

Vice President Koung, in turn, thanked China and other international partners for supporting Liberia’s election to the Security Council for the 2026–2027 term.

He outlined Liberia’s priorities during its tenure, including strengthening the participation of women and young people in peace and security initiatives, addressing the connections between climate change, conflict and natural resources, promoting regional security, and advancing Security Council reform and peacekeeping.

Koung also solicited China’s continued support for Liberia’s December presidency.

Both officials reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the Liberia-China strategic partnership and translating diplomatic engagements into practical economic and development benefits for their respective populations.

The meeting was held at the Xijiao State Guest Hotel in Shanghai and attended by Shanghai Mayor Zhu Zhongming; Chinese Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Miao Deyu; Liberia’s Ambassador to China, Dudley McKinley Thomas; and Executive Chairman of the Liberia Special Economic Zones Authority, Prince A. Wreh.

Other members of the Liberian delegation included Samuel Nagbe, Executive Director of the Rural Renewable Energy Agency; Deputy Chief of Staff for Administration Macdonald Metzger; Press Secretary Richmond Neufville; and J. Wesley Washington, Minister Counselor at the Liberian Embassy in China.

World.title: Liberia: The Economy Grew. So Did Poverty. And Nobody Can Say What the State’s 47 Companies Cost
World.content:
MONROVIA — On paper, 2025 was a good year for Liberia. The economy grew 5.1 percent, its strongest pace in the five years the World Bank charts. Inflation ended the year at 4 percent. The budget deficit narrowed, and export earnings leapt by nearly 58 percent on the back of gold and iron ore.

By Rodney D Sieh

Yet by the Bank’s own estimate, more Liberians slipped into extreme poverty — from 34.6 percent of the population in 2024 to 36.1 percent in 2025.



That contradiction sits at the heart of Beyond Growth, the 7th edition of the World Bank’s Liberia Economic Update, released in October. Its diagnosis is blunt: Liberia is growing in the places where few Liberians work, and stalling in the places where most of them do. And it turns a spotlight on an institution that rarely features in growth debates — the state’s own portfolio of 62 government-owned entities, whose finances, the report says, the government itself cannot reliably see.

Growth that skips the household

The 2025 numbers were driven by mines, not markets. Industrial output jumped 10.8 percent, powered by a 42 percent surge in iron ore production as a major project scaled up and a 17 percent rise in overall mining output. Gold, iron ore and rubber now account for 92.8 percent of everything Liberia sells abroad; gold alone is 61.8 percent.

The sectors where Liberians actually earn a living moved the other way. Manufacturing shrank 2.8 percent. Agriculture, which still employs about 39 percent of the workforce, slowed to 2.6 percent growth from 3.4 percent, and farm labour productivity has fallen about 1.1 percent a year since 2014.

The labour market tells the rest. Some 78 percent of workers are in what the Bank calls vulnerable employment — informal self-employment or unpaid family work. Wage jobs account for just 20.9 percent of employment, a share that has barely moved in two decades. About 55,000 people join the labour force each year, but the economy creates roughly 50,000 jobs.

Firms are too small to absorb them. Some 86 percent are micro-sized and nearly 89 percent are one-person operations. Liberia registers about two new limited liability companies per 10,000 adults a year — roughly 165 times below the global average, the report says.

Prices compounded the squeeze. Food inflation collapsed after rice prices fell and the government cut the wholesale price of a 25kg bag from US$16.75 to US$14.00. But non-food inflation climbed to 9.9 percent, driven by services, healthcare and housing — costs that hit urban wage earners hardest. The Bank expects poverty to ease to 33.2 percent in 2026 if farming recovers.

Stability bought with the capital budget

Monrovia’s fiscal numbers improved. The deficit narrowed to 2.1 percent of GDP, domestic revenue rose to US$830 million (15.9 percent of GDP), and public debt eased to 55.1 percent of GDP. Domestic revenue now covers 69.3 percent of public spending, up from 59 percent.

But the Bank is plain about how the books were balanced. As donor grants fell from 7.8 to 4.9 percent of GDP, capital spending was cut from US$406 million to US$297 million — from 8.5 to 5.7 percent of GDP. Interest payments, meanwhile, rose from US$49 million to US$87 million.

Cutting the investment Liberia needs to break its jobs trap, the report says, is “precisely the wrong adjustment.” It points instead to money left on the table: tax exemptions worth about US$240 million in 2024, more than 40 percent of tax revenue; a mining sector from which Liberia captures only 15–20 percent of available fiscal value, against 50–60 percent in peer countries; and a domestic capital budget that has historically been only about one-third executed.

The gap matters because the government’s ARREST Agenda development plan needs roughly US$8.4 billion over five years, at a time when concessional finance is shrinking and Liberia remains at high risk of overall public debt distress.

The black box: 47 state firms, few accounts

The report’s second half is its sharpest. Liberia’s government owns 62 entities — 47 operating, 15 dormant — running power, ports, petroleum, water, transport, hospitals, universities and regulators. They control assets worth roughly a quarter of GDP. Yet in 2024 only 19 submitted financial returns to the state’s oversight bureau, and 26 of the 47 active entities report nothing at all. Just 13 percent file compliant quarterly reports.

Where auditors have looked, the picture is grim. Only 17 of the 47 have had even one General Auditing Commission audit since 2019. Of 36 financial-statement opinions issued for FY20–FY24, 25 were adverse, seven qualified and four clean. All ten compliance audits came back adverse.

The self-reported numbers that do exist flatter the portfolio. The 19 reporting firms booked a combined US$29.0 million profit in 2024, but US$19.7 million of that was pension accumulation at the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP). Strip out US$15.1 million in government subsidies and a US$16.7 million donor grant to the electricity utility, and the group posted a loss of about US$2.7 million.

The bigger risk sits off the subsidy line. Government on-lent or guaranteed US$423.3 million of state-enterprise debt as of end-2025 — debt that lands on the treasury if a company cannot pay. The report also finds firms that did not remit workers’ income tax for years: the Liberia Civil Aviation Authority paid nothing until a marginal sum in 2024. Auditors found NASSCORP could not link US$4.1 million of 2022 deposits to any contributor.

Governance is part of the problem. A 2023 Bank review of eight state firms found ministers on every board and some directors missing three-quarters of meetings. Presidential performance contracts are signed directly with chief executives, bypassing boards. The old Bureau of State Enterprises oversaw this portfolio on less than US$1 million a year.

Its successor, the State-Owned Enterprises Authority of Liberia (SEAL), formally took over on August 23, 2026. The Bank calls it timely but flags weaknesses: no governing board, three political appointees with loosely defined tenure, and funding from a 0.25 percent levy on the very firms it polices. A House-passed bill barring sitting officials from state boards, reported by FrontPageAfrica in March and cited in the Bank’s report, still awaits Senate action.

LEC: the utility at the centre of the risk

No entity illustrates the problem better than the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC). It holds about 77 percent of all liabilities reported by state firms, and its accounts have drawn adverse audit opinions year after year.

LEC reported modest losses of about US$3.5 million over 2022–2024. But that was only after booking roughly US$50 million in grant income. Without it, the Bank estimates, losses would have run US$17–20 million a year. Its equity fell from US$51.0 million to US$30.4 million in 2024, as liabilities climbed to 95 percent of assets.

The utility’s biggest deadbeat is its owner. Of US$34.0 million owed to LEC at end-2025, about 91 percent was owed by government ministries and agencies, most of it more than a year old. In December 2025, core government paid 0.3 percent of what it owed, against about 21 percent for customers overall. The government, the report notes, is at once LEC’s shareholder, regulator, least reliable customer and lender of last resort.

Businesses pay the price. More than 90 percent of Liberian firms now own a generator, up from 73 percent in 2017. Auditors also found LEC operated for at least five years without documented board minutes or adopted by-laws. The planned expansion of the Mount Coffee hydropower plant from 88 to about 130 megawatts by 2028 offers relief — if the utility can be run to use it.

What the Bank prescribes — and what to watch

The Bank is careful not to overclaim. It says it has not established that state firms cause Liberia’s jobs problem. Its argument is narrower and harder to dismiss: without accounts, audits and a register of who sits on which board, no one can say what the portfolio costs, what it delivers or what risk it poses to the treasury.

Its fix is deliberately unglamorous. By end-2027, it wants every entity classified as commercial, public-service or hybrid; a published register of entities and directors; a minimum annual reporting template for all 47 operating firms; and audit firepower focused on the five biggest exposures — LEC, NASSCORP, the National Port Authority, the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company and the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation — with private auditors brought in under the Auditor General’s oversight. By June 2028, it wants government’s tangled money flows with those firms reconciled, public-service obligations costed, the first public aggregate report on state enterprises, and a legal inventory of the 15 dormant companies.

The wider outlook is cautiously positive but exposed. The Bank projects growth averaging 5.3 percent a year over 2026–2028, inflation of 7.0 percent in 2026 and a VAT launch in early 2027. But global growth is forecast to slow to 2.5 percent in 2026 as the Middle East conflict lifts oil prices. A 15 percent fall in gold and a 20 percent fall in iron ore prices would wipe about US$295 million off export earnings, with reserves covering only about two months of imports.

For a country that has heard many reform plans, the test is simple. Growth figures can be announced. Whether the state can account for its own companies — and pay its own electricity bills — will show whether Liberia’s boom is starting to reach the people living through it.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai’s Anti-Corruption Credibility Tested as Indicted Gbarpolu Superintendent Gets Presidential Commissioning
World.content:
President Boakai commissioning indicted Gbarpolu County Superintendent Zinnah

MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s commitment to fighting corruption is facing renewed public scrutiny following his decision to commission Gbarpolu County Superintendent Sam K. Zinnah, who is among five individuals indicted in connection with the controversial US$425,000 Yellow Machines procurement scandal.

By Augustus D.R. Bortue

The controversy has intensified as the corruption case remains unresolved, with the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission (LACC) reporting that proceedings scheduled to commence on September 14, 2026, at the 16th Judicial Circuit Court in Bopolu were postponed after a member of the defense reportedly submitted an excuse for nonappearance.



The latest development has renewed concerns among citizens and political stakeholders about the pace of justice in a case involving public development funds intended to improve infrastructure in one of Liberia’s least-connected counties.

While an indictment does not constitute a conviction, critics argue that the President’s decision to commission an official facing unresolved corruption charges raises questions about the administration’s judgment, consistency and commitment to public accountability.

The controversy also revives an earlier demand by Gbarpolu Senator Botoe Kanneh for indicted county officials to be temporarily relieved of their duties while facing prosecution.

The US$425,000 Controversy

The case centers on US$425,000 allocated from Gbarpolu County’s Social Development Fund for the procurement of three heavy-duty machines: a bulldozer, an excavator and a motor grader.

The equipment was intended to support road construction, rehabilitation and other infrastructure projects across the county.

On September 8, 2025, the LACC announced that the Grand Jury of the 16th Judicial Circuit Court had returned a True Bill on all counts of the indictment against five individuals: Superintendent Zinnah, former Superintendent J. Keyah Saah, former Fiscal Superintendent Anthony Yorkor, former Project Management Committee Chairman Robert Benda and City Lion Inc. Chief Executive Officer Omaru Sheriff.

According to the Commission’s allegations, the procurement process involved irregularities, questions about the quality of the equipment supplied and possible violations of public procurement and financial management requirements.

The LACC also raised concerns about whether the machines delivered met the specifications and represented value for the public funds invested.

Reports that the equipment has remained largely non-operational, with concerns about oil leakages and other defects, have further intensified public demands for answers.

However, the allegations remain subject to judicial determination. All five defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty by a competent court.

Boakai’s Commissioning Decision Under Scrutiny

The decision to proceed with Zinnah’s commissioning has become a focal point in the broader debate about the credibility of the Boakai administration’s anti-corruption agenda.

Critics argue that although an indictment does not automatically disqualify an individual from holding public office, the circumstances demand careful consideration by the Presidency.

They question whether the President was fully briefed on the LACC indictment before commissioning the superintendent and what considerations informed the decision.

The controversy is particularly sensitive because the Boakai administration has repeatedly presented accountability and the fight against corruption as central pillars of its governance agenda.

However, the legal distinction between an indictment and a conviction remains important. Zinnah has not been convicted of the charges, and his constitutional rights must be protected throughout the judicial process.

The question confronting the administration, therefore, is not whether the President should pronounce judgment on an accused official, but whether the government has adequately addressed the public confidence concerns arising from the commissioning.

Critics have also drawn comparisons with the case of Abdullah Kamara, former Chairperson of the Liberia Telecommunications Authority, whom President Boakai suspended after his indictment by the LACC. Kamara was subsequently acquitted by the court.

They argue that the differing circumstances surrounding the two cases warrant an explanation of the standards guiding presidential decisions involving public officials facing corruption allegations.

Trial Postponement Fuels Public Frustration

The latest postponement has added another layer to the controversy.

According to the LACC, its prosecution team traveled to Gbarpolu County on September 14, 2026, expecting the trial to commence, but was informed by the Clerk of Court upon arrival that the matter had been postponed.

The Commission said it had been notified that a member of the defense had submitted an excuse for nonappearance before the prosecution team arrived in Bopolu.

The LACC described the development as one of the challenges affecting the timely prosecution of corruption-related cases but reaffirmed its readiness to proceed through the judicial process.

The postponement has raised questions about when substantive proceedings will begin and whether the five defendants will be available to face trial.

It also comes amid growing impatience among residents who believe the case should not be allowed to linger while the equipment purchased with county development funds remains largely unusable.

Youths Demand Speedy and Impartial Trial

On September 14, 2026, concerned citizens and youths in Gbarpolu staged a peaceful demonstration and issued a statement demanding a speedy, transparent and impartial trial.

In their statement, the youths expressed concern over what they described as continued delays in the proceedings, calling on judicial authorities to ensure that the case is handled without unnecessary postponements.

They emphasized that their demonstration was peaceful and lawful, adding that the people of Gbarpolu deserve accountability over public resources allocated for their development.

Their demands reflect growing concerns that prolonged judicial proceedings could further weaken public confidence in the institutions responsible for investigating and prosecuting corruption.

Senators Had Earlier Called for Zinnah’s Recusal

The controversy surrounding the indicted county officials is not new.

In 2025, Gbarpolu Senator Botoe Kanneh called on the Senate to engage the Executive Branch to ensure that Superintendent Zinnah and other indicted officials were temporarily relieved of their duties pending the court’s determination.

In a communication to the Senate Plenary, Kanneh said the indictment and ongoing judicial proceedings had generated deep concern among citizens, local leaders and development stakeholders.

She warned that the situation could undermine public trust in the justice system and the integrity of public service.

Citing the Code of Conduct for public officials, Kanneh argued that the Senate should take cognizance of the LACC indictment and consider engaging the Executive Branch to temporarily relieve the indicted superintendent of his responsibilities while the case proceeded.

The communication was referred to the relevant Senate committees for investigation and appropriate action.

The Senate subsequently mandated its Committees on Judiciary and Internal Affairs to investigate concerns surrounding the indictment of Gbarpolu County’s local leadership, including Superintendent Zinnah.

However, the committees’ findings, recommendations and any subsequent decisions by Plenary have not been made public.

More recently, another Gbarpolu Senator, Amara Konneh, has also called for the speedy trial of the case, adding to pressure on the judicial authorities to ensure that the matter is resolved.

Zinnah Insists on Judicial Process

For his part, Superintendent Zinnah has maintained that he respects the rule of law and is prepared to respond to the allegations through the courts.

In a letter dated July 14, 2026, addressed to LACC Executive Chairperson Cllr. Alexandra K. Zoe, Zinnah declined an invitation to appear before the Commission for further discussions about the yellow machines.

The invitation, dated July 9, was for a meeting scheduled for July 16, during which the LACC intended to obtain additional information about the equipment, including its current condition and the circumstances surrounding its assembly.

The Commission had requested that Zinnah attend with his legal counsel and the individual or individuals who initially assembled the machines.

However, the superintendent argued that the matter was already before the Sixth Judicial Circuit Court and should therefore be addressed through the judicial process.

He maintained that participating in discussions outside the courtroom while the case was pending could compromise the integrity of the proceedings.

Zinnah subsequently reaffirmed his willingness to cooperate with the legal process and respond to the allegations in accordance with the law.

He has not publicly responded to the latest concerns raised by citizens over his commissioning or renewed calls for him to recuse himself while the case remains before the courts.

Gbarpolu Wants Value for Its Money

Beyond the political debate surrounding the President’s decision, the central concern for residents remains the condition of the three machines and whether the county received value for its US$425,000 investment.

The equipment was procured to address infrastructure challenges, particularly poor road connectivity that continues to affect communities across Gbarpolu.

Residents deserve an independent technical assessment establishing the machines’ current condition, compliance with contractual specifications, actual market value and the cost of restoring them to operational condition.

Such an assessment would help establish whether the county received what it paid for and identify the appropriate remedies if procurement violations or contractual breaches are proven.

The government must also ensure that the equipment’s condition is properly documented and that public resources are protected while the judicial process continues.

A Test of Institutional Consistency

Analysts say the controversy presents President Boakai with an opportunity to clarify his administration’s position on public officials facing corruption allegations and demonstrate that accountability standards apply consistently across government.

They called on the Presidency to explain the circumstances surrounding Zinnah’s commissioning and whether any consideration was given to the pending indictment.

For the people of Gbarpolu, the expectations are straightforward: public money must deliver public value, the courts must determine the truth, and every public official must remain accountable under the law.

The administration’s credibility will depend not only on what it says about fighting corruption, but also on how consistently its institutions and leadership act when accountability questions arise within its own ranks.

World.title: Liberia: Joint Chambers Reconstruction Estimated at Over US$10M as Speaker, Deputy Cite Lack of Funding
World.content:
MONROVIA – More than one year following the severe incident of destruction at the Joint Chambers of the Liberia Legislature, Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon and Deputy Speaker Thomas P. Fallah jointly toured the destroyed segment and expressed disappointment over the condition.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

During the tour, Deputy Speaker Fallah, specifically, expressed profound sorrow over the state of the facility, noting that rebuilding the heavily damaged structure will demand significant financial resources and extensive construction work.



The tour comes ahead of a multi-stage damage assessment that will involve both government estimators led by the Ministry of Public Works and international experts.

While financing remains a concern, both leaders confirmed there is no plan of taking out loans to fund the necessary repairs.

Uncertainty Hangs Over Renovation Process

Addressing inquiry from Legislative reporters during the tour, Speaker Koon provided a response that somewhat dashes all hope and expectations that the renovation process is far from happening.

Speaker Koon tells the public that in the first place there is no money now neither had any money being budgeted towards this projected which is estimated around US$10M.

He pointed out that the shutdown of the Joint Chambers continues to undermine and impair the function of the Legislature, especially during the SONA [State of the Nation Address].

“It depends on how soon the estimate can be given to us, so we can commence. We don’t have money budgeted, but we are not going to take a loan for this place, because this place is undermining our work and impairing the function of the Legislature, especially during the SONA – the State of the Nation Address. We have to find other places and secure them to have the President’s address,” Speaker Koon intoned.

Sad Moment

In remarks, Deputy Speaker Fallah described the destruction as a “sad,” “embarrassing,” and “frustrating” and warning that the building will have to be rebuilt from scratch.

Deputy Speaker Fallah, who has been at the Capitol for the past 18 to 20 years, asserted that it was his first time entering the building since the incident.

“This is a sad moment, very sad. Today is my very first time honestly entering this place to see the level of destruction that took place. I feel so sad as a national leader, as a statesperson, to have known how this place was in the past and to see it like this today,” he stated.

US$10 Million to Rebuild

The Deputy Speaker estimated that restoring the building to the standard required would cost at least $10 million.

“I am not a technician, I am not an engineer, but I know I have been involved in construction. To see something like this tells me that to bring it to the standard we need will cost us nothing less than US$10 million. We are constructing from scratch, because it is not secure, so you have to do a lot of work,” he asserted.

Though the cause of the incident is yet to be established, but the Lofa County Electoral District #1 Representative stressed that destruction of public property must never happen, whatever the political disagreement.

“There should be no point in time when we destroy state property or facilities that belong to the state, even private property. That should not be the case.”

“The Legislature is the theatre of disagreement. We all come from different political persuasions, different political backgrounds, but we should never resort to destruction,” Deputy Speaker Fallah, among other things, indicated.

World.title: Liberia: Wife, Family of Convicted NSA Agent Peter Bon Jallah Appeal to U.S. Ambassador, Raise Questions Over Trial
World.content:
Monrovia-The family of former National Security Agency, NSA, Peter Bon Jallah has appealed to the United States Ambassador to Liberia, seeking international attention to what they described as serious concerns about the fairness of his trial and the handling of evidence that they believe deserved greater judicial scrutiny.

By Willie N. Tokpah

In separate communications dated October 26, Bon Jallah and his wife, Shirley Jallah, called on the U.S. Embassy in Monrovia to take note of the circumstances surrounding his conviction on charges of statutory rape and kidnapping and consider whether appropriate diplomatic or human-rights channels could help bring their concerns to the attention of relevant authorities.



The appeals came three days after Criminal Court ‘E’ at the Temple of Justice found Bon Jallah guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping involving a 16-year-old boy, while acquitting him of gang rape.

The conviction has triggered questions from the defendant’s family, which maintained that important aspects of the defense’s case, including medical findings, forensic evidence, witness testimonies, telephone records and observations relating to the alleged crime scene, were not adequately addressed in the court’s determination.

In an appeal addressed to the U.S. Ambassador, Bon Jallah described the verdict as raising serious questions about the impartial evaluation of evidence and requested that the Embassy consider whether the matter could receive attention through appropriate diplomatic or human-rights mechanisms.

His wife, Shirley Jallah, separately appealed for assistance, questioning the sufficiency of the prosecution’s evidence and whether the defense’s arguments and witnesses received adequate consideration.

Family Turns to Washington for Attention

In his October 26 communication, Bon Jallah specifically requested that the United States Embassy take note of the concerns surrounding his trial and consider whether appropriate channels were available to raise questions about due process and judicial accountability.

He acknowledged that the United States cannot interfere in Liberia’s judicial proceedings but argued that judicial independence should operate alongside transparency, accountability and respect for fundamental rights.

“My intention in raising these concerns is not to undermine the Liberian judicial system but to advocate for fairness, accountability, and public confidence in the administration of justice,” Bon Jallah wrote.

He urged the Embassy to consider directing the concerns to relevant organizations or authorities if direct diplomatic engagement was not possible.

His wife made a similar appeal, saying she was deeply troubled by the circumstances surrounding her husband’s conviction and believed that questions remained about the evidence presented during the trial.

She specifically raised concerns about forensic testing, the handling of evidence and what she described as insufficient consideration of the defense’s arguments.

The family’s appeal effectively seeks to bring the case to the attention of an international diplomatic mission, although the U.S. Embassy has no judicial authority to overturn a Liberian court’s verdict or direct the outcome of an ongoing legal process.

JFK Medical Center Report at the Center of Dispute

One of the principal issues raised by Bon Jallah concerns the medical examination conducted at the John F. Kennedy Medical Center following the alleged incident.

The family argued that the medical report contained findings that deserved closer consideration by the court, particularly regarding the reported absence of certain physical signs associated with the allegations.

Bon Jallah questions whether the court adequately explained how the medical findings were weighed against the complainant’s account and the other evidence presented during the trial.

The defense’s concerns also extended to the forensic evidence and the interpretation of findings presented by the prosecution. According to reporting on the court proceedings, the prosecution presented forensic evidence involving DNA profiles associated with biological material recovered from clothing exhibits.

However, the defense challenged the significance and interpretation of the findings, including their ability to establish when or how the biological material was deposited. The medical and forensic evidence, therefore, became an important part of the competing arguments presented during the trial.

The family maintained that these issues should receive particular attention in any review of the proceedings.

Defense Witnesses and Questions About Their Testimonies

Another important aspect of the family’s appeal concerns the testimonies presented by witnesses called by the defense. According to the court proceedings reported by FrontPage Africa, the prosecution presented 13 regular witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses, while the defense presented eight regular witnesses and three subpoenaed witnesses from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Orange GSM and the John F. Kennedy Medical Center.

The involvement of witnesses from these institutions was significant because their testimonies formed part of the evidentiary record surrounding the medical examination, telephone records and other issues raised during the proceedings.

Bon Jallah’s family believed that the defense presented evidence that challenged important aspects of the prosecution’s allegations and deserved careful consideration.

The family is particularly concerned about whether the court adequately addressed the evidence and explanations offered by the defense witnesses before reaching its conclusions.

The exact substance of each witness’s testimony and how the judge evaluated it will be important in assessing these concerns against the official trial record.

Telephone Records Raise Questions About Defendant’s Whereabouts

Bon Jallah also raised concerns about telephone records that, according to his understanding, did not place him at the alleged crime scene at the relevant time. He believed the records were important to the defense’s effort to establish his whereabouts and should have received detailed consideration in the court’s evaluation of the evidence.

The issue is particularly relevant because telephone records and related technical evidence can assist in examining a person’s movements and communications, although such records do not automatically establish a person’s precise physical location.

The family argues that if the records were properly presented and admitted, their significance should have been clearly addressed in the court’s final reasoning.

Judge’s Visit to Alleged Crime Scene Also Questioned

The family has also questioned the circumstances surrounding a reported visit by the presiding judge to the residence where the alleged incident was said to have occurred.

Bon Jallah maintains that the physical conditions of the residence raised questions about certain descriptions provided during the complainant’s testimony.

He is concerned about whether observations made during the visit were properly documented and considered in the court’s final decision. The family argues that where a judge personally observes the location associated with disputed testimony, any relevant observations must be handled in accordance with applicable evidentiary and judicial procedures.

They are seeking clarification on whether the reported discrepancies were adequately addressed in the proceedings.

Wife Questions Sufficiency of Prosecution’s Case

In her separate appeal, Shirley Jallah questioned whether the prosecution sufficiently established her husband’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. She expressed concern that the defense’s arguments and evidence were not given adequate consideration and raised questions about the fairness and impartiality of the proceedings.

She also asked the U.S. Embassy to consider whether any appropriate assistance or guidance could be made available within the limits of its diplomatic mandate.

Her appeal emphasized that the family was not asking the United States to interfere in Liberia’s judicial system but wanted concerns about due process and fundamental human rights to receive appropriate attention.

Embassy Appeal Puts Due Process in Focus

The appeal to the United States Embassy places the case within a broader discussion about judicial accountability, due process, and public confidence in Liberia’s justice system.

Although the U.S. Embassy cannot substitute itself for Liberia’s courts, the family is asking the diplomatic mission to consider whether concerns involving the fairness of the proceedings may appropriately be brought to the attention of relevant human-rights institutions or other competent authorities.

The appeal also raises an important question about the availability of independent legal remedies when defendants believe that material evidence or defense arguments were not adequately considered.

For Bon Jallah and his family, the immediate concern is whether the verdict adequately reflects the totality of the evidence presented during the trial. Their request to the U.S. Ambassador is therefore not simply an appeal for diplomatic sympathy but a call for attention to questions they believe should be examined through established legal and accountability mechanisms.

World.title: Liberia: NPA Unveils Measures to Ease Port Congestion as Importers Protest Delays, Rising Fees
World.content:
Dukuly announces direct Maersk shipping to Monrovia, extended port operations, plans to clear stranded containers and $280 million investment initiative as businesses demand urgent relief from mounting costs and prolonged shipping delays.

MONROVIA — National Port Authority (NPA) Managing Director Sekou A. Dukuly has announced a series of measures to address congestion, prolonged cargo delays and rising port-related costs at the Freeport of Monrovia, following protests by Liberian businesswomen and importers demanding urgent government intervention.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh



Speaking at a press briefing at his office at the Freeport, Dukuly acknowledged that the port is operating below its required capacity, leaving hundreds of containers stranded and imposing additional financial burdens on importers.

He disclosed that approximately 700 containers have remained at the port for more than 30 days, describing the situation as unacceptable for a country whose economy depends heavily on maritime trade.

Among the immediate interventions, Dukuly announced that shipping giant Maersk has agreed to bring vessels directly to Monrovia, a move intended to reduce transit times and additional costs associated with transshipment through other West African ports.

Previously, some cargo shipments destined for Liberia were routed through regional ports before being transferred onto smaller vessels for delivery to Monrovia. The arrangement has contributed to prolonged shipping schedules and additional handling requirements.

The direct-shipping arrangement is expected to shorten delivery times and reduce logistical complications for importers. However, its actual impact on shipping costs and delivery schedules will depend on the frequency of direct services and effective implementation.

Dukuly also announced plans to clear approximately 700 containers that have remained at the port for extended periods, suspend ongoing berth repairs to allow two vessels to berth at a time, and extend working hours to improve cargo handling.

He said the NPA is exploring the possibility of granting additional free days to importers facing mounting demurrage and storage charges because of delays.

In a further proposal aimed at addressing the financial consequences of the congestion, Dukuly said the NPA could engage the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) and commercial banking institutions to provide short-term relief to affected businesses.

He proposed microeconomic support measures, including easing loan repayment obligations and extending repayment periods for importers whose capital remains tied up in goods they have been unable to retrieve from the port.

According to Dukuly, such engagement could help reduce the financial pressure on businesses while the NPA works to resolve the operational challenges.

The proposal comes amid complaints from importers who say they rely heavily on commercial bank loans, often secured against their homes and other personal properties, to finance their businesses. Prolonged shipping delays, combined with demurrage, storage fees and accumulating loan interest, have reportedly threatened their ability to sustain operations.

On infrastructure, Dukuly disclosed that capital dredging at the port is expected to begin within two to three weeks. The exercise is intended to improve navigational depth and allow larger vessels to access the port, potentially increasing its cargo-handling capacity.

He also said APM Terminals, the port’s terminal operator, has ordered additional equipment expected to arrive in Liberia soon to strengthen cargo-handling operations.

The NPA is further opening an unpaved section of the port yard to accommodate additional containers and create more space for incoming vessels.

Beyond these immediate interventions, Dukuly said the authority is working with the Liberia Revenue Authority, Ministry of Commerce, CTN, MedTech and other stakeholders to automate port operations.

The proposed system would allow Import Permit Declarations and other documentation processes to be completed online, reducing physical transactions, administrative bottlenecks and delays in cargo clearance.

In another major announcement, Dukuly disclosed that President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has established the Inter-Ministerial Concessions Committee, which he said has attracted approximately US$280 million in direct capital investment for the port.

The investment is expected to support efforts to modernize the Freeport of Monrovia and strengthen its competitiveness as a regional maritime and commercial gateway. However, details of the investment, including its financing structure, implementation timeline and specific projects, were not immediately provided.

Business Community Demands Government Intervention

The announcements follow growing frustration among Liberian importers, particularly women-owned businesses, over prolonged shipping delays, port congestion and escalating demurrage, storage and administrative charges.

On Tuesday, representatives of the China Business Women United with One Voice and the Consortium of Liberia Importers petitioned the National Legislature and the NPA, warning that the situation is threatening the survival of local businesses.

Reading the petition on behalf of the business community, advocate Sriya Musu Momolu said shipments originating from Asia and China are reportedly taking between six and seven months to reach the Freeport of Monrovia.

She explained that many importers depend on commercial bank loans, often secured with personal homes and other properties, to finance their businesses. Extended shipping timelines, she said, have left their capital tied up for months, making it difficult to repay loans, meet rental obligations and fulfill tax responsibilities.

The petition also highlighted problems associated with expired Delivery Orders, which require importers to pay renewal fees and additional administrative charges before retrieving their goods.

The businesswomen argued that importers should not be forced to shoulder demurrage and other penalties for delays beyond their control.

They called for a legislative inquiry into shipping companies over transit delays and surcharge structures. They also demanded that shipping lines and terminal operators waive reissuance fees and demurrage charges arising from expired Delivery Orders.

Other demands include mandatory shipping arrival timelines, streamlined container-clearance procedures, enforcement of the Liberianization Policy to protect local businesses from unfair foreign retail competition, and the development of a long-term national logistics policy.

Receiving the petition on behalf of the Legislature, Montserrado County District No. 8 Representative Prince Toles pledged to bring the concerns before his colleagues for consideration.

Toles, who identified himself as a fellow businessperson, described the grievances as concerning and emphasized the need for swift legislative and administrative intervention.

Pressure Mounts on Port Authorities

The protest and petition have placed renewed pressure on the NPA and other government institutions to demonstrate that the country’s principal commercial gateway can effectively handle the demands of importers and shipping companies.

The Freeport of Monrovia is central to Liberia’s import-dependent economy, serving as a major entry point for food, fuel, construction materials, machinery and other essential commodities.

Prolonged delays can increase the cost of doing business as importers incur additional storage, demurrage, transportation and administrative charges. Such expenses can ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher prices in local markets.

While Dukuly’s proposed interventions could improve cargo movement and reduce delays, their effectiveness will depend on timely implementation, adequate equipment, improved coordination among government agencies and greater transparency in port operations.

For the protesting importers, the immediate concern remains the cost of retrieving goods already stranded at the port and the financial pressure accumulated during months of shipping delays.

World.title: Joseph Sitali joins Kitwe Utd coaching bench
World.content:
After a 20-year hiatus from Garden Park, former Super League star Joseph Sitali has returned to his boyhood club Kitwe United, this time as an assistant coach.

Chingalika have appointed Sitali to assist interim head coach Chisala Mwandama in the 2026 transitional National League season.

Sitali launched his playing career at Kitwe before switching to Power Dynamos after the club’s demotion around 2006.

After playing for Power, Don Bosco in DR Congo, Nkana and Mighty Mufulira Wanderers, Sitali hung up his boots at Shinde Stadium and was given a coaching role.

Sitali was an assistant coach at Mighty until June 2025.

Speaking to Lusaka Times Sports, the former midfield dynamo expressed his happiness to join the Kitwe bench.

“I am happy to join the Kitwe United coaching bench. This is my team and this is the team that made me,” Sitali said.

“I have come back at my parent club as a way of paying back. I accepted to come back here because of what this team has done for me,” he said.

Kitwe are enjoying good form in the National League and currently share top spot with Forest Rangers.

“For me to come back where it all started I believe God is saying something. I am here serving the club with my whole heart,” Sitali said.

Kitwe have 14 points from seven matches having posted four wins, two draws and one defeat.

World.title: Law marker calls for cancer screening
World.content:
Lima Constituency Member of Parliament Kelvin Kunda has called on Zambians to prioritise regular cancer screening, warning that late detection continues to contribute to cancer-related deaths.

Mr Kunda has said that early detection remains critical in improving treatment outcomes urging members of the public not to wait until they experience symptoms before seeking screening services.

Speaking during the Rotary Club of Maluba’s Free Annual Cancer Screening event at Twikatane Mall in Barlastone Park in Lusaka today, Mr Kunda said cancer is a major health concern requiring collective efforts from Government, the private sector and communities.

He cited estimates from the International Agency for Research on Cancer indicating that approximately 16,600 Zambians are diagnosed with cancer annually, while nearly 9,800 die from the disease.

Mr Kunda mentioned that many people continue to lose their lives because cancer is detected at advanced stages when treatment is more difficult and costly.

“Not knowing does not protect you. Knowing does,” he said, urging people to overcome fear, stigma and misconceptions surrounding cancer screening,” he said.

He said early detection improves chances of successful treatment, reduces the financial burden on families and helps to prevent some cancers, particularly through screening for cervical cancer.

Mr Kunda has commended the Rotary Club of Maluba for sustaining its free cancer screening and awareness initiative for 22 years, noting that about 4,400 people have been educated on cancer prevention and have been screened through the programme.

He has called for more partnerships to expand access to screening services, particularly in underserved communities calling on churches, community health volunteers and other local groups to promote awareness.

Meanwhile, Rotary Club of Maluba President Chanja Makai said the club is targeting to screen 700 people during this year’s initiative.

Ms Makai said the annual programme has been running for 22 years, with prostate and breast cancer screening introduced alongside cervical cancer screening as the initiative expanded.

She said the services are being provided free of charge in partnership with health professionals from Kanyama Level One Hospital and CDH, with screening available for breast, cervical and prostate cancer.

“We are hoping to capture about 300 men and 400 women. So men will be testing for both prostate and breast cancer,” she said.

Ms Makai has encouraged members of the public to attend with their families, adding that screening is quick and can help detect cancer even among people who are not experiencing symptoms.

She said the club has also heard testimonies from cancer survivors who have lived cancer-free for several years after diagnosis and treatment, demonstrating the importance of early detection.

And Synergy Seeds Zambia Chief Executive Officer Brian Mhango said the company is proud to partner with the Rotary Club of Maluba and other stakeholders in making cancer screening services accessible to communities.

Mr Mhango said the initiative reflects the importance of promoting good health as a foundation for strong families, productive workplaces and thriving communities.

“Early detection saves lives, and screening is one of the most important steps we can take towards protecting our health,” he said.

He has urged members of the public not to wait until they feel unwell before taking their health seriously.

World.title: 2027 budget to be judged by results-Nkoma
World.content:
Government said the 2027 National Budget will be measured by results and not pronouncements.

Minister of Industry Noel Nkoma said the Budget will be judged by the businesses that grow the investments and materialise jobs among others.

He was speaking at the Zambia Institute of Chartered Accountants (ZICA) 2027 Post-Budget Analysis Dinner in Lusaka.

Mr Nkoma said the National Budget is the Government’s most powerful tool for driving national development, as it reflects Government’s priorities, aspirations and policy direction.

He said the 2027 Budget comes at a pivotal moment in Zambia’s economic transformation journey and has been crafted around the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He said the agenda seeks to stimulate economic expansion, support enterprise development, create jobs, increase productivity, attract investment and improve the quality of life for all citizens.

The Minister added that it was fitting for stakeholders to gather after the presentation of the Budget to analyse its provisions and understand its implications for the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He said the budget process is strengthened by stakeholder participation both before and after the Budget is presented.

“Before formulation, Government undertakes extensive consultations with business associations, professional bodies, civil society, academia and other key stakeholders to ensure the Budget reflects the realities of the economy and responds to the needs of citizens and industry,” he said

Mr Nkoma said discussions at forums such as the ZICA dinner help businesses understand emerging opportunities, enable investors to assess likely economic trends and allow stakeholders to align their plans with national development priorities.

He said such engagements strengthen collaboration between Government and the private sector, which remains a critical pillar of Zambia’s economic transformation agenda.

The Minister said the Government recognises that sustainable economic growth cannot be achieved through public sector interventions alone, but requires a vibrant and competitive private sector capable of investing, innovating, producing and creating employment.

He said the Budget therefore seeks to empower businesses, improve the operating environment and unlock opportunities for entrepreneurship and industrial development.

ZICA President Joseph Matimba, stated that the Budget comes at an important time as Zambia seeks to consolidate macroeconomic stability while accelerating growth, stimulating investment and addressing the challenges facing people.

He named the cost of living, unemployment, poverty, energy security and low productivity as critical areas requiring sustained attention.

“The National Budget must therefore be assessed not only in terms of fiscal allocations and policy measures, but also in terms of its ability to stimulate productive economic activity, support enterprise development and improve the livelihoods of ordinary Zambians,” Mr Matimba said.

He said the industrial sector has a particularly important role to play, noting that a stronger manufacturing base, increased local production and greater value addition are essential to creating jobs, reducing dependence on imports and strengthening Zambia’s competitiveness in regional and international markets.

Mr Matimba said the Budget must also be viewed within the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda, which seeks to accelerate economic transformation and create inclusive growth through expanding production and investment in agriculture, mining, energy, manufacturing and tourism.

Meanwhile, ZICA Chief Executive Officer, Anthony Bwembya, said that the National Budget is more than a statement of Government’s revenue and expenditure priorities, but reflects national aspirations and provides a framework for stimulating investment, supporting industrial development, creating employment and improving livelihoods.

“Through sound financial management, transparency, accountability and professional advice, our members contribute to strengthening public financial management, supporting business growth and building confidence in our economy,” Mr Bwembya said.

World.title: Mundubile, Makebi Zulu Wait On Tuesday Ruling After 70 Days In Mukobeko
World.content:
Mundubile Bail Fate Rests On Tuesday Ruling As Tonse Condemns 70-Day Detention

The High Court will rule on Tuesday, 10 November, on whether Brian Mundubile and 17 others can proceed with their bid for constitutional bail. The State has asked the court to throw out the application on a technicality, arguing that it was filed in the wrong form. Opposition leaders are describing the prolonged detention as cruel and illegal.

A panel led by Mr Justice Mulenga reserved its ruling after hearing arguments in chambers on a preliminary issue raised by the State. Mr Mundubile is the losing presidential candidate of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP). He is joined in the application by his former running mate Makebi Zulu, Lusaka business executive Harry Findlay and 15 others. The group sued the State alleging gross violations of their constitutional rights. They then applied for constitutional bail, asking to be released either unconditionally or on reasonable conditions set by the court.

Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha, State Counsel, raised the preliminary issue. He urged the court to dismiss the bail application on the grounds that it had been wrongly commenced as a civil application instead of a criminal one. The State’s position is that the form of the filing goes to the heart of the court’s authority to hear the matter at all.

Acting Chief State Advocate Chibesa Mulonda developed that argument on behalf of the State. He submitted that the court could not grant constitutional bail when the application had been brought in civil rather than criminal format. He contended that, in those circumstances, the court had no jurisdiction to hear the application.

The defence pushed back hard. Lawyers for Mr Mundubile and the 17 others include three State Counsel: Bonaventure Mutale, Chifumu Banda and Sakwiba Sikota. They urged the court to reject the objection, sustain the application and hear it on its merits. The State maintained its position that the application should be dismissed for being irregularly filed.

The ruling leaves two possible paths. Mr Justice Mulenga said that if the preliminary issue did not succeed, the court would proceed straight to the substantive bail hearing on the same day. A ruling in the State’s favour would end the application in its current form and send the detainees’ lawyers back to refile.

Outside the courtroom, the opposition has escalated its language. Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance secretary general Muhabi Lungu said the continued incarceration of Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and the others at Mukobeko Maximum Prison for more than 70 days, without a plea before a High Court judge, was cruel. In a television interview, he said the detention was illegal because the country was not under a state of emergency.

“It’s not right and fair to charge Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 17 others and keep them in prison for 70 days without a plea before a judge. It’s not right; it’s illegal. We are not under a state of emergency. 70 days is not 48 hours, especially when the state says it has been probing this case for the last three years ahead of the arrest,” Mr Lungu said.

Mr Lungu accused the State of dragging its feet in the treason matter while the accused remained behind bars. He framed the choice facing prosecutors in stark terms: prove the case or free the accused.

“You can clearly see the State is dragging its feet in the treason matter while our leaders suffer. If you don’t have evidence, let them go, release them. If you have evidence, let the trial start and do it expeditiously so that the whole world sees what you accused them for,” he said.

The Tonse official went further and described the detention as an abuse of state power. In his view, it was aimed at punishing dissent rather than delivering justice. He said the opposition’s reading was that the Government wanted to demonstrate its power to punish.

“Our speculation is that government just wants to show that it can punish you, that abuse, that dictatorship, its cruelty, it’s not governance,” Mr Lungu said.

He tied the case to the final report of the European Union (EU) election observer mission, which he said confirmed that Zambia’s democratic space was shrinking. Mr Lungu said the mission was correct that the boundaries between the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) and the police had been unclear during the election. He cited uneven policing, misuse of public resources and questions over the independence of the electoral body. He added that former Botswana president Ian Khama and other outside observers had issued similar warnings.

“It’s wrong to jail people arbitrarily and then question why international observers say there’s shrinking democracy,” Mr Lungu said. “The police act selectively in Zambia under this government, one rule for those that support the government of the UPND, another that restricts those that have divergent views.”

The alliance is also demanding that the treason trial be opened to live coverage. Mr Lungu said past treason trials involving army generals, such as the late Christon Tembo, were covered openly. He said the present case should be held to the same standard.

“Here we are with a treason trial of civilians, namely Brian Mundubile; our leaders, including the media, are barred from covering the proceedings. Give us live coverage,” he said.

Access to the court itself has become a point of friction. Green Party leader Peter Sinkamba said blocking the Lusaka High Court premises had become a culture under the United Party for National Development (UPND) government whenever there was a case involving Mr Mundubile. Mr Sinkamba said he had gone to the court to file documents but met obstruction from police officers manning the premises during the bail hearing.

Tuesday’s ruling now carries weight well beyond the 18 applicants. If the court upholds the State’s objection, the detainees face further delay while the application is refiled. If it rejects the objection, the court will move straight to whether Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and the others should be released while their case proceeds. Either way, the decision will shape the course of the most closely watched prosecution of the post-election period

World.title: Here Is Who Pays More Under Zambia’s 2027 Budget Tax Measures
World.content:
High earners, small companies, mobile money users and mining shareholders face a heavier tax load from January 2027. Finance and National Planning Minister Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane has proposed a package of revenue measures expected to raise an extra K10.8 billion. The package raises Value Added Tax (VAT) to 16.5 per cent from 16 per cent and adds a new top Pay As You Earn (PAYE) rate of 39.5 per cent. It also lifts corporate income tax on lower-rated income, increases the mobile money levy across all bands and sharply raises duties on plastics.

Dr Musokotwane set out the measures when he presented the K284.8 billion 2027 National Budget to Parliament. He said the successful implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda required strong, sustainable and predictable domestic revenue. The proposals, he said, would balance support for productive economic activity with the need for individuals and businesses to contribute fairly to national development. The measures would take effect on January 1, 2027.

The new PAYE band is aimed at the top of the income ladder. Individuals earning more than K37,000 a month will pay a top marginal rate of 39.5 per cent on the portion of income above that line. Dr Musokotwane moved to reassure most salaried workers that their payslips would not change under the measure.

“In simple terms, those earning K37,000 per month and below will continue to be taxed under the current regime and will therefore not be affected by this measure. Only the additional income above K37,000 per month will be taxed at 39.5 per cent,” Dr Musokotwane said.

Companies will also pay more. The corporate income tax rate will rise by five percentage points on income currently taxed at 20 per cent and below. VAT moves to 16.5 per cent, which the minister described as part of the Government’s commitment to strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation. Because VAT applies to most goods and services, it will touch nearly every household budget.

Mobile money users will reach deeper into their wallets. The minister proposed to increase the mobile money levy across all bands, so every transaction tier will cost more. For the millions of Zambians who send, receive and save money on their phones, this is likely to be the measure they feel most often.

The mining sector faces a new set of charges. Dr Musokotwane proposed to raise withholding tax on dividends paid by mining companies to 15 per cent from zero, and to introduce a five per cent export duty on zinc concentrates. Mining, mineral processing and exploration licence fees, area charges and related fees will also rise. He said this would align Zambia’s licensing regime with international good practice.

Plastics are the target of the steepest increases in the package. Customs duty on single-use plastics will double to 200 per cent from 100 per cent. An additional duty of K8 per bottle will be introduced on plastic bottles, and the extra duty on selected plastic articles will rise to 30 per cent from 15 per cent. The measures are framed as part of the Government’s environmental sustainability agenda.

A cluster of import duties is designed to shield local industry. Customs duty on imported ceramic tiles will rise to 40 per cent from 25 per cent. Selected imported aluminium bars, rods and profiles will attract a 20 per cent selected goods sales tax and 25 per cent customs duty. The selected goods sales tax on imported meat, including beef, sheep and goat meat, will rise to 30 per cent from 20 per cent.

Shoppers will also see the effect on cooking oil and packaging. Crude soya bean and sunflower oils will attract 15 per cent customs duty and a 10 per cent selected goods sales tax to encourage local production. The selected goods sales tax on imported cement packaging and woven bags will be harmonised at 30 per cent. The minister also proposed ending the customs duty exemption and VAT zero-rating on energy-saving appliances. Second-hand clothing and handbags will be excluded from the duty relief given to approved public benefit organisations.

The package is not all tightening. Dr Musokotwane proposed a 100 per cent customs duty suspension and a VAT exemption on imported raw materials used to manufacture sanitary products locally. Customs duty will also be suspended on safari vehicles, hospitality equipment and communications infrastructure. That relief supports the target of five million international tourist arrivals under President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

Small-scale gold miners received a direct incentive to trade through official channels. The minister proposed to cut mineral royalty for artisanal and small-scale miners who sell to Government-approved aggregators to three per cent from six per cent. The measure is meant to pull a largely informal trade into the tax net. It sits alongside plans for a state gold trading agency to aggregate production.

Businesses that report losses year after year will face a narrower minimum alternative tax. Dr Musokotwane said the regime would apply only where a business recorded losses for three consecutive years.

“This will ensure that only businesses with a persistent pattern of loss declaration are brought into the alternative tax net while allowing businesses facing recurring downturns to recover and return to profitability,” Dr Musokotwane said.

The tax drive supports a budget that leans more heavily than ever on money raised at home. Domestic revenues of K233.7 billion will fund 82.1 per cent of spending, up from 58.7 per cent in 2021 and 76 per cent in 2024. Borrowing will account for K41.9 billion and grants from cooperating partners for K9.2 billion. The minister was blunt about the reasoning.

“There are no donors to pay, we must pay ourselves,” Dr Musokotwane said.

Debt remains a heavy claim on that revenue. The Treasury has set aside K67.6 billion for debt service in 2027, made up of K50.8 billion for domestic debt and K16.8 billion for external debt. Debt service sits within K90.5 billion, or 31.8 per cent of the budget, allocated to general public services.

Early reaction from economic and business voices was broadly positive. International Monetary Fund (IMF) Resident Representative for Zambia Dr Reginald Darius described the budget as growth-oriented and said revenue mobilisation would be critical to preserving fiscal stability and debt sustainability. Zambia Association of Manufacturers president Ashu Sagar said the increase in certain taxes was a move to support the social sector. Zambia Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ZACCI) chief executive officer Emmanuel Mumba said the incentives for manufacturing were a plus for local value addition.

To give effect to the measures, Dr Musokotwane proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act, the Customs and Excise Act and the Value Added Tax Act, among other laws. Parliament will now debate the proposals before they take effect in the new year.

World.title: E-government and decentralization key to improved service delivery
World.content:
Government has said deliberate investments in e-government and decentralization are driving public service transformation and anchoring the Grow Zambia agenda.

Speaking at the Association of Public Administration and Management conference, Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa commended the Association for Public Administration of Zambia (APAZ) and partners for organizing the conference, saying it comes at a time when all institutions must align to the next phase of national development.

Mr Kangwa said the government has invested deliberately in e-government and service digitization, noting that citizens can now access several services online.

“Today, citizens can complete end-to-end processes for tax payments, road service licenses, land rates, and ground rent without unnecessary delays,” he said.

He cited the recent launch of the online passport application system by the Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security and the planned roll-out of the digital national registration card, saying, “they are the result of deliberate planning and execution aimed at making public services faster, transparent, and accessible.”

Mr Kangwa said the second major milestone is the implementation of the decentralization policy, stating that, Decentralization sits at the heart of President Hakainde Hichilema’s development agenda, adding that devolving functions, resources and decision-making to local authorities is empowering communities to manage their own development.

He said the targets set by government are not theoretical, pointing to the transformation of the former Rocky Gardens in Lusaka West into one of Africa’s biggest industrial parks by the Wonderful Group conglomerate, which is now producing packaging materials and fertilizer, including a new urea plant commissioned by the President on October 16, creating over 6,000 jobs and projected to bring in US$5 billion by 2029.

“You must make sure the private sector feels the facilitation and enabling role that we play as public administration,” he said.

He urged public service workers to embrace changes in systems and structures, break down silos, and build institutions that deliver consistently for citizens.

Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development permanent secretary for administration Gabriel Pollen said its partnership with the Association for Public Administration of Zambia (APAZ) was born out of the passion for duty demonstrated by the association’s leadership.

Dr Pollen said when the APAZ team visited his Ministry, he saw an opportunity to champion a partnership that would reflect the practicality of the public sector for the development of the country, and worked with the office of the Secretary to the Cabinet to ensure the conference took place.

“Seeing public administrators and public administration enthusiasts in one room gives me hope about the future that it holds,” he said.

Dr Pollen expressed concern over the low response from local authorities, who are the main stakeholders of the conference, but said the inaugural conference will give special momentum going forward, and encouraged staff in the Ministry of Local Government and all local authorities to affiliate with professional associations such as APAZ because regardless of backgrounds, all are public administrators.

Association of Public Administrators of Zambia (APAZ) president Mudonda Sikawala said the organisation is focusing on transforming into a professional association backed by an Act of Parliament to regulate thousands of practicing but unregulated administrators.

He said the association, formed by public administration enthusiasts in 2020, has grown to over 150 members across five provinces, adding that it needs the Secretary to Cabinet’s guidance and wisdom as its new patron to move to the next phase.

He said efforts are focused on transforming APAZ into a professional association backed by an act of parliament, in order to attain the same recognition already achieved by professions such as accountancy, lawyers and other professions.

Mr Sikawala assured the government of APAZ’s readiness to support the Grow Zambia agenda, recommending that the Ninth National Development Plan and the next five budget cycles be synced to the agenda for policy coherence and easy monitoring.

He announced that 14 individuals and organisations are being awarded this year, and thanked ZESCO and the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development for their support ahead of a bigger event in June 2027.
