World.title: Carlota de Limón: The Mexican cocktail that transported me to my mother’s kitchen
World.content:
“You have to try one of these; it’s like a refreshing key lime pie,” a hotel guest at the bar said. I walked over to the friendly group, all with the same drink in hand. The cocktail in front of them resembled a blended piña colada that was pale yellow and frothy on top, garnished with a thin lime wedge on the rim.

My friend and I were staying at the Dreams Estrella del Mar in Mazatlán, Sinaloa, for a few days to check out the hotel and all its amenities. After the nightly show, we stopped by the bar for a drink and tasted what would ultimately be the most memorable part of the trip.

The cocktail was tangy from the lemon, sweet from the sugar, and instantly took me to something very familiar. The creamy texture and the balance of tart and sweet also felt familiar, as if I had tasted this combination many times before.

Then it hit me: It was a dessert my mom used to make growing up, and one I’ve always requested when I’m home. It was a favorite of mine that she called “lemon dessert,” which I know now as a Carlota de Limón.

Back in my mother’s kitchen

Carlota de Limón is a Mexican icebox cake made with lemon juice, Galletas María (sweet, thin vanilla cookies), and a creamy mixture of evaporated and condensed milk. Layered and chilled until set, it has the perfect balance between sweet and tangy.

It was one of my favorite desserts growing up. I remember eating it by the spoonful, freshly made and the day after, as well as the feeling of disappointment when it was gone. It wasn’t reserved for special occasions, and my mom made it regularly whether we were having dessert at home or sharing a meal with guests. It was a dish that was made on a whim, ingredients almost always on hand, and one that didn’t last long.

In other words, it was always a hit.

My mother’s kitchen was where our family came together and where some of our deepest conversations happened. While water boiled for pasta or soup simmered in spices, we would all gather around the island, almost like magnets pulling us closer, filling the space with conversation, laughter and connectedness. That feeling is still there today when I visit my parents, especially around the holidays or special occasions.

An unexpected connection

At the hotel, I pulled up a bar stool and watched the bartender make another drink. Curious about its inspiration, I struck up a conversation with him. He was 23 and working his first hotel bartending job, where he had been experimenting with flavors and creating cocktails, something he found to be a fun, creative outlet.

When I described the dessert the cocktail reminded me of, he recognized the Carlota de Limón, a favorite of his, too. He had been experimenting with ingredients to create the drink, combining Licor 43, the vanilla and spice notes echoing the María cookies, and the fresh lemon juice, sugar and heavy cream to match the creamy layer. He would then shake it vigorously with ice until the mixture turned frothy and cold, adding a simple lime wedge as the finishing touch.

What began as an experiment in flavors had unexpectedly recreated something familiar to me. The bartender didn’t know my personal backstory of the dessert, but his experimentation with a new cocktail and my memories of my mother’s kitchen had led us to the same place.

Why flavors stay with us

Research from the National Library of Medicine has a name for the way a familiar smell or taste can bring back a personal memory: the Proust effect, named after the French writer Marcel Proust. The theory is that taste and smell can trigger autobiographical memories, leading to powerful emotions. Research on the brain’s olfactory pathways also shows direct connections between smell processing and the regions involved in emotion and memory, which makes sense given my strong and positive response to the citrus cocktail.

To me, Carlota de Limón was more than just a dessert; it was something my mother made regularly, in a kitchen where conversations and laughter occurred. The flavor was familiar, but so was everything I associated with it.

When I returned home, I found myself thinking less about the resort’s beautiful pools, manicured grounds or nightly shows, and more about that cocktail. A drink I’d encountered on vacation that had brought back a dessert so familiar that I hadn’t thought much about what it meant to me until that moment.

On the drive home from the airport, my husband asked how the trip went. My answer was simple: “Do we have any lemons? I have a drink in mind.”

Sandra Lee is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: My family always travels during Día de Muertos. Here’s what we’ve enjoyed most
World.content:
There are certain magical aspects of living in Mexico that simply cannot be replicated elsewhere — its foods, traditions and seasons. And because of Mexico’s vast geography and cultural topography, many of those elements can be heightened by being in the right place at the right time.

In that regard, nothing compares to Día de Muertos: A time of year in which colors are blooming, communities are celebrating and honoring loved ones, and regional gastronomy, customs and superstitions are on display for everyone to be collectively immersed in.

Beyond the obvious, increasing importance of the Mesoamerican holiday in Mexico for so many native families and local households, Día de Muertos means something especially personal for me and my family since it marks our anniversary of having moved to Mexico from California. The holiday always reminds me of arriving in Mexico after having gained dual citizenship and being received by festive parades, open-armed friends and relatives, and getting a dose of Mexico’s fullest, most complex flavors that have come to define what we most enjoy about living on this side of the border.

Building our own annual tradition

My wife’s and my own appreciation for Día de Muertos extends further back, years before we had fully relocated to Mexico. In 2019, we visited my mom, who is Mexican-born and was living on my abuelo’s ranch in Oaxaca at the time. We spent a month traveling the state of Oaxaca with her. The highlight? A full week of Día de Muertos in Oaxaca City.

I’ll never forget when we arrived, hopped off the bus, dropped our things off and went into the loud, colorful streets as Oaxaqueños had already kicked off their days-long celebration in the middle of the afternoon. A man wearing a Spider-Man mask saw us standing among the crowd, and as we soon found out would be a common occurrence and part of the local hospitality, he offered to pour out a shot of mezcal from the bottle in his hand.

As an outsider, there is no warmer welcome on the planet than someone picking you out of the masses on the street and pouring you mezcal. It’s a spirit and energy that would come to embody every Día de Muertos holiday we’ve experienced — the sense of connection and togetherness.

Since then, we’ve turned it into our own tradition to celebrate the holiday in different parts of Mexico as often as we can.

The regional nuances of Día de Muertos

My wife recently shared a visual map with me that outlines the different kinds of pan de muerto that are prepared throughout Mexico, based on each state’s history and gastronomic influences. Her point, besides nudging me to pick up another round of pan de muerto for our house, was that Mexico offers more to try than we know, especially whenever Día de Muertos rolls around.

It’s true. Everywhere we’ve been during this season has always presented a new way through which to experience and understand the multidimensionality of how the holiday is celebrated and revered.

Nearby, in the town of Naolinco, Veracruz, and its surrounding mountain communities, the festival is largely centered on the cempasúchil. This year, the community of San Pablo Coapan welcomed thousands of visitors for its fifth annual Festival del Cempasúchil, in which the local cempasúchil farms open to the public with a festival-like array of activities, food and Instagrammable photo ops.

The flower fields are decorated with playful calaveras that are decorated in Veracruzano style, ranging from a 25-foot-tall Jarocho skeleton to a human-sized fútbolero in the afterlife wearing a Tiburones Rojos soccer uniform from the 1990s (a team that no longer exists but certainly evokes memories for anyone who recalls the historic Veracruz team and grew up watching Liga MX).

In the pueblo of Naolinco proper, just a few miles up the mountain, Día de Muertos is celebrated with “La Cantada” (or a townwide serenade), where locals go around singing from the cemeteries to the streets throughout the night.

Major cities and regional rituals

Of course, there are the more globally popular and large-scale interpretations of Día de Muertos that can be seen in Oaxaca or Mexico City. In both cases, the holiday draws countless international and domestic visitors who join in on the fun and traditions as local families honor their deceased relatives with a mix of humility and bombast.

In both Oaxaca and Mexico City, expect massive gatherings of happy-go-lucky tourists and locals, as you’ll have to shuffle your way around the crowds and generally pay higher prices. The celebrations are bigger, louder and, to a degree, more capably geared toward tourism than other locales. I’d say for starters, both Oaxaca’s capital and Mexico City are a comfortable entry point into Mexico’s sprawling multiverse of Día de Muertos, as they provide broadly appealing and easy-to-navigate celebrations, both of which my family has enjoyed and experienced ourselves multiple times.

Of course, we still have a bunch of places to visit on our wishlist that I’ve been told about by my Mexican family members and other travelers. In the Huasteca jungles, “Xantolo” brings the holiday to life with “La Viejada,” a regional masked dance in which townspeople dress up as elders (similar to Veracruz’s “El Viejo del Año Nuevo” custom at the end of every year) to remember their relatives.

1 of 17

Indigenous customs from Huasteca to Campeche

In parts of Michoacán, there is a lake procession where the Purépecha fishermen use torches to light their path across the water and celebrate with all-night vigils.

Choo Ba’ak, a bone-washing ritual that happens every year in the Campeche pueblo of Pomuch, is part of Hanal Pixán (the Maya Day of the Dead) and offers an idiosyncratic version of the holiday unlike the contemporary mainstream version that is usually portrayed.

National Geographic described the ceremony as such: “…families wash the tombs and clean the bones of their deceased. After the cleaning they keep the ossuaries, or the box where the bones are deposited, open so the skulls and bones receive sun and air, as dictated by tradition. Relatives also arrange, paint and adorn the ossuaries and cover them with an embroidered white tablecloth bearing the name of the deceased.”

In Huaquechula, Puebla, unique altars — three to four stories tall, resembling a pyramid — are on display inside homes, with each layer of the altar representing a different aspect of life and death (the earth, the heavens and a celestial summit). The elaborate designs are typically defined by white cloth and marigolds.

As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me, you’d need more than a few lifetimes to truly experience all that Mexico has to offer regionally for Día de Muertos.

Our highlights from this year in the mountains of Puebla

The Pueblo Mágico of Cuetzalan del Progreso is tucked away in the northernmost edge of the state of Puebla, high up in the Sierra Norte mountains.

Unlike the majority of Puebla, which is commonly known for its arid plateaus and Talavera pottery in its state capital and surrounding areas, northern Puebla offers a microclimate and culture of its own that more closely resembles the humid, tropical and high-altitude Indigenous communities of Papantla in northern Veracruz, which is located just a few miles away on the other side of the mountain.

It’s not what one might think of when thinking of Puebla. And yet, it’s where regional customs for Día de Muertos are flourishing. We drove roughly four hours north of Xalapa (or about five hours northeast from Mexico City) to experience it for ourselves this year.

We weren’t disappointed, to say the least.

The town’s architecture alone is worth the winding mountain curves that one must navigate to reach the small, ages-old village that is — because of its elevated location in the mountains — famously drenched in drizzly mist and rainfall. The narrow alleys and steep, cobblestone paths (which all lead to the gorgeous Parroquia de San Francisco de Asís and its Totonac voladores, who perform their flying ritual on a sky-high wooden pole at the center of the plaza) resemble a miniature version of Guanajuato’s capital city, without the overcrowded tourism and with a hyper-local texture.

Flying globos de Cantoya into the night

I was told by a couple of young locals that families don’t commonly celebrate Día de Muertos by visiting the graveyards overnight (which is the tradition elsewhere). Instead, they light “globos de Cantoya” (miniature hot-air balloons made from paper and other materials) and send them off into the night.

From groups of high schoolers to older professionals who’ve mastered the craft, the town gathers on Día de Muertos weekend, as everyone takes turns setting up and sending off hundreds of their custom, artisanal balloons. The balloons — and their makers — vary in style, decoration and success (often, the small balloons will self-combust in flames and come burning back to earth, which can sometimes cause fires in the area). But generally, it’s a safe and spectacular tradition to witness in person.

The tradition, as it was explained to me in the pueblo, is meant to represent a path back to the heavens for the souls who are visiting their altars to enjoy the ofrendas laid out. Each globe, as it ascends brightly and colorfully into the night sky, is meant to guide family members back to the spiritual realm.

In recent years, Cuetzalan has turned the tradition into a legitimate state-funded festival, known locally as “El Vuelo del Quetzal” (The Flight of the Quetzal), and officially as Festival Internacional de Globos Artísticos de Papel. Surprisingly, the festival is only in its second year of formal operation, which helps it retain a charmingly niche, DIY feeling.

Local flavors and looking ahead

During the day, it is all preceded by local dances, voladores, Catrina costume contests and the general ambiance of a Pueblo Mágico worth its salt: excellent food, tianguis and a dense number of historic stairways and nooks to explore.

Among the standouts in town, you cannot skip TAOL, which is led by Chef Adriana Márquez and offers elevated, accessible takes on local dishes, including tlayoyos, chilpozontle, itacate, pipián, coffee and more. It’s the kind of chic eatery that would draw lines out the door in Mexico City, but since it’s hidden behind an unassuming stone exterior in Cuetzalan, it is able to offer ample space and friendly prices for what I would consider among the best cuisine I’ve tasted this year.

Paired with Día de Muertos activities and the hordes of costumed kids making their rounds on Halloween night to ask for their calaverita at local shops, which my son participated in, a few nights in Cuetzalan is a slept-on destination for late October and early November.

Though we elected to stay home last year to dedicate our time and resources to building and decorating an altar inside our home — with the help of my mom, who supplied many photos of our relatives — we’ve enjoyed going on the road to see how others embrace the spirit of the tradition.

I’m already thinking about where we might end up next year and what it will impart.

World.title: Why Tuesday’s US midterm results are a historic opportunity for Mexico-US relations: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Most of us intently watched Tuesday night’s midterm election results in the United States, regardless of political affiliation. As the MND team is committed to remaining apolitical, I will not weigh in on my personal thoughts on the results. I will, however, comment on what they mean for Mexico and for Mexico-U.S. relations.

It’s important to understand that the hardline approach of the Trump administration over the past two years against both Mexican immigrants and Mexico effectively silenced leaders on both sides of the border. Mexico was constantly on the defensive against the U.S. on tariffs, cartels, deportations, the rights of Mexican citizens abroad and many other topics. Mexican Americans, regardless of status, watched with anxiety as their communities came under threat from aggressive ICE raids. For many people and for Mexico in general, it was a time to keep your head down and stay quiet. The focus became on surviving the storm rather than thriving, leading or growing.

But the midterm election results have dramatically changed that dynamic.

First of all, I am happy for Mexican Americans. They will hopefully no longer have to fear the heavy-handed tactics often deployed by members of ICE. I recently wrote about the death of the 18th Mexican-American in ICE custody here: Yet another Mexican national dies in the custody of ICE: A perspective from our CEO.

People living in the United States — either legally or illegally — shouldn’t have to fear for their lives at the hands of the government. The data shows that the raids have often gone far beyond focusing on criminals, as the administration suggested it would do. Too many good people have been demonized by ICE as the agency has become increasingly extremist.

I am also happy for Mexico. The country has been the brunt of countless threats by the Trump administration on everything from tariffs to immigration to drug policy and cartels — despite historic cooperation from the Sheinbaum administration on many of these issues. Businesses on both sides of the border have had to deal with near-constant tariff threats, which oftentimes defy standard logic and strategic rationale for the North American region. Both Trump and members of his administration have repeatedly claimed that Mexico is run by the cartels, that President Sheinbaum is “afraid of the cartels,” and threatened to take unilateral action in the country. Hopefully, the unprecedented cooperation will continue and the unhelpful threats will diminish.

I am happy for the states of California and Texas, which both elected Mexican American governors. These two states — the largest and most economically prosperous in the United States — now account for more than half of the people of Mexican origin in the United States. Mexican Americans represent 40% of the total population in those states, which, if they were stand-alone counties, would be the fifth- and eighth-largest in the world in terms of GDP. Children of Mexican immigrants to the U.S. now lead both states. The newly elected lieutenant governor of Nevada is also of Mexican heritage.

Mexican Americans stood up, voted, and were heard — loudly and clearly. Their collective action presents a tremendous opportunity for Mexico. Let me give two examples:

1. I recently wrote about the huge, untapped opportunity that the Mexican diaspora in the U.S. represents for Mexico. The engagement of Indian American businesspeople with India stands in stark contrast to the lack of engagement of many Mexican American businesspeople with Mexico. Post-election, the timing is perfect for this to change. The opportunity for Mexican American businesses to further connect with Mexico to find talent, suppliers or customers is massive and could unleash economic growth in both countries.

2. It’s time for Mexico and the U.S. to think BIG on binational projects and initiatives. If not at the national level, most certainly at the state level. Some great examples already exist or are in process. In California, think of the Tijuana airport, which actually straddles the border into California. The airport has experienced phenomenal growth and is a perfect example of how the two countries can work strategically to develop closer ties. In Texas, think of the newly-opened second railway between Laredo and Nuevo Laredo or the proposed expansion of the World Trade Bridge from eight to 18 lanes. Think of the soon-to-be-opened Pharr project adding a four-lane bridge in Reynosa, or the Colombia-Solidarity highway projects to better connect Nuevo León and Laredo. Or even consider the Green Corridors planned project for an autonomous system to transport cargo from Monterrey to Laredo.

It’s a historic time for real leadership — strategic, long-term, big thinking that can foster engagement and economic prosperity between the two countries. Far too much time has been lost dividing, threatening and silencing bilateral collaboration and cooperation. The current circumstances offer an opportunity to take the relationship to a whole new level. Leaders on both sides of the border, stand up! The time is now.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Mexico City’s Quintonil named best restaurant in Latin America
World.content:
Quintonil, a contemporary Mexican restaurant in Mexico City, was recognized as the best restaurant in Latin America and the fourth best globally in the 2026 edition of The World’s 50 Best Restaurants, presented Wednesday at the Municipal Theatre of Lima, Perú.

Led by married couple Chef Jorge Vallejo and restaurateur Alejandra Flores, Quintonil was the only Mexican representative among the top 50 in the ranking.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The 50 Best Restaurants (@theworlds50best)

“With a reputation for weaving fresh, local ingredients and traditional Mexican flavours and techniques into modern preparations, [Quintonil] has cemented its place as a Mexico City classic,” 50 Best said.

Asador Etxebarri, a Basque restaurant in Atxondo, Spain, was ranked best in the world.

Despite securing a place in the top five, Quintonil dropped one spot in the rankings, falling from third to fourth place this year.

Founded in 2012 by Vallejo and Flores, Quintonil has built its concept around Mexican fresh local produce and a contemporary interpretation of traditional flavors and techniques. Many of its ingredients are sourced from an urban garden just 30 meters away from the restaurant.

Located in the high-end neighborhood of Polanco, the restaurant is named after an edible wild plant belonging to the amaranth family, widely used in traditional Mexican cuisine and featured in some of the dishes and drinks served there.

The power duo brings complementary expertise to Quintonil: While Vallejo leads the kitchen, Flores oversees the service experience in the dining room.

“Quintonil is the setting for chef Jorge Vallejo’s boundary-pushing Mexican cuisine and his wife Alejandra Flores’ exceptional hospitality,” 50 Best said.

50 Best highlighted dishes including roasted duck with coconut manchamanteles mole (a fruit and chile sauce) and a beetroot reduction, wild mushroom chileatole soup with cacahuazintle (a traditional corn variety) and beans, and ice cream made with honey from stingless melipona bees, served with papaya and lavender marmalade.

The tasting menu costs around 4,900 pesos (US $233) featuring four pairing options that include wines from around the world, Mexican wines, a selection of terroir-driven wines and rare finds, and a non-alcoholic option.

It also features a cocktail menu incorporating Mexican ingredients.

The recognition from 50 Best adds to Quintonil’s list of accolades, which includes two Michelin stars, a distinction it shares with only one other restaurant in Mexico: Pujol, also located in Mexico City.

With reports from El País

World.content:

Formula 1 · São Paulo Grand Prix

Published Saturday, November 7, 4:56 p.m. ET (6:56 p.m. São Paulo) · Source: Formula 1 timing and results, OpenF1 timing data, Polymarket

The rain nearly won qualifying at Interlagos, but Lando Norris beat it. Norris, McLaren’s British driver, took pole position for Sunday’s São Paulo Grand Prix 2026 with a lap of 1:27.470, his third pole in a row at the São Paulo circuit.

In plain English Qualifying is Saturday’s timed shoot-out that sets Sunday’s starting order, and pole is first place. It has three knockout rounds, Q1 to Q3.

Norris Wins a Wet Gamble at Interlagos

Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc was fourth (1:28.289) and Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson fifth (1:28.321). Audi’s Nico Hülkenberg was a surprise sixth and Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar seventh, with Haas’s Oliver Bearman, Aston Martin’s Fernando Alonso and Williams’s Alex Albon made the top ten.

Q2 ended early when Câmara, a Brazilian rookie making his Formula 1 debut for Haas, crashed into the barrier with less than a minute left. He was classified 13th.

In Q3 the sky darkened and Alonso was first out on intermediates, the tyre for damp tracks. The best conditions had passed with seven minutes left, and Russell was furious when his team told him to abandon a lap.

Penalties Will Reshuffle Sunday’s Grid

Formula 1, the series organiser, says Russell loses five places and Leclerc ten. Hamilton needs a new power unit, the engine and hybrid system, and joins Verstappen and Pérez at the back, and Verstappen did not run in Q2.

Norris keeps pole, but the order behind him will change once the FIA, the sport’s governing body, publishes the official grid. That helps midfield drivers such as Lawson and Hülkenberg.

On Polymarket, a prediction market where traders bet real money, Antonelli was the favourite to win Sunday’s race at 39.5%, ahead of Norris at 33.0%, Verstappen at 13.5% and Russell at 9.9%. The market had US$125,266 traded at 4:51 p.m. ET, and these prices are bets, not polls.

The next test is Sunday at noon ET (9:00 a.m. PT), when Norris tries to turn pole into a win. Apple TV is the exclusive US broadcaster this year.

After Mexico City, champion Antonelli has 380 points, ahead of Verstappen on 261 and Hamilton on 259. Mercedes leads Ferrari 630 to 504 in the teams’ standings.

What Is Not Known

The FIA had not published the official starting grid when we wrote this, so the exact places of Russell and Leclerc after their penalties are unconfirmed. Sunday’s weather and any further penalties are also unknown.

The race starts Sunday, November 8, at noon ET (2:00 p.m. São Paulo, 9:00 a.m. PT). In the United States it is shown live on Apple TV.

Lando Norris of McLaren took pole with a 1:27.470 in rain-hit qualifying at Interlagos. Mercedes’ George Russell was second, but has a five-place grid penalty.

Brazil Health

World.title: Bolivia State Telecom Eyes Near Full Reach
World.content:
Bolivia Telecom

Entel, the state-owned phone and internet company of landlocked Bolivia, says it wants coverage close to 100% of the country by 2030, while admitting that gaps remain today.

Bolivia’s state telecom company says it wants to reach close to every corner of the country by 2030. Entel, the Empresa Nacional de Telecomunicaciones, set out the goal at a forum in La Paz this week.

For readers abroad, the plan tests whether state-led investment can narrow a deep digital gap in a poor, mountainous country. General manager Jorge del Solar said Entel already has a presence in 335 municipalities, the local council areas that run towns and rural districts, but gaps remain.

Key Facts Who: Entel S.A., Bolivia’s state telecom company, whose board president is Álvaro Bazán.

What: A goal of coverage close to 100% of Bolivia’s national territory by 2030.

Context: A new atlas from SDSN Bolivia, a development research network, reports household internet access rose from 10% in 2012 to 74% in 2024.

Open: How the coverage goal is measured, what it costs and the yearly milestones.

Power Index: Bolivia ranks 13th of 14 in Bolivia ranks 13th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 27.9 points (November 2026 edition).

Three Pillars for 2030

Entel’s board president, Álvaro Bazán, said the company’s strategy rests on three pillars. The first is connectivity, which he described as meaningful access that improves lives, not just wider coverage.

The second is technological transformation, where Entel takes on a major role in Bolivia’s digital development. The third is integration, which means strengthening the country’s links with the rest of South America.

Under the first pillar, Entel plans to come close to 100% coverage of the national territory by 2030. Del Solar said the goal is to come as close as possible to 100% of Bolivia, calling it complex, long-term work.

What the Atlas Shows

This week SDSN Bolivia presented the Atlas of the Sustainable Development Goals in Bolivia 2026. SDSN Bolivia is the Bolivian arm of the Sustainable Development Solutions Network, a global research network, and it produced the atlas with the Universidad Privada Boliviana, a private university.

The atlas compares more than 340 municipalities and other territorial units between 2012 and 2024, and holds more than 100,000 data points. It reports that the share of Bolivian households with fixed or mobile internet rose from 10% in 2012 to 74% in 2024.

Municipalities with more internet access also show better results on poverty, education, health and employment. SDSN Bolivia’s Lykke Andersen stressed that this is a correlation and that deeper research is needed to show cause.

In Plain English

Entel is Bolivia’s national phone and internet operator, run by the state. The name is similar to Chile’s Entel, but this is a separate company that serves Bolivia.

A municipality is a local government unit with an elected mayor and council. The Sustainable Development Goals are the United Nations targets on poverty, health, education and other areas.

What It Means for You

Readers in the United States should treat the 2030 goal as a stated ambition, not a funded plan. It shows a state company trying to narrow Bolivia’s digital gap, especially in rural areas.

If the goal is met, more Bolivians could go online for work, school and health services. See our Bolivia coverage for how state-led investment fits the wider economy.

What Is Not Known

Entel did not say how it measures coverage, whether by population, territory or municipalities. It also gave no cost, funding plan or year by year milestones.

The atlas figures come from SDSN Bolivia and we have not checked them independently. Andersen described internet access as reaching roughly 75% of the population, a slightly different measure from the household figure above.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Entel’s goal for Bolivia?

Entel, Bolivia’s state telecom company, aims to come close to 100% coverage of the national territory by 2030. It has not said how it measures that figure.

How many Bolivian households have internet?

SDSN Bolivia’s 2026 atlas reports that 74% of households had fixed or mobile internet in 2024, up from 10% in 2012. The figures come from the atlas, not from Entel.

Is this the same Entel as the Chilean company?

No. The name is similar, but this is Bolivia’s state-run Empresa Nacional de Telecomunicaciones, a separate company that serves Bolivia.

World.title: Ambev Courts Young Brazilians With an App
World.content:
Brazil Business

Zé Delivery, the brewer’s own ordering app, gives Ambev a close view of young buyers. Across Brazil, premium and lighter beers are growing fast while mainstream beer falls.

Ambev, the Brazilian brewer, says its own delivery app is helping it reach young adults of legal drinking age. Michelob Ultra, a beer brand many Americans know, grew more than five-fold in volume in Brazil last quarter.

The app is called Zé Delivery, and in the third quarter its total sales grew about 16%. Ambev reported this on 29 October 2026 in its quarterly results release.

Key Facts Who: Ambev, a Brazilian brewer whose brands include Skol, its mass-market lager, Stella Artois and Michelob Ultra.

What: Zé Delivery, Ambev’s drinks-delivery app, grew total sales about 16% in the third quarter.

Why the App Matters to Ambev

Zé Delivery is Ambev’s own app for ordering drinks in Brazil. About 80% of its users are Gen Z and Millennials, the two youngest adult generations, according to Ambev’s results release of 5 May 2026.

Ambev says the app keeps it close to new trends and speeds up its test-and-learn cycle on new products. In plain words, the company can try an idea on real buyers and quickly see what works.

In the first quarter the app was an innovation hub for the launch of Skol Zero Zero, a no-alcohol beer. Almost 90% of consumers said their view of the brand was neutral or better after trying it.

Zé Marketplace, where extra products beyond beer are sold, is nearly 20% of total platform GMV. So close to one fifth of the app’s sales value now comes from the marketplace, which widens the range beyond beer.

Across Brazil, Ambev’s premium beer volumes grew in the high teens. Balanced Choices more than doubled in volume, and no-alcohol beer grew in the forties percent.

What It Means for You

For US readers, the app shows Ambev building a direct line to young customers. It also shows demand moving toward premium and lighter drinks, which matters when the company’s mainstream beer is shrinking.

Ambev says the app gives it a direct relationship with a large base of young adults of legal drinking age. That base is where it tests new products and promotions.

Anyone who follows Brazil’s consumer market can watch whether premium and lighter beers keep gaining while mainstream beer falls. That split is the clearest signal in the latest release.

Ambev does not break out Zé Delivery buyers by generation in the releases we reviewed. The 80% figure combines Gen Z and Millennials and comes from the May release.

What is Zé Delivery?

Zé Delivery is Ambev’s own app for ordering drinks in Brazil. It also hosts Zé Marketplace, which sells products beyond beer.

How fast did the app grow in the third quarter?

How many app users are Gen Z?

Ambev said in May 2026 that about 80% of the app’s users are Gen Z and Millennials. It did not repeat or split that figure in October.

World.title: Nigeria Oil Firm Denies Gas Link to Outages
World.content:
Nigeria Power

Nigeria’s state oil company says its pipelines can still deliver gas to power plants, setting up a public dispute with the grid operator over why electricity output fell.

Nigeria’s state oil company has rejected claims that its gas pipelines are behind a fall in the country’s electricity output. NNPC Limited, formally the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited, said in a statement that, by its own records, its gas transport network shows no constraints.

Nigeria is a major African oil producer, so a weak grid hurts business and the oil-linked economy. US investors who follow Nigeria’s power and gas sector will want to know who is right.

Key Facts Who: NNPC Limited, Nigeria’s state oil company, and the Nigerian Independent System Operator (NISO), which runs the grid.

What: NNPC denies that gas pipeline limits explain the fall in electricity generation.

Why: Gas-fired plants are a main source of Nigeria’s grid power, so supply gaps hit business.

Next: NNPC wants a joint review by gas suppliers, transporters, power generators and the grid operator.

What NNPC Said

The statement was issued in Abuja and signed by Andy Odeh, the company’s Chief Corporate Communications Officer. NNPC posted it on 7 November 2026.

It said the records of NNPC Gas Infrastructure Company Limited, the subsidiary that runs the pipelines, show no transport constraints that could explain the drop.NNPC said its gas production volumes are up about 10% so far in 2026. It gave no baseline and no figure for gas delivered to power plants.

It added that ‘gas supply availability is therefore not a challenge’.

A line of flags along a fenced roadside in Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. File photo, 2019. (Photo: Kritzolina, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why the Two Accounts Differ

The reply followed a statement dated 5 November 2026 from the Nigerian Independent System Operator, known as NISO, which runs the national grid and sends power to distribution companies, the firms that sell electricity to homes and businesses. NISO blamed the decline in generation on limited gas availability and reduced water inflows to hydroelectric stations.

NNPC argued that open pipelines do not prove that every stage of the gas to power chain works. Gas production, commercial supply arrangements and actual deliveries to each power plant must be assessed separately, it said.

It also pointed to the readiness of generating units and to plant maintenance schedules. Actual gas offtake, meaning how much gas a plant takes, was named as a further factor.

NNPC called for a coordinated review involving gas suppliers, transporters, power generators and NISO. The aim, it said, is to identify the specific constraints and the interventions needed.

Nigeria’s grid has struggled for years with outages, which is the context for this dispute. See our explainer on Nigeria’s power cuts for why the problem keeps getting worse.

What It Means for You

For businesses in Nigeria, the dispute matters because unreliable power raises costs and disrupts work. Until the cause is clear, the risk of further cuts stays on the table.

For investors abroad, the question is whether gas, power plants or water is the weak link. The answer shapes how they judge Nigeria’s grid, its gas sector and the oil-linked economy.

Gas-fired plants are a main source of grid generation, so any gap between supply and delivery shows up quickly. A clear public review would help households, lenders and companies see where the fix must come.

What Is Not Known

NNPC’s statement did not publish current generation figures in megawatts or the exact gas volumes delivered to plants. The two accounts differ, and no joint review had been announced in the reports we saw.

NNPC did not say how much of the drop is due to water levels at hydroelectric stations. That leaves the weight of each cause open.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does NNPC say gas pipelines caused Nigeria’s power drop?

No. NNPC says its pipelines remain available to deliver gas to power plants nationwide, and its subsidiary’s records show no transport constraints.

What did the grid operator say?

The Nigerian Independent System Operator, in a statement dated 5 November 2026, blamed the decline on limited gas availability and reduced water inflows to hydroelectric stations.

What does NNPC want to happen next?

It wants a coordinated review involving gas suppliers, transporters, power generators and the grid operator to identify the specific constraints and the interventions needed.

Sources NNPC Limited statement (posted 7 November 2026); NISO statement (5 November 2026), as quoted in NNPC’s reply and reported by Nigerian media.

World.title: Peru Promises Police Their Back Pay Bonuses
World.content:
PERU · SECURITY

Key Facts What happened Peru’s finance minister said in the past few days that unpaid risk bonuses for police will be paid.

Who Elmer Cuba, finance minister, and Interior Minister César Astudillo, whose ministry (Mininter) oversees the police.

How much Up to S/2,150 (Peruvian soles) a month per officer, about US$625 at S/3.4406 per US dollar.

Why it matters Cuba says funds are budgeted; Astudillo says his ministry cannot pay yet. No payment date has been given.

As of Saturday 7 November 2026, 21:00 GMT

Peru’s finance minister has promised that police officers working in emergency zones will receive their delayed risk bonus, but no date, total or decree has been announced yet.

Elmer Cuba, Peru’s Economy and Finance Minister, gave the promise in an interview with a Peruvian radio and television station. He was sworn in on Tuesday 28 July 2026 under President Keiko Fujimori.

What We Know

The payment in question is the Bonificación por Alto Riesgo a la Vida, a bonus for high risk to life. It goes to officers and non-commissioned officers (sub-officers) of the Peruvian National Police (PNP) who serve in areas under a state of emergency.

The bonus can reach S/2,150 a month (about US$625 at the market rate of S/3.4406 per US dollar on Friday 6 November 2026). S stands for the Peruvian sol, the national currency.

The bonus applies to officers serving in areas covered by the government’s emergency decrees. Officers there carry the risk that the bonus is meant to recognise.

On Thursday 5 November 2026, Interior Minister César Astudillo spoke on the same subject. He said “the bonuses will be paid” and that there will be “no clean slate”.

Astudillo added that his Interior Ministry, known as Mininter, is working with the Economy Ministry to secure financing. He also said Mininter does not have the funds at the moment.

According to Astudillo, recovered money has already gone to salaries, year-end obligations and per diems, which are daily allowances for staff on duty. Neither minister has announced a payment date.

In Plain English

The Economy and Finance Ministry, called MEF in Peru, controls the national budget and releases money to other ministries. The Interior Ministry oversees the police.

A bonus can be approved on paper and still go unpaid until the finance ministry moves the cash. That gap between a promise and a transfer is what officers are now waiting on.

A Precedent for Paying This Bonus

This would not be the first time the finance ministry has paid for this bonus. It has funded this bonus through budget transfers before.

One example is S/43.5 million (about US$12.6 million at today’s S/3.4406 per US dollar) paid in 2023 under Supreme Decree 090-2023-EF. A supreme decree is a government order issued in the president’s name.

What Is Not Known

Cuba says the money is in the public budget, while Astudillo says his ministry cannot pay yet. The two statements have not been reconciled, and neither minister has said which budget line would cover the cost.

No payment date has been announced, and no total amount has been published. Nobody has said how many officers are owed or which budget line will cover the cost.

It is also unclear whether a new decree is needed to release the funds. Until one appears, or the transfers begin, the promise remains a statement of intent.

What It Means for You

For police officers and their families, the practical question is timing rather than principle. Both ministers now say the bonus will be paid, which narrows the dispute to how and when.

Travellers and expats in emergency zones should keep following official guidance. Our guide to Peru’s emergency mode after the Trujillo attack in August explains what the rules mean day to day.

Investors watching Peru’s security picture can look at how fast the money moves. Our earlier report on the police chief’s resignation in September shows the pressure on the force.

A prompt transfer would show that the new government can match its words with cash. A long delay would leave officers in dangerous zones waiting, and we will follow the next announcement from either ministry.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the police risk bonus in Peru?

It is the Bonificación por Alto Riesgo a la Vida, a monthly payment for police officers and sub-officers serving in emergency zones. It can reach S/2,150 (about US$625 at S/3.4406 per US dollar).

Who said the bonuses will be paid?

Economy and Finance Minister Elmer Cuba said in the past few days that they are in the public budget. Interior Minister César Astudillo said on 5 November that the bonuses will be paid and there will be no clean slate.

When will officers receive the money?

No payment date has been announced. Officials have also not said how many officers are owed or what the total cost will be.

Do the ministers agree on funding?

Cuba says the money is in the public budget, while Astudillo says his ministry lacks funds right now. The two statements have not been reconciled.

Sources: Statements by Peru’s Economy and Finance Minister Elmer Cuba (interview published 7 November 2026) and Interior Minister César Astudillo (5 November 2026); Decreto Supremo 090-2023-EF, published in the official gazette El Peruano on 12 May 2023; exchange rate S/3.4406 per US$ (market close, 6 November 2026).

World.title: Colombia Leader Backs Aide After Home Entry
World.content:
COLOMBIA · POLITICS

Key Facts What happened Three people with judicial records were found inside the home of presidential official Carlos Ríos on 28 October.

Who Ríos directs Dapre, the presidential administration department that runs the president’s office; President Abelardo de la Espriella backs him.

Why it matters Colombia is a close US partner, and its new government is pushing an anti-corruption agenda.

What is not known Arrests are unconfirmed, no suspect is named, and any link to his corruption allegations is unproven.

As of 7 November 2026, 21:00 GMT

Colombia’s president has publicly defended a senior aide after three people with criminal records were found inside the aide’s home, though the facts of the case remain unclear.

Three people with judicial records were found inside the home of one of Colombia’s senior presidential officials, and on Saturday 7 November 2026 the president said he stands behind him. The official is Carlos Ríos, director of Dapre, the Departamento Administrativo de la Presidencia de la República, which runs the president’s office and administration.

For readers in the United States, the story matters because Colombia has long been a close partner of Washington in the region. The government says it will keep pursuing the use of public funds and will not give way to pressure.

What We Know

The Government says protection authorities found the three people inside Ríos’s home on Wednesday 28 October 2026. The Presidency of Colombia, the president’s executive office, says their records include homicide and eight aggravated thefts.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Abelardo de la Espriella (Colombia) Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Government made the matter public on Tuesday 3 November 2026. Miller Soto, the Presidency’s spokesman, said the three were found inside the residence, not outside it.

On Saturday 7 November, President Abelardo de la Espriella, a conservative lawyer who took office in August 2026, wrote on the social network X that anyone who messes with Ríos messes with the president. He added that no member of what he called “our pack” would be left alone or unprotected.

The president also said the denunciations must be investigated “to the last consequences”. He added that the Government will not allow threats, intimidation or fear to silence those who denounce corruption.

His message is aimed at anyone who might try to pressure an official who speaks out. For another recent presidential warning, see our report on his message to two San Andrés leaders.

Why Ríos Was Already in the News

On Wednesday 21 October 2026, a week before the entry, Ríos spoke in a debate of the Senate’s Second Committee, which deals with foreign affairs and defence. He alleged irregular service contracts tied to 48 women under the previous government of Gustavo Petro.

He also alleged an “instrumentalización de mujeres”, meaning a use of women. The allegations concern the previous government of Petro, the leftist former president.

What Is Not Known

Arrests are not confirmed, because official accounts say only that the three were identified and placed at the disposal of the authorities. No suspect has been named, and it is not known who the three people are or why they were there.

Authorities must still establish how they got in. The Attorney General’s office, Colombia’s national prosecutor, has opened a preliminary inquiry into the Dapre contracts, and we found no statement from it on the entry.

The Presidency has linked the entry to Ríos’s allegations and asked the authorities to establish whether the two are related. That link is unproven.

No link has been established between the entry and Ríos’s allegations in the Senate. Until investigators say otherwise, the two events should be read as separate.

In Plain English

Dapre handles the administration of the president’s office, so its director sits close to the centre of government. Protection authorities are the state bodies that guard senior officials and their homes.

“Instrumentalización de mujeres” is Ríos’s phrase for using women as tools, and it remains an allegation, not a court finding. The same is true of the contract claims.

What It Means for You

If you follow Colombia as an investor, traveller or policy watcher, the immediate lesson is about politics, not markets. A new conservative government is pressing corruption claims against its predecessor, and one of its senior officials has now been touched by a security incident.

Three things are worth watching: whether prosecutors confirm an investigation into the entry, whether the identities of the three people are released, and whether the Presidency produces evidence of a link. Until then, the president’s words are a statement of support, not evidence of what happened.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Carlos Ríos?

Carlos Ríos is the director of Dapre, the department that runs the president’s office and administration. He spoke in a Senate committee on 21 October 2026.

What did the Government say happened at his home?

It says protection authorities found three people with judicial records inside his home on 28 October 2026. It made this public on 3 November.

Were the three people arrested?

That is not confirmed, as official accounts say only that they were identified and placed at the disposal of the authorities. No suspect has been named.

Is the entry linked to his corruption allegations?

No link has been established. Authorities must still determine how the three got in and whether it relates to his allegations.

Sources: Presidency of Colombia and its spokesman Miller Soto, statements of 3 and 7 November 2026; Senate of Colombia, Second Committee debate of 21 October 2026.

World.title: Drones Hit Colombian Army Base, 3 Dead
World.content:
COLOMBIA · SECURITY

Key Facts What happened Drones with explosives hit an army base; the Army reports 3 soldiers dead and 8 wounded.

Where Santa Rosa del Sur, a gold-mining town in southern Bolívar, northern Colombia.

Who No group has claimed it and the Army names no suspect; some reports point to the ELN, a guerrilla group.

Why it matters Colombia works closely with the United States on security, and Washington lists the ELN as terrorist.

As of Saturday, 7 November 2026; all casualty counts are preliminary.

Explosive-laden drones hit an army base in northern Colombia on Saturday, and the Army reports three soldiers dead while the culprits remain unknown.

Drones carrying explosives struck an army base in northern Colombia around midday on Saturday, 7 November 2026. The Army says three soldiers died and eight were wounded.

The target was the Cantón Militar, an army base in Santa Rosa del Sur, a gold-mining town in southern Bolívar department. For readers in the United States, the strike matters because Colombia is one of Washington’s main security partners in South America.

What We Know

The Army’s First Division, a regional command, reported the attack on social media. It said unmanned aircraft fitted with explosives hit the base.

The division called the strike a serious violation of international humanitarian law and of human rights. It asked the public to pass on information through Colombia’s anti-terrorism hotline, Line 107.

The Army counts three soldiers dead and eight wounded, with other personnel also hurt. All counts are preliminary.

Reports put the wounded at 30 to 35, including a figure of 35 given by the town’s mayor, Milton Olaya. The Army has not confirmed those figures, and a military source called all counts preliminary.

President Abelardo de la Espriella condemned the attack. He ordered more operations to find those responsible.

His government has not yet said who it believes carried out the attack. No official attribution has been made, although some reports point to the ELN.

Colombian Army soldiers on duty beside a road near the Sisga reservoir in Cundinamarca. File photo: Petruss / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

In Plain English

The ELN is a Colombian left-wing guerrilla group that the United States designates a Foreign Terrorist Organization. The Clan del Golfo, also called the AGC, is a large drug-trafficking gang that operates in the same part of the country.

FARC dissident groups, armed factions that rejected the 2016 peace deal with the FARC, a former rebel army, are also present in southern Bolívar. The area is a gold-mining region, and all three groups operate there.

A Pattern of Attacks in Santa Rosa del Sur

This is not the first strike on soldiers in this municipality. On 7 October 2024, an explosives attack wounded nine soldiers in Santa Rosa del Sur.

In August 2025, an ELN drone attack in La Pradera, in the same municipality, killed one soldier and wounded seven. Four soldiers reported missing were later found alive.

In May 2026, drone attacks with explosives in rural Santa Rosa del Sur and Arenal del Sur killed one soldier and wounded four, according to the First Division. For another recent case of this tactic, see our report on drone bombs hitting a Colombian police station.

Our report on a security meeting over illegal gold mining in southern Bolívar gives more background. Several armed groups contest the area.

What Is Not Known

The biggest open question is who carried out the attack. No group has claimed it, and the Army has not named any suspect.

The number of drones and the exact time of the strike are not confirmed. The identities of the dead and the damage to the base are also unknown.

Colombia’s Defence Ministry has not yet given its own account in the reports we could confirm. The gap between the Army’s wounded count and the local figure of more than 30 has not been explained.

What It Means for You

For readers in the United States, Colombia has long worked closely with Washington on security. The ELN is on the US list of terrorist organisations.

Travellers and investors should note that southern Bolívar is a gold-mining region where several armed groups operate. Drones fitted with explosives have been used against troops there more than once since 2025.

The next signals to watch are an Army update on casualties and any claim of responsibility. The president has ordered more operations, and the Army says the damage is still being assessed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Santa Rosa del Sur?

Drones fitted with explosives hit the Cantón Militar army base around midday on Saturday, 7 November 2026. The Army reports three soldiers dead and eight wounded.

Who is responsible for the attack?

No suspect has been officially named, and no group has claimed the attack. Several armed groups, including the ELN, operate in the area, and some reports point to the ELN.

How many people were hurt?

The Army counts eight wounded, plus other personnel. Reports put the wounded at 30 to 35, but the Army has not confirmed that, and all figures are preliminary.

Why does this matter to Americans?

Colombia has long worked closely with Washington on security. The United States also designates the ELN a Foreign Terrorist Organization.

Sources: Colombian Army First Division (statement on X, 7 November 2026); Office of the President of Colombia (7 November 2026); US Department of State list of Foreign Terrorist Organizations.

World.title: Fire Chief Says Fernández Gave No Order on Ambulance Deal, but a Memo Cites Her
World.content:
The director of Costa Rica’s Fire Department, Héctor Chaves León, said last night that President Laura Fernández gave no instruction on how to buy 40 ambulances now under review by anticorruption prosecutors. Internal procurement documents, however, cite a presidential instruction as the basis for the emergency purchase.

The Fire Department, known here as the Cuerpo de Bomberos, awarded the contract on Sept. 28 to the SGSV-Bem Estar consortium for $13.88 million, about $347,000 per vehicle. It invited only that consortium to submit an offer, using Article 66 of the General Public Procurement Law, which allows exceptional contracting in emergencies.

The consortium joins SGSV Soluciones Tecnológicas Integradas with the Brazilian ambulance maker Bem Estar. Two people linked to SGSV, its legal representative and regional sales director and a company officer who has held that post since 2015, bought political debt bonds from Fernández’s Pueblo Soberano party during the presidential campaign. According to the Supreme Elections Tribunal (TSE), the purchases totaled 43 million colones and 9 million colones, or roughly $95,600 and $20,000.

The TSE has opened a preliminary administrative inquiry into the economic solvency of the two campaign financiers. The inquiry began on Sept. 17 and was expanded on Nov. 4. Separately, the Deputy Prosecutor’s Office for Probity, Transparency and Anticorruption (FAPTA) opened a case on its own initiative on Nov. 2 into alleged influence peddling against the public treasury. No one has been charged, and the investigation is at a preliminary stage.

At a press conference yesterday, Chaves said Fernández had not told the Fire Department which contracting method to use, how many ambulances to buy or which suppliers to consider. He said those were the institution’s own decisions and asked anyone claiming otherwise to produce written evidence such as emails or messages, adding that none exists.

Chaves acknowledged that the president asked in July for prehospital emergency care to be strengthened. He said it was the government’s Health Sector Council that later instructed the Fire Department to speed up the process.

A recommendation report addressed to Chaves and dated Sept. 25, three days before the award, states that the urgent purchase was carried out under the instruction of President Fernández and a July 31 agreement of the Health Sector Council. The report traces that reasoning to a Sept. 4 memo from the department’s Operations Directorate, and a Sept. 10 compliance report from its procurement office treats the presidential instruction as the trigger for the urgency.

Asked about the document, Chaves said it refers to the president’s general instruction to promote prehospital care in the country, not to the purchase method or the choice of suppliers. Two local suppliers that had submitted quotes during the department’s market study were not invited to bid. Comercializadora Técnica Industrial del Oeste (Cotisa) offered all 40 units for $11.57 million, or $2.31 million less than the winning price, while AutoStar Vehículos offered $13.74 million. The Fire Department rejected both, citing delivery times of 240 days as excessive.

Chaves said the speed of delivery was vital. He said the competing offers ranged from 240 to 280 days, while the Brazilian manufacturer proposed 100 days, and that he expects the units next March, whereas other purchasing routes could have pushed delivery into 2027 or 2028.

Under the contract, the supplier is to deliver one prototype first and the remaining 39 ambulances within 100 days of the department’s approval of that prototype. An inspection of the prototype at the factory in Brazil is scheduled for Nov. 19 and 20. The Fire Department has acknowledged that its own failure to specify the exact color code for its red fleet altered the contract schedule, and it approved an extension.

The tender required proof that the bidder had built at least 200 ambulances for five clients over the previous two years. Bem Estar submitted certificates for 210 units for two Brazilian clients. AutoStar asked for the procedure to be annulled over what it called serious defects, and the Fire Department rejected the request as untimely.

Chaves said the ambulances would be advanced life support units equipped with ultrasound, defibrillators and ventilators, assigned to the Southern Zone, Limón, Guanacaste, the Northern Zone and the Central Valley. He said the country handles about 50,000 accidents a year. He also said the Fire Department dealt only with the Brazilian manufacturer, which then sought out a Costa Rican partner to form the consortium.

Chaves said he had sent the full procurement file to the Prosecutor’s Office and to FAPTA, and that he is willing to cooperate with the Comptroller General’s Office. The file is public and can be consulted on the government’s SICOP procurement platform.

Gabriela Chacón, executive president of both the National Insurance Institute (INS) and the Fire Department, announced at Casa Presidencial on Oct. 7 that the 40 ambulances had been awarded and were expected to enter service in February 2027. On Nov. 2, she said she did not know the details of the procedure and attributed its approval to the department’s director or to its administration.

SGSV has won at least five public contracts since 2022, four of them through special procedures, and it was part of a consortium that bid in 2024 for the contract behind the digital marchamo vehicle sticker, a tender the INS later declared void. Opposition lawmaker Claudia Dobles of the Coalición Agenda Ciudadana described the links between the president’s campaign financiers and the winning consortium as vulgar and sharply questioned the process.

The contract remains in force while prosecutors and electoral authorities carry out their reviews and none of the people or companies involved has been accused of a crime.

World.title: Red Tide Spreads in Costa Rica’s Gulf of Nicoya and Cooking Won’t Make Shellfish Safe
World.content:
If you plan to order oysters, mussels or pianguas anywhere around the Gulf of Nicoya, ask where they came from first. Costa Rica’s National Animal Health Service (SENASA) has widened the zones where selling and eating these shellfish is banned because of a toxic red tide. The new restrictions cover shellfish harvested on the western shore of the gulf between Playa Blanca and Punta Curú.

They also cover the coastal strip from the mouth of the Jesús María River to the sugar dock at Punta Morales. This is not a new alert. Red tide restrictions have been in place in the gulf since June 12, according to researchers at the National University (UNA), and the restricted zones have grown as lab tests find toxins at new points.

SENASA based this latest expansion on the recommendation of an interagency commission that includes UNA’s Marine Phytoplankton Laboratory. The ban applies to bivalves, the two-shelled mollusks such as oysters, mussels and pianguas. They feed by filtering seawater, so when toxic algae bloom, the toxins build up in their flesh.

The hard part is that you cannot tell a contaminated shellfish from a safe one. UNA specialists say the toxins do not change how the shellfish look, smell or taste. Cooking does not destroy them either, so a well-cooked plate is no safer than a raw one. The algae involved can produce paralytic, diarrheic, amnesic and neurotoxic toxins, according to UNA. The species identified as the source of the paralytic toxins in the gulf is Pyrodinium bahamense.

SENASA has warned in earlier advisories that eating contaminated bivalves can cause anything from digestive problems to neurological effects and, in severe cases, death. If you feel tingling or numbness around your mouth, nausea or dizziness after eating shellfish, get medical care right away and tell the doctor what you ate.

UNA experts say the current event may be linked to El Niño. Warmer seas and a more layered, stratified water column can favor the growth of Pyrodinium bahamense. The species also has a dormant stage in seabed sediments that works like a bank of seeds. Those cysts need to be stirred back up by ocean processes tied to winds and tides before they germinate, and UNA says that part of the cycle still needs study.

The same warm-water conditions are already weighing on the gulf’s coastal communities, where El Niño has left fishermen with catches too small to pay for fuel. Until the restrictions lift, buy shellfish only from sellers who can tell you exactly where it was harvested. At restaurants and ceviche stands, ask about the source. If no one can give you a clear answer, skip the oysters, mussels and pianguas.

The measure covers bivalve mollusks only. Authorities continue to monitor the algal blooms and have redrawn the restricted zones each time new test results come in.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Grynspan Wins 12 of 15 Votes in Eighth UN Secretary-General Poll
World.content:
Former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan widened her lead in the race to become the next UN secretary-general on Thursday, winning 12 “encourage” votes from the 15-member Security Council in its eighth informal straw poll, according to leaked results reported by the UN-focused news site PassBlue.

Grynspan also received three “discourage” votes. In the seventh poll on Oct. 30, she had 11 “encourage” and four “discourage” votes, so Thursday’s result added one supporter and removed one objection. Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, stayed in second place with nine “encourage,” four “discourage” and two “no opinion” votes, unchanged from the previous round. Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett received eight, five and two, cutting her “discourage” count from six.

The newest entrant, Türkiye’s Feridun Sinirlioğlu, secretary general of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe and a former foreign minister, drew three “encourage,” eight “discourage” and four “no opinion” votes in his first poll. The United Arab Emirates’ Lana Nusseibeh received seven, six and two, according to the same tally.

Further back, Uganda’s Olara Otunnu received four “encourage” votes and Ecuador’s María Fernanda Espinosa three. Ivonne A-Baki, also from Ecuador, received one “encourage” vote against 14 “discourage.”

Council members again used ballots of the same color, which hides whether any “discourage” votes came from the five permanent members that hold a veto: the United States, China, Russia, France and the United Kingdom. PassBlue reported widespread speculation that the United States has consistently discouraged Grynspan and that Russia may have joined it this time.

The only color-coded poll so far, held Oct. 16, showed Grynspan, Grossi and Rodrigues Birkett each with two “discourage” votes from permanent members. An outside expert told PassBlue that China may be pushing to keep the polls undifferentiated to give the Latin American candidates more time to build support. To be recommended to the General Assembly, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favor in the Council and no veto from a permanent member. The 193-member General Assembly then makes the appointment.

Time is short since Secretary-General António Guterres’s second term ends Dec. 31 and the Council’s president for November, Latvian Ambassador Sanita Pavļuta-Deslandes, warned this week that the window to agree on a candidate is closing. No date has been set for the next straw poll, and it is not yet known whether it will be color-coded.

Sinirlioğlu was scheduled to hold a public dialogue with the General Assembly on Friday and an informal meeting with Council members on Monday. President Laura Fernández asked for support for Grynspan’s candidacy this week at the Ibero-American Summit in Madrid. Grynspan was Costa Rica’s second vice president from 1994 to 1998, led the Ibero-American General Secretariat from 2014 to 2021 and has headed UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) since 2021. Costa Rica formally nominated her on March 3.

If she is chosen, she would be the first woman to lead the United Nations since its founding in 1945, and the first Central American.

World.title: Five Costa Rica Regions on Yellow Alert as Saturday Rain Hits Soaked Ground
World.content:
If you live in or are traveling through the Central Valley, the Pacific coast or the Northern Zone, you are now under a yellow alert for rain. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) raised five regions from green to yellow yesterday, and the National Meteorological Institute (IMN) expects another wet day today on ground that can barely take more water.

The regions on yellow alert are the North Pacific, Central Pacific, South Pacific, Central Valley and Huetar Norte, which covers the Northern Zone. The Caribbean stays on green. That is a step up from yesterday morning, when the whole country was still on green alert even as the chance of a tropical depression was fading.

Why the upgrade? It comes down to soil. CNE president Alejandro Picado said the low-pressure system off the Pacific coast kept pushing showers and storms ashore from Thursday night. Soils on the Pacific slope are now 80% to 95% saturated, according to the commission. When the ground is that full, rain runs straight into rivers, ditches and drains instead of soaking in.

The numbers from Thursday night into yesterday show how fast it adds up. The IMN recorded 20 to 50 millimeters (0.8 to 2 inches) across Guanacaste and Puntarenas in 12 hours. Hojancha took 111 mm (4.4 inches) and Barú 56 mm (2.2 inches). Yesterday morning, local emergency crews handled incidents in San Carlos, Fraijanes, Poás, Alajuela and Sarapiquí, mostly overflowing sewers. The CNE said no one had to be evacuated.

For today, the IMN said the low near the Pacific coasts of northern Costa Rica and Nicaragua will keep the atmosphere unstable. Expect rain from early morning along the Pacific coast. In the afternoon, showers and thunderstorms spread to several regions, including the Caribbean and the Northern Zone. The Central Valley should get scattered rain, with occasional thunder in the east.

Guanacaste is the area to watch this weekend. The IMN warned that rain along the Pacific coast can come in bursts of 30 to 60 mm (1.2 to 2.4 inches) within six hours, especially in the North Pacific. Isolated gusts can reach 80 km/h (50 mph), which is enough to bring down branches, signs and power lines.

It will stay cool in the capital. The IMN forecast a high of 24.7 C (76 F) and a low of 18.5 C (65 F) in San José today. Liberia should reach about 33 C (91 F), and Quepos about 28 C (82 F).

The storm system itself is weakening. In yesterday’s outlook, the U.S. National Hurricane Center cut the odds of a tropical depression to 30% over both the next 48 hours and the next seven days. That is down from 40% on Thursday night and from the 60% chance it carried earlier in the week. The center said conditions will turn increasingly hostile over the weekend, but warned the system can still bring heavy rain to parts of Central America.

So what should you do? Plan outdoor time for the morning, when storms have been weaker. Never drive or walk through a flooded street, river or ravine, because you cannot judge depth or current until you are in it. On mountain roads, slow down for fog, fallen trees and small landslides, which are more likely when hillsides are this wet.

On the coast, the risk is on the water too. The CNE asked small fishing boats and tourism operators to watch sea conditions closely. That follows several days of rough surf on the Pacific beaches. If a boat tour or surf lesson is in your plans, ask the operator about conditions before you go.

Yellow alert means local emergency committees are active and ready to respond, not that a disaster is under way. Forecasts for systems like this can change quickly, so anyone with weekend plans should check the latest IMN update before heading out and call 911 in an emergency.

World.title: Costa Rica Removes Don Pepe Figueres Monument After Protest Vandalism
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Ministry of Culture and Youth removed the bronze monument to former President José Figueres Ferrer from San José’s Plaza de la Democracia on Friday morning, less than four weeks before the country marks the anniversary of the army abolition Figueres declared in 1948.

Culture Minister Jorge Rodríguez Vives ordered the temporary removal after the sculpture was defaced during demonstrations in recent weeks. A crew from the state power company CNFL lifted the figures by crane, and the pieces were taken to the National Museum’s José Fabio Góngora facility in Pavas, where specialists will clean and restore them.

Rodríguez described the decision as difficult but necessary to protect the ensemble from further damage. He acknowledged freedom of expression and peaceful protest as pillars of Costa Rican democracy but said exercising those rights cannot come at the expense of the nation’s heritage.

The minister said he expects those responsible to cover the cost of restoration, subject to the findings of the competent authorities, adding that damage to national heritage should not go without consequences. He also said the figures will not return to the plaza until there are guarantees they will not be vandalized again. The ministry characterized the removal as a temporary conservation measure, not a surrender of public space to vandalism.

The National Museum, which administers the plaza, has filed criminal complaints with the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) and the San José prosecutor’s office. According to the museum’s preliminary technical assessment, the latest incident left graffiti, spray paint and scratches on the bronze figures themselves, whereas damage in October mainly affected the monument’s base.

The museum has warned it cannot guarantee a full return to the sculpture’s original condition, because the paint penetrated surfaces already worn by age. Specialists expect the work to take several weeks. Rodríguez put the cost of the initial cleaning alone at about 1 million colones (roughly $2,000). The ministry said the total cost will be determined once its technical and economic assessment is complete, and it has not announced a date for the monument’s return.

The damage occurred during protests against budget cuts to public education and university funding. The most recent incident followed a student demonstration in the plaza on the night of Monday, Nov. 2. María Ortega Zamora, president of the student federation at the State Distance University (UNED), said four hooded people dressed in black arrived around 1 a.m. and began defacing the monument. She denied that students were responsible.

The removal drew a sharp response from the National Liberation Party (PLN), which Figueres founded in 1951. Álvaro Ramírez, head of the PLN’s legislative caucus, likened the move to a dictator’s playbook, writing on social media that it erased memory, disrespected history and removed symbols of the country’s democracy.

Ramírez argued that a nation’s historical memory cannot be treated as an obstacle and that defending it is part of defending democracy. He said the PLN will demand that the restored statues be returned to the Plaza de la Democracia as testimony to Costa Rica’s history.

The dispute adds to tensions between President Laura Fernández’s administration and opposition parties, including the PLN, as the education budget protests continue. The ensemble, by Costa Rican sculptor Marisel Jiménez Rittner, was unveiled on April 28, 1998. Its four bronze elements depict Figueres, a girl with a violin symbolizing culture, a boy with a book representing education, and a sledgehammer recalling the abolition of the army.

This is not the first time the monument has left the plaza. It was moved to the National Museum’s gardens in 2008 during a renovation of the square, and its original sledgehammer had been stolen. After restoration by museum specialists and the sculptor, it was reinstalled in December 2016, when the space was renamed Plaza de la Democracia y de la Abolición del Ejército.

The plaza sits beside the National Museum, the former Bellavista barracks where Figueres declared the army abolished on Dec. 1, 1948. Army Abolition Day commemorations have traditionally included a floral offering at the monument, and it remains unclear whether the figures will be back in place for this year’s ceremony.

Figueres, popularly known as Don Pepe, led Costa Rica three times and remains one of the defining figures of its modern history, closely tied to the institutions, social reforms and unarmed democracy that shaped the country’s identity.

World.title: A Proposed 15% Tax Would Reach Costa Rica Residents’ Foreign Dividends and Interest
World.content:
Costa Rica residents who earn interest, dividends, rent or capital gains outside the country would pay a 15% tax on that income under a bill the government has sent to the Legislative Assembly, a change tax specialists say would break with the country’s long-standing territorial tax system.

The bill, presented by the Finance Ministry on Sept. 22, would tax five types of passive income earned abroad by Costa Rican tax residents: interest, dividends, royalties, rent and capital gains. It would apply to individuals as well as companies, trusts, investment funds and other structures that are tax residents in Costa Rica.

The proposal sets no minimum threshold. Daniel Pelecano, director of tax and legal services at Grant Thornton, said that means small and large investors would be taxed on the same terms. Costa Rica has generally taxed income based on where it is generated rather than where the earner lives. A 2023 reform, Law 10.381, taxed some foreign passive income, but only for certain entities in multinational groups that failed to meet economic-substance requirements.

The new bill would repeal those limits and make tax residency the deciding factor for passive income. It keeps the territorial rule for active income, such as earnings from work or a business. In the bill’s statement of reasons, the Finance Ministry argues that the 2023 rules reached very few taxpayers. It also says residents receiving the same foreign dividends or interest are treated differently depending on whether they belong to a multinational group.

The ministry says the bill takes into account tax already paid or withheld abroad in order to avoid double taxation. Tax specialists say the mechanism works as a deduction rather than a direct credit, with the foreign tax subtracted from the income before Costa Rica applies its own rate.

Tax lawyer Gabriel Zamora Baudrit illustrated the effect with $100 in US dividends that have already had $30 withheld. Costa Rica would apply its 15% rate to the remaining $70, collecting $10.50 and bringing the combined tax burden to 40.5%. Under a direct credit capped at the Costa Rican amount, the $30 already paid would exceed Costa Rica’s $15 charge, leaving nothing more to pay. Zamora said the bill’s formula falls short of that standard and amounts to a new tax on residents’ foreign passive income, not simply a 15% rate.

Companies that already pay corporate income tax would follow a different route.
