World.title: Nine killed in road accident in southeastern Türkiye
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. At least nine people have been killed and five others injured in a road accident in Türkiye’s southeastern Van province.

According to the local administration, Van Governor Ozan Balci announced the casualties.

The accident occurred on Saturday, shortly after rainfall, on the Van–Ozalp highway, where a minibus collided with a truck.

"According to preliminary information, nine of our citizens lost their lives in the accident, five of them women. Another five people were injured and hospitalized," the governor said.

The circumstances and causes of the accident are under investigation.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Victory Day commemorated in Mexico (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. A commemorative event marking Azerbaijan’s Victory Day was held in Mexico on November 7, 2026.

The day symbolizes the end of nearly 30 years of occupation of Azerbaijani territories as a result of the 44-day Patriotic War, led by Supreme Commander-in-Chief, President Ilham Aliyev.

According to the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Mexico, the official ceremony took place at the Mexico-Azerbaijan Friendship Park, located on the historic Paseo de la Reforma, one of Mexico City’s most prominent avenues. The park features a monument depicting a map of Azerbaijan.

The event served as a symbol of the strength of the Azerbaijani people and national pride.

During the ceremony, the Symphony Orchestra of the Mexican Navy performed the national anthems of Azerbaijan and Mexico. A wreath was also laid at the monument depicting the map of Azerbaijan.

The event was attended by representatives of the Embassy of Azerbaijan in Mexico, members of the Azerbaijani diaspora, and representatives of the Mexican public.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev: The leader who achieved what no one else could
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. Azerbaijan is celebrating Victory Day. Six years ago, on November 8, 2020, Supreme Commander-in-Chief and President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev announced the liberation of Shusha.

Today, it is clear that Azerbaijan did not simply win a war. It brought to an end a conflict that had been considered insoluble for 30 years. As recently as 2019, Karabakh was cited as an example of a problem with no solution in sight – and seemingly no prospect of one in the future. President Ilham Aliyev, however, had a different view.

To understand the scale of this achievement, one need only look around the world. Cyprus has remained divided since 1974. The Annan Plan, on which the international community spent years of work, was rejected in a 2004 referendum, and the island has remained divided by a demarcation line ever since. Transnistria has been frozen in conflict since 1992, while Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region have remained unresolved since the early 1990s. The Minsk agreements on Donbas were intended to provide a diplomatic solution but proved to be little more than a pause before a major war. Serbia and Kosovo signed agreements in Brussels and Washington but have yet to establish normal relations. India and Pakistan have spent decades fighting over Kashmir, periodically exchanging strikes, with neither side able to secure victory or reach an agreement. Ethiopia and Eritrea signed a peace deal in 2018, for which Ethiopia's prime minister received the Nobel Peace Prize, yet the region was plunged into war again just two years later.

In all these cases, influential politicians, major powers, and respected mediators were involved. Some relied on negotiations, only to see them turn into an endless process without results. Others relied on force, which brought temporary gains that could not be consolidated. Almost no one managed to see the process through to the end.

The Karabakh conflict required solving three distinct challenges, each of which would, on its own, be considered a major achievement in a political career.

The first was military. It was not enough simply to win the war; it had to be won before the international community could intervene and prevent the achievement of its objectives. The 44 days of fighting in 2020 were the culmination of 17 years of preparation – in the military, economic and diplomatic spheres, as well as in relations with Türkiye, Russia, the West, and neighboring countries. The war began when Azerbaijan was ready for it and ended when its main objectives had been achieved. Knowing when to stop is a skill no less rare than knowing how to win.

The second challenge was bringing the conflict to a definitive end. After 2020, armed formations and a Russian peacekeeping contingent remained in Karabakh. Many believed at the time that this status quo would persist for years. The anti-terrorist measures in September 2023 lasted less than a day, and by spring 2024, the peacekeepers had left Azerbaijani territory. The country's sovereignty was fully restored, with no gray areas or "special arrangements" remaining.

The third challenge was diplomatic – and perhaps the most difficult. Military victory almost always creates the conditions for another conflict: the defeated side harbors resentment, seeks revenge, and waits for circumstances to change. This was the case with Germany after World War I and with dozens of other local conflicts that followed. Ilham Aliyev did what victorious leaders rarely do: he turned victory into a negotiating position, and that negotiating position into peace. On August 8, 2025, the leaders of Azerbaijan and Armenia signed a Joint Declaration at the White House in the presence of the US President, while the two countries' foreign ministers initialed a peace agreement. A year after the Washington meeting, there is no gunfire along the border, and discussions between Baku and Yerevan are focused on transport, trade, and reopening communications.

The main lesson of Karabakh is not that force solves everything. If that were true, many powerful countries would have resolved all their outstanding conflicts long ago. The lesson is that force works only when backed by a clear political objective and an understanding of what comes next.

From the outset, Ilham Aliyev said that Azerbaijan wanted neither someone else's land nor endless hostility. It wanted its own territory and peace on its own terms – in accordance with international law and the principle of territorial integrity. This position did not change during years of fruitless negotiations, throughout the war, or in its aftermath. That is precisely why victory did not turn into endless confrontation, and why peace does not look like a temporary ceasefire.

Speaking at the World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku in October, the President recalled that the Karabakh negotiation format had initially been structured not to resolve the conflict but to freeze it, and that major powers appeared to have accepted this approach. They made one mistake: they failed to take into account what the Azerbaijani people wanted and what the Azerbaijani state was determined to achieve.

Today, the world is going through perhaps its most difficult period since the Cold War. Conflicts that were considered manageable for decades are once again turning into open hostilities. Leaders are searching for formulas that would allow them to end wars without creating new ones. In almost every case, those formulas are proving elusive.

Against this backdrop, Azerbaijan's path stands out as an exception. In six years, the country has moved from war to the full restoration of its sovereignty, and from there to peace recognized in Washington, Brussels, Moscow, and Beijing. Many leaders have faced and continue to face similar challenges: occupied territories, fruitless negotiations, and indifference from international institutions. Many have tried to resolve them through force, while others have relied on diplomacy. Ilham Aliyev has proved to be one of the very few leaders capable of combining the two and seeing the process through to the end.

That is why November 8 is more than a day of remembrance and pride. It is a day to recall that no conflict is frozen forever. What is often lacking is the political will to unfreeze it and the wisdom to build peace afterward. President Ilham Aliyev has shown that both can come together in one leader.

Happy Victory Day!

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: November 8, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 8. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 43rd day of the Second Karabakh War:

- President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, victorious Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev addressed to the nation from the Alley of Martyrs on November 8 announcing that the city of Shusha was liberated from occupation.

- Supreme Commander-in-Chief Ilham Aliyev congratulated General Hikmat Mirzayev on victory.

- President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Alley of Honors and the Alley of Martyrs.

- President Ilham Aliyev received Turkish Foreign and National Defense Ministers.

- First Vice President Mehriban Aliyeva congratulated the people of Azerbaijan on the occasion of the liberation of Shusha on her official Instagram page.

- Armenian troops were forced to retreat, suffering losses.

- The list of Armenia's military equipment destroyed in one day has been announced.

- Armenia violates ceasefire on state border.

- Armenian troops fired on Tartar, Aghdam and Aghjabadi.

- A video of the liberated Balasoltanli village of Gubadli has been released.

- The Azerbaijani Army is increasing the advantage of the front in the direction of Khojavand.

- High-ranking Armenian officials were destroyed in the direction of Khojavand.

- A video of the liberated Tsakuri village of Khojavand has been released.

- Heavy blows were inflicted on the Armenian troops as a result of the operation carried out by the Azerbaijan Army in the Khojavand direction of the front.

- The Azerbaijani Army has full control over the city of Shusha.

- Video footage of the liberated Vejnali village of Zangilan region was released.

- A video has been spread of Armenian troops fleeing from the Khojavand direction of the front.

World.title: Controversial sale of Sydney's Victoria Barracks scrapped
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has vowed to keep Victoria Barracks in Sydney in public hands, following widespread backlash after plans for the heritage-listed site to be sold off.

The site and three others, including Victoria Barracks Melbourne, Fort Queenscliff and Point Cook (RAAF Williams), will be transferred from Defence to the Finance department.

Victoria Barracks in Sydney is one of the most high-profile of 67 Defence sites that were due to be sold after an independent estate audit in February this year, in a bid to generate $1.8 billion for the government.

The projected sale of the site, with it's 166-year history, spurred widespread backlash from all sides of the political spectrum, with the Coalition, Greens, teal independents and One Nation condemning the move.

Former prime minister John Howard, joining a recent protest against the sale, accused the government of "indifference to our proud national and military history".

Mr Albanese said the site was no longer for sale.

"Victoria Barracks Sydney has a special place in our nation's history — and we will be keeping it in public hands," Mr Albanese said.

"This program creates opportunities to open Defence's historic sites and buildings to the public, and to commemorate our nation's history."

Inside the battle over defence real estate A plan to sell defence sites around the country has become a political headache for the federal government.

Defence is the country's biggest landholder, with 70 major bases and 3.8 million hectares of land.

Defence Minister Richard Marles said personnel would be moved off the properties and they would be opened up to the public, adding that Defence sites needed to be "fit for purpose".

"Given the strategic landscape we face, we cannot afford to be wasting money," he said.

"We need to look at how we best use defence money for defence capability."

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the heritage of each of the sites was protected by law and public ownership would ensure they would be preserved for future generations.

Mr Albanese, Mr Marles and and Senator Gallagher are due to give an update about the Defence estate audit later today.

World.title: Council wants government to reject 'ugly, out-of-date' town centre plan
World.content:
A council in Melbourne's outer north has slammed an updated plan for a town centre next to a train station, with one councillor describing it as a "glorified drive-through".

There is already a shopping centre at the site next to the train station at the end of the Mernda line, and several river red gums.

The updated plan for the rest of the town centre at Mernda has been submitted through the Victorian government's development facilitation program, meaning it will bypass the council and go to the planning minister for approval after the November state election.

The City of Whittlesea will object to the plan, saying it is too car-dominated at the expense of a walkable town centre, and does not provide enough housing.

Part of the town centre site, as seen in council documents. (Supplied: City of Whittlesea)

The plan for the 24-hectare site on the corner of Plenty Road and Bridge Inn Road includes buildings of up to 10 storeys housing retail, public space and between 298 and 368 homes, including some affordable housing.

It also includes 628 street-level car parks.

"Mernda Town Centre will be a vibrant, mixed use, green and people-focused destination," the plan reads.

'A glorified car park'

The council disagreed, and said the plan was a significant change from the one it endorsed in 2009 and amended in 2018.

"The type of retail proposed is more akin to a homemaker centre which is more suitably located on the outer edge of a town centre, where car use is reliant," council officers said in a report to councillors.

At an unscheduled meeting, councillors voted to write to the state government, calling for the plan to be scrapped.

"Council's endorsed vision is for the site to become Mernda's primary retail and commercial town centre, with more homes, quality buildings, community facilities, attractive streets and safe walking routes for pedestrians," the City of Whittlesea said in a statement.

"The landowner's revised proposal moves significantly away from that vision."

Jarrod Lappin is unhappy with the number of car spaces. (Supplied: City of Whittlesea)

Councillor Jarrod Lappin described the plan as "isolated, car-centric, a glorified drive-through".

He said the retail aspect of the plan was particularly disappointing.

"It seeks big-box-style storage buildings which are spread out across the site, only broken up by rows and rows of car parks," he said.

Not enough housing

Cr Lappin said the plan for up to 368 homes was not enough, with council officers finding between 777 and 1,450 homes could fit on the site.

"It's uninspired, it's negligent and it's a dramatic under-utilisation of this central and important piece of land which is a shared asset for this community," he said.

"This plan … is only designed to turn a profit quickly."

Council officers noted the state government had a plan to increase density around transport hubs, like train stations.

"A proposal for less housing, in a location designated for higher housing density of housing is inconsistent with the intentions of Victoria's Housing Statement, state planning policy and risks directing more housing to less appropriate locations," officers found.

Expert says 'ugly' plan is 'from the 1950s'

RMIT Centre for Urban Research Professor Jago Dodson said he understood the council's concerns.

"Looking at the plan as it is currently proposed, a large area of the plan is surface car parking," he said.

Jago Dodson says the plan is outdated. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"It's effectively just producing a pretty ugly and inefficient suburban big box development next to a rail station, which is a real wasted opportunity."

He said town centres, especially in growth areas, were an important opportunity to set the community up for sustainable transport.

"If you have a town centre that's very car-dependent, then that will tend to drive, so to speak, people to use their cars to get there," he said.

Professor Dodson said communities deserved better.

"This is a type of development from the 1950s, we're in the late 2020s, we should be doing far better than this," he said.

"I really hope the professional planners who work in the state agencies have given some pretty clear advice to the minister that this is an out-of-date, retrograde development.

"It would be embarrassing, from my point of view, if professional planners were actively endorsing this kind of development."

A spokesperson for the government declined to comment on a planning application during the caretaker period.

In a statement, developer Dorman Capital rejected the council's characterisation of the project as "simply untrue".

Dorman Capital said council officers continued to refer to a development plan "dating back decades without any consideration to how their vision would be economically viable today".

Managing director Nicholas Dorman said the company had met with council officers for nearly two years and made a number of concessions, which had failed to satisfy council.

"We have never been afforded the opportunity to meet with Councillors and everything they were presented at their Unscheduled Council Meeting [on Thursday] rested mostly on the planning officer's interpretation of our proposal," Mr Dorman said.

"If we are forced to start again, Mernda may be waiting another two decades for a town centre."

The ABC contacted the opposition for comment, as well as the town planner, Tract.

World.title: The artist keeping Indigenous language alive on Aussie coins
World.content:
The next time you reach for a gold coin, artist Ryhia Dank hopes you'll discover something new about First Nations culture.

The Sunshine Coast-based Gudanji/Wakaja and Kalkadoon artist has illustrated a collection of $1 and $2 coins with six native animals and their names in language.

"I want the kids back home to pick up the coin and say, 'Oh, that's the crocodile that's floating down the river, or the brolgas that are dancing there'," Dank said.

Ryhia Dank chose "nardurna" to honour the matriarchal culture of her people. (Supplied: Ryhia Dank)

Dank — who creates under the name nardurna meaning "woman" — is from Borroloola in the Gulf of Carpentaria region in the Northern Territory.

She said the collection offered an opportunity to share the Gudanji language, and encourage others to learn about the Country on which they live.

However, her greatest hope is keeping the language alive.

"There aren't many speakers of the Gudanji language left, like a lot of languages all around Australia that are unfortunately dying down."

The collection includes six coins featuring animals native to Borroloola Country. (Facebook: Indigenous Literacy Foundation)

Keeping language alive

Animals shown on the coins: Marraji, the red kangaroo

Jagurrugurru, the emu

Mardumbarrayi, the saltwater crocodile

Darrmanji, the brolga

Gulamandarrina, the long-necked turtle

Jurrgubadi, the goanna Source: Royal Australian Mint

First Languages Australia, the peak body for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island language communities, said of the more than 700 documented, unique languages, fewer than 100 were used today in "everyday context".

Senior program officer Ella Woods said language revitalisation must be led by the communities who own and speak the languages, alongside governments and institutions.

"Being able to have language custodians involved in those processes is really essential".

Ella Woods is a Yugambeh woman working to support communities across Australia to strengthen their languages. (Supplied: First Languages Australia)

She said storytelling and art played an important role in strengthening languages.

"It's a beautiful way for not only communities to be able to reconnect … but also for non-Indigenous people to be able to see those languages represented through artwork and song and dance and storytelling."

University of Queensland linguistics professor Felicity Meakins said that visibility played an important role in encouraging younger generations to learn and use the traditional language.

Professor Felicity Meakins's work focuses on Indigenous languages, language contact and revitalisation. (Supplied: Felicity Meakins)

" You can't be what you can't see. "

She pointed to examples such as the translation of Bluey into Yolŋu Matha and children's books written in Gurindji.

"It's extremely important for those young lives because they're seeing that their language is important, their culture is important, and this has a really huge influence on their feeling of wellbeing."

Professor Meakins said initiatives that brought First Nations languages into everyday spaces, including currency, also played an important role.

"Because [coins are] such an everyday thing that all of us use, means that those languages have a public space that they wouldn't necessarily have."

Bringing Country to currency

The Our Animals, Our Country coins were released as a collection this week with some $2 coins already in circulation.

The gold coins might only be worth $1 or $2, but the stories engraved carry generations of culture, identity and knowledge. (Supplied: Indigenous Literacy Foundation)

The project was a collaboration of the Australian Mint, Australia Post and the Indigenous Literacy Foundation (ILF), of which Ms Dank is an ambassador.

For almost 20 years, the foundation has supported literacy in remote communities, donating more than 150,000 books to approximately 508 communities.

"It's an amazing opportunity for us just to focus on language — the power of it, the visual storytelling that goes with the written word and to have this celebrated across the country on a coin is incredible for us," chief executive Ben Bowen said.

Wiradjuri man Ben Bowen says the Indigenous Literacy Foundation has published 31 books featuring up to 50 different languages to help children connect with their languages. (Supplied: Indigenous Literacy Foundation)

Mr Bowen said while a disconnect between Elders and youth could create barriers to passing language down, the artwork and language on the coins could help to change that.

"I think this is a beautiful way for us to start conversations and spark that curiosity and all be willing to learn more," he said.

A connection to home

Reflecting on her Northern Territory mob nearly 3,000 kilometres away from the Sunshine Coast, Dank became emotional as she recalled loved ones — living and passed — who had inspired her work.

"I wanted to make sure that these animals were relatable for my family back home and community."

And she's looking forward to sharing the coins with her grandmother when she's next back home.

"Like most grannies, mine loves playing cards, so I'll be taking a few for her to play with and she can see her animals on there."

World.title: Moesha Johnson's Open Water World Cup winning streak continues
World.content:
The Cancún leg of the Open Water Swimming World Cup may have been the start of a new season.

But for dominant Australian Moesha Johnson, absolutely nothing changed.

Following a stunning 2025/26 season in which Johnson won every single open water event she entered, the 29-year-old started the 2026/27 campaign with yet another double gold medal-winning weekend in Mexico, underlining a dominance rarely seen in top level international sport.

In Friday's 10km race, Johnson set out her stall early by claiming the $US1,000 ($1,455) bonus for winning the sprint lap, before easing up.

"After the sprint lap the goal was just to drop back and relax," Johnson told World Aquatics.

"I haven't got the big endurance work behind me for this season so far, so my endurance strength isn't quite there.

"I really wanted to practice my open water skills, get in the pack, just play around a little bit."

After recovering amidst the melee of the main group, Johnson made her way back to the front and powered to victory, finishing in a time of 2 hours, 3 minutes and 31 seconds, 13 seconds ahead of Japan’s Airi Ebina and Italy’s Ginevra Taddeucci.

St Peter's Western swimmer and World Cup debutant, 22-year-old Jacqueline Davison-McGovern, finished in seventh place.

After her success in the 10km, Johnson backed up to win a second gold medal in the 3km elimination race.

Johnson won the 1,500m heat, the 1,000m semifinal and the 500m final dash to make it two-from-two to start the year.

"For me this was a bit more of a closure to 2026 rather than a start to the new season," Johnson said after the 10km.

"We haven't had our normal preparation so I didn't know where I was at, but today I gave myself every opportunity to finish 2026 as my year on top.

"I know people might have come to expect [winning] from me, but it's not that easy to be on top every single race.

"It's really stressful and it takes a lot of work, and it's something that I'm really proud of now.

"Hopefully, the increasing standard keeps lifting the professionalism of our sport and the girls around us and it's just as entertaining as ever."

World.title: Youth crime policy rejig, UFC return among Victorian party pledges
World.content:
Low and mid-level youth offenders would be sentenced to age-targeted rehabilitation detention if Victoria's Labor government is re-elected this month.

The $200 million program would see young offenders removed from the community for up to 12 months and be held around-the-clock in a secure residential youth justice facility.

Minister for Crime Prevention Paul Edbrooke singled out Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre as a destination for offenders, a controversial facility re-opened by the Allan government earlier this year.

Paul Edbrooke said reforming the use of Malmsbury Youth Justice Centre would be a key part of Labor's new youth crime policy. (ABC News)

He said jail time in youth detention already existed for serious youth crime, but there was no strong option for lower-level offending.

"It provides that tougher new option that isn't jail but keeps them off the streets," Mr Edbrooke said.

"It puts structure in their lives; Going to school, getting a trade or a skill.

"It gives them a chance to turn their lives around and stop them going down the wrong path."

In October 2025, Corrections Minister Enver Erdogan said the decision to reopen Malmsbury came amid a 46 per cent rise in remand rates following bail reform in March.

Initially 30 beds of the more than 100-bed facility were made available under the re-opening plan at an operating cost of more than $141 million over five years.

Mr Edbrooke said rehabilitation shouldn't be a choice.

"We've had parents ask for this. They know that kids at risk of reoffending won't get better on the streets," he said.

"We're looking at the program being able to treat up to nearly 500 kids over two years with capacity to be scaled up over time."

UFC to return to Melbourne under Liberal government

Meanwhile the Victorian opposition is today focusing on major events.

If elected later this month, it pledges to establish a $40 million Major Events Attraction Fund to bring big sporting and entertainment events to Melbourne.

Among those events is the UFC — the ultimate fighting championship.

The pledge includes working with global sporting powerhouse TKO which also manages the WWE and Zuffa Boxing.

Liberal leader Jess Wilson said hosting the events would help boost the economy by supporting small business and creating more jobs.

"This isn't just about putting on a great show," she said.

"It's about filling our hotels, packing our pubs, supporting small businesses and creating more jobs for Victorians.

"Melbourne is the sporting capital of the world, and under my government, we're going to make sure it stays that way."

Shadow Minister for Major Events and Tourism David Southwick said if the Liberal Party formed government, UFC could be in Melbourne as early as next year.

"Our plan is to potentially bring all three codes [UFC, WWE and Zuffa boxing] to Melbourne over four years," he said.

"That would be the first time ever Australia would be able to host three different codes in Victoria."

He said it would bring close to $300 million into Victoria's economy.

"It really is the economic driver that underpins all of this. The jobs, the visitation to Melbourne and to Victoria," Mr Southwick said.

"These have huge viewerships. We could have a billion homes all around the world in 60 different languages broadcasting from Melbourne being able to showcase Melbourne to the rest of the world."

One Nation federal leader Pauline Hanson campaigning in Swan Hill on Saturday. (ABC News)

Meanwhile, federal leader of One Nation, Pauline Hanson, hit the campaign trail in Swan Hill as part of the minor party's push to win the National Party-held seat Murray Plains.

The electorate and its predecessor constituency was held for more than two decades by former National Party state leader Peter Walsh, who is retiring at the state election.

World.title: Guns, traps and baits to target 'ballistic' NSW feral pig problem
World.content:
From the front line of the feral pig fight, Walgett farmer Enid Coupe's assessment is blunt: "They've just gone ballistic. There are just pigs everywhere.

"The pigs are killing lambs, they're destroying waterholes, spreading disease … and absolutely [causing] hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of damage."

According to the National Feral Pig Action Plan's latest report, the pests cost Australian agriculture more than $190 million annually, with Queensland and New South Wales suffering the biggest losses.

Enid Coupe says exploding feral pig numbers are causing widespread damage to crops, livestock and land. (ABC News: Brigitte Murphy)

Ms Coupe said recent favourable seasons had fuelled a pig population boom, creating a problem that could no longer be tackled by individual landholders alone.

NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty believes a new program across 600,000-hectares in the Walgett Shire, in north-west NSW, will help tackle the problem.

It brings together 120 landholders as well as state government land managers, who will use baiting, trapping and aerial culling to reduce feral pig numbers across five priority management areas.

Ms Moriarty said consultation with local farmers and community leaders had been central to developing the plans, which are rolling out this month.

"We want local buy-in, we want local people to be running this program with the support of the New South Wales government," she said.

She said feral pigs remained a significant biosecurity challenge across the state.

"We've taken out 1.1 million feral pigs since we've been in government," Ms Moriarty said.

"I don't say that as a point to say, 'Wow, look how much we've done.' I say that to give people a sense of the problem that we have in New South Wales."

One in, all in

The minister said the key to the program's success was all landholders being good neighbours.

"Pigs don't stop at the fence line … and we all have a responsibility to be tackling this issue," she said.

Ms Coupe welcomed the new coordinated approach and said landholders who failed to manage pests contributed to the growing problem.

"This trial of Walgett, where we're going to be under the LLS hammer and looked at and we have to do our bit, I think is excellent," she said.

"Because farmers who aren't doing their share are the reason why we've got such a big problem."

Ms Moriarty said the program was focused on cooperation rather than punishment, but warned compliance powers remained available for landholders who refused to meet their obligations under the Biosecurity Act 2015.

Penalties of up to $220,000 for individuals and $440,000 for corporations can be applied.

"If people refuse, if they don't get involved, it's not fair to the people who are doing it, it's not fair to taxpayers," she said.

The minister said the state government had committed $60 million to pest animal management over three years, including $16.3 million this financial year, with a significant portion of that funding supporting the Walgett program.

Tara Moriarty says a new feral pig control pilot near Walgett will bring together landholders and public land managers. (ABC News: Alexander Lewis)

Coordinated control key to reducing numbers

Ms Moriarty said success would be measured through environmental, agricultural and productivity outcomes, rather than simply the number of pigs removed.

North West Local Land Services invasive species team leader Peter Dawson said tens of thousands of pigs are now estimated across the Walgett Shire alone

"Coming off the back of the previous drought, we saw numbers basically explode," he said.

A Local Land Services staff member puts grain in a trap to lure feral pigs. (ABC News: Juno Robertson)

Mr Dawson said the pilot would focus on five priority management areas in the Walgett local government area using a coordinated and integrated approach.

He said the program aimed to bring together landholders, National Parks, Crown Lands and other land managers, who had often been conducting pest control independently.

"If we're not communicating, we can't coordinate," he said.

He said baiting, trapping, ground shooting and aerial culling would all be needed to reduce pig numbers.

"There's no one silver bullet here for anything," he said.

Peter Dawson says coordinated action across 600,000 hectares is critical to reducing record feral pig numbers. (ABC News: Juno Robertson)

That sentiment echoed by the National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS).

Northern Inland branch director John Whittall said NPWS was responsible for about 65,000 hectares, or a little over 10 per cent of the 600,000-hectare trial area.

While some landholders have criticised public land managers in the past, Mr Whittall said National Parks had maintained ongoing feral pig control programs.

"Over the past 18 months for example, at Narran Lakes, which is in Walgett [LGA], we've controlled about 4,000 pigs," he said.

"We know that feral pigs that just don't stay in the one place ... move around and can reproduce quite quickly.

World.title: This was once a favourite swimming spot, but locals fear it may never return
World.content:
David Godfrey-Smith longs for the day when the ankle-deep puddle near his doorstep returns to the brilliant blue lagoon where he once learned to swim.

But he fears that day may never come if a recent application to extract millions of litres upstream is approved.

Henderson Lagoon, at Falmouth on Tasmania's east coast, was once a haven for paddling, kayaking and family holidays.

But the lagoon, which is fed by a series of inland streams and intermittently opens to the ocean, has become a trickle.

The region has experienced very low rainfall this year — with a nearby weather station at Fingal receiving just 10mm in September, 10.2mm in August and 18.2mm in July.

David Godfrey-Smith believes the Falmouth community would help fund a water management plan for the area. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Another weather station at St Helens received 5mm in September, 25.2mm in August and 36.4mm in July, according to Bureau of Meteorology data.

But Mr Godfrey-Smith, along with other locals like Michael Di Giovanni, suspects poor water regulation is partly to blame and further extraction could be devastating.

"I think that the way the system is at the moment, there are a few that might say it may never recover," Mr Di Giovanni said.

" But if this [water allocation] is approved, it almost definitely won't recover. "

Falmouth resident Michael DiGiovanni worries the lagoon will never recover if more water is extracted upstream. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

The recent application to vary an existing water licence to take an additional 360 million litres from Ferntree Glen Creek, upstream of Henderson Lagoon, was lodged by Cooltrans Pty Ltd, which is directed by a nearby farmer.

Data on LISTMap shows Cooltrans has a number of current licences to draw irrigation water from two other creeks and another unnamed tributary, which feed the lagoon.

Cooltrans declined to comment.

Mr Godfrey-Smith said many locals wrote submissions against the current application, which is currently being assessed by the Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE).

He said he hoped that assessment was based on current data that accounted for recent climatic and land use changes, and considered impacts to environmental flows.

He said a group of concerned residents were even considering putting up around $50,000 of their own money to fund a water management plan for the area, despite that being a state government responsibility.

Locals are concerned about the future of Henderson Lagoon, on Tasmania's east coast. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Call for more water management plans

Henderson Lagoon is among many catchments in Tasmania without a formal water management plan.

These plans are legally binding documents that can set catchment-specific rules for allocating and managing water.

But NRE's website lists only 11 formally adopted plans in the state, some of which are due for review.

Some locals say Henderson Lagoon used to be turquoise-blue. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Environment Tasmania's freshwater campaigner Lucy Tremain said the plans provided targeted environmental protections, which she said were particularly important as demand for rural water intensified.

She believed this was partly driven by a Tasmanian Government commitment to increase the value of its agricultural sector to $10 billion by 2050.

"If we're looking to increase agriculture ... [water management plans] are a key piece of infrastructure that needs to be rolled out broadly across the state," Ms Tremain said.

Todd Dudley is concerned about the future of Henderson Lagoon. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Todd Dudley, president of the North East Bioregional Network, said the recent low rainfall and climate change should prompt the state to take a more precautionary approach to allocating water.

"But the government's going in the opposite direction," he said.

TasFarmers chief operating officer Neil Grose, however, said NRE had been "very active" in managing stressed catchments, particularly those on the east coast which had been dry for years.

"Certainly the discussions we have had with NRE, even in recent weeks, have been very precautionary," he said.

" They're very cautious around allocating water. "

TasFarmers chief operaring officer Neil Grose says no farmer wants to see the environment degraded through agricultural practices. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

He also said the idea that water was being prioritised for agriculture, rather than the environment, was a "misconception".

"There wouldn't be many farmers who would say it's too easy to get extra water," he said.

"It is a rigorous process, as it should be."

State Water Minister Gavin Pearce was contacted for comment.

Henderson Lagoon pictured with blue water in 2024. (Supplied)

An NRE spokesperson said Tasmania’s irrigated agriculture sector has grown over recent decades, supported by private investment, irrigation scheme development and the state's rural water strategy.

While they said water demand had generally grown as well, they said actual annual water use varies according to seasonal conditions, commodity markets and water availability.

It said all water licence applications were assessed under the Water Management Act 1999, with consideration given to water availability, environmental impacts, other water users and community submissions received as part of the assessment process.

Community could fund plan

Mr Godfrey-Smith said if the state did not produce a water management plan for the area, the community would do it.

Falmouth resident David Godfrey-Smith would love to see Henderson Lagoon restored. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

He estimated it would cost community members around $50,000 and require commitments from all stakeholders.

"This is an environmental jewel here, and the state government should be helping the community look after it," he said.

"But if push comes to shove, we'll do the study ourselves."

The NRE spokesperson said it supports community involvement in water management planning.

Locals say Henderson Lagoon would often link to the ocean, as it does in this picture taken in 2024. (Supplied)

Concern for future generations

David Cannon has lived in Falmouth for 47 years and worked for decades as a commercial fisherman, often leaving his six-metre dinghy in Henderson Lagoon overnight.

He said the lagoon used to flow through to the ocean much of the time, but for the last two years it has been virtually landlocked.

Henderson Lagoon was a long way from reaching the ocean. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

While machinery is at times used to open the lagoon to the ocean — which the ABC understands is often to prevent saltwater intrusion on private land — Mr Cannon worries this may also have a detrimental impact.

NRE said the practice was managed through an established protocol, which included specific water level triggers, and was designed to balance environmental health with public safety, infrastructure protection and the risk of inundation to surrounding properties.

But Mr Godfrey-Smith said this protocol should be reinvestigated and updated, as part of a new water management plan.

Some locals dispute the use of machinery to open Henderson Lagoon to the ocean. (Supplied)

He worries that without stricter management, future generations will never experience the region at its best.

"I learned to swim here, my kids learned to swim here," he said.

"It'd be really nice if their kids, our grandchildren, could learn to swim here too.

World.title: Wet-weather chaos in qualifying for Brazilian Grand Prix
World.content:
Oscar Piastri will start the F1 São Paulo Grand Prix from 10th place on the grid after a chaotic wet-weather qualifying session at Interlagos.

The Australian only jumped into the top 10 due to grid place penalties meted out to his rivals, however, in a wet and wild session that was twice red-flagged, and delayed by 80 minutes as torrential rain teemed down on the circuit.

Piastri was only 12th fastest in the tricky conditions, missing out on Q3.

For the third year in a row, Piastri's McLaren teammate Lando Norris will start on pole.

"It's been a long day," Norris said.

"To be on pole here two years in a row… Different conditions to last year, but I am very happy.

"It was about getting two laps in, not making any mistakes and yeah, it has been a very good day.

"This was my first time driving the car in the wet, but I think I figured it out."

The entire grid dealt with atrocious conditions. (Getty Images: Clive Mason)

George Russell, who fumed at his team for telling him to back off during a flying lap, qualified second, but will start seventh after taking a five-place grid place penalty for a power unit change.

That puts world champion Kimi Antonelli on the front row of the grid after he qualified third.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was fourth fastest but has a 10-place grid drop, promoting Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson to third, with Audi's Nico Hulkenberg fourth.

Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, Oliver Bearman, Fernando Alonso and Alex Albon all made up the rest of the top 10 on track.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton will start from the back row of the grid after both veterans took grid-place penalties.

However, with wet weather forecast for race day, both men will back themselves to make their way through the firled to the front places.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the F1 São Paulo Grand Prix on Monday morning, with lights out at 4am AEDT.

What happened to Oscar Piastri?

Piastri was struggling on the wet-weather tyres and was delayed in changing to intermediates as the track dried during a brief window in the weather.

Then, once he changed to the correct tyres, a crash to debutant Rafael Camara meant that Q2 was brought to a premature end.

That left the Australian in 12th place and unable to participate in the final phase of qualifying.

World.title: PM backtracks on historic Defence properties sale
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsVictoriaDefence PM backtracks on historic Defence properties sale James Costa Updated November 8, 2026 — 9:27am ,first published 8:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The federal government has backed down on its decision to sell off historic Defence properties, including the Victoria Barracks in Melbourne, which together would have raised $3 billion for the Defence Department. The sale of the heritage properties, including the Victoria Barracks in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, was met with sharp backlash from Returned and Services League branches and former prime minister Paul Keating, when the government announced in February that it planned to fully or partially sell 67 defence sites for an estimated $3 billion – or $1.8 billion after costs. The heritage-listed Victoria Barracks in St Kilda Road. Penny Stephens The Victoria Barracks site in Southbank – across the road from the Shrine of Remembrance – along with Fort Queenscliff on the Bellarine Peninsula and the RAAF base in Point Cook will be spared from the sale. The sites will remain publicly owned, with the government opening them up to public access.



“This program creates opportunities to open Defence’s historic sites and buildings to the public, and to commemorate our nation’s history,” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement. In a statement, Defence Minister Richard Marles said the government could not “afford to be wasting money”. “It is more important now than ever that we have a Defence Force which is focused on keeping Australians safe, and that involves a fit-for-purpose defence estate. “By moving personnel off these sites, and working to open them up for the public, we are ensuring that the history of Victoria Barracks is one that can be protected and returned to all Australians.”



Related Article Defence Marles wants Defence out of $3 billion sites ‘as soon as possible’ Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher will hold a press conference in Sydney on Sunday afternoon to announce the backtrack and next steps for the 63 other Defence sites that will be divested. In September, The Age reported that Marles insisted he would not back down from selling defence properties, labelling one of the locations “the oldest wine cellar in Sydney”. “It matters that we have a government which is willing to make difficult decisions,” he told reporters at the time. “Let’s be clear about Victoria Barracks Sydney. Most members of the army have never been to Victoria Barracks Sydney. Victoria Barracks Sydney is effectively off limits to the people of Sydney and the people of Australia.”

World.title: The real-life couple behind the movie everyone is talking about
World.content:
If Wicker has something real to say about relationships, thank its husband-wife creators.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Wicker has been generating all sorts of buzz for its funny, sexy and decidedly kooky take on marital and sexual relations. So it’s perhaps little wonder that the people behind it, writer-directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, are themselves a couple. “I’ll give you Alex’s biographical information and he can give you mine,” volunteers Wilson. Loading “Eleanor lived in Melbourne and then came to New York to study,” begins Fischer. “From Adelaide,” she interjects. “Then London, then Melbourne, then to New York, to study at the Actors’ Playhouse,” the American Fischer resumes.



“The Neighbourhood Playhouse,” she corrects. She pauses briefly, then adds: “I’ll tell you my stuff.” “It’s like The Dating Game,” he says, referring to the 1960s TV show. Related Article Cinema Total basket case: How Alexander Skarsgård became the perfect husband in Wicker “I know,” she says, laughing. “The price is not right, Alex.” It’s rather endearing that they aren’t in total sync. It helps explain why Wicker – a feminist fable set in a vaguely medieval England, about a woman who conjures the ideal husband, who just happens to look like a basket – is so astute in its clear-eyed skewering of relationship dynamics. The movie was a popular choice to open the Melbourne International Film Festival in August, but the chatter has really picked up in the last few weeks, with thirst memes about a willowy Alexander Skarsgård and think pieces and an entirely understandable fascination with the mechanics of making love with a man of wood. Something Wicker this way comes … but what of the couple behind it?



Married writer-directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer on the set of their film Wicker with Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman and Elizabeth Debicki as the Tailor’s Wife. Roadshow The pair met in New York in late 2015, and almost immediately decided to try working together. “Eleanor was like, ‘I have this movie idea, what do you think?’,” says Fischer. “She asked if we would write together, and I thought that would be fun, and then we did.” “And then we kept doing it,” she says. “Now we’re married, we have a kid [aged four], we have two movies.” They work alone and with other people, too. “But most things we write together,” says Wilson. Do you always agree? Did you bicker over Wicker? “Writing with somebody is way more fun than writing alone,” says Fischer. “Writing alone can be torture.” “We enjoy making each other laugh and trying to impress each other, so it tends to make the work better because we’ve got an immediate audience we have to show our work to,” Wilson says. “You’re always thinking, ‘is this going to be funny?’ At least that’s how we wrote Wicker. We were mostly focused on making each other laugh throughout that process.”



Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer at the LA premiere of their movie last month. AP Photo/Jordan Strauss The film is adapted from a short story, The Wicker Husband, written by Ursula Wills. While the essential elements were all there in the 14-page source material, “there was not a tonne of character specificity, and it was very scant in dialogue, which is an incredible gift to people who love writing dialogue and love digging into character,” Wilson says. “So we really pulled apart the village and the couples and tried to figure out exactly what each couple’s thing was, and dived into that.” They didn’t divide the characters by gender. It was more a case of each taking the bit they felt inspired to work on that particular day. “It’s sometimes a little more fun to write in the other gender’s voice and put yourself in that mindset,” observes Wilson. Fischer wrote some “brilliant” stuff for the Tailor’s Wife, the bitter, judgmental and ultimately envious character played by Elizabeth Debicki. “And the Baker Man [who asks the Wicker husband to sleep with his own wife because he feels incapable of satisfying her needs] just poured out of me.” Was any of the stuff in the film drawn from your own lives or experiences? “Probably, but I couldn’t tell you,” says Fischer. “I think it’s drawn from our psyches,” says Wilson. “I think it’s all in there somewhere. I think a lot about the Tailor’s Wife. I’ve always felt very close to her, even though she’s obviously not the best character in the movie. There’s something about her that I feel is justified, a deep-rooted anger that I had that needed to be resolved in a character in that way.”



Loading Anger about what? “Domestic labour, the mental load, for sure.” For independent filmmakers with just one prior feature to their name – the comedy Save Yourselves!, in which a couple on a retreat completely miss the fact that the planet has been invaded by aliens; released in 2020, COVID killed it at the box office, but made its theme of isolation seem eerily prescient – Wilson and Fischer have had a dream run with Wicker. And much of that, they readily acknowledge, is down to its female lead. From the outset, they’d had Olivia Colman in mind as the Fisherwoman, a stoic and lusty outsider who dares to ask for what she wants, and gets it. But, says Fischer, “we were told she probably won’t read this, she’s probably not going to do it, just go to somebody who’s more likely.” “But we just gave it a shot anyway,” says Wilson, “and we’re very lucky that she happens to be the kind of person who reads scripts and follows her heart…”

World.title: Six killed after gunman opens fire on tourist hotspot in Krakow
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropePoland Six killed after gunman opens fire on tourist hotspot in Krakow Updated November 8, 2026 — 8:28am ,first published 3:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Polish man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow on Saturday and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him, authorities said. The attack, which Poland’s defence minister described as an “act of terror,” happened in Main Square, which is in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town and is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city. Emergency workers at the scene of the deadly shooting. Getty Images The 25-year-old attacker drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each stop with an automatic weapon, authorities said. Although they didn’t release his name, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man holds “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views. “Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” Kierwiński said at a news conference.



Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said drone footage appeared to show three bodies inside the home of the man behind the mass shooting. He said the two women and one man appear to be close members of the gunman’s family. Sixteen people were injured in the attack, including the suspect, two police officers and five foreign nationals. It’s unclear how many of the injured were shot. Two of them were treated and released within hours of the mass shooting. Police lock down market square in Krakow. AP The attacker wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, and used a military-type long gun, Krakow police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said. Police found many other weapons and ammunition in his car. He kept firing at the police even after being shot himself, she said.



The attacker engaged in a “wild ride” around Main Square, which is why people were wounded at several locations, Cisło said. Cisło added that the gunman acted alone and that the public is safe. Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy. “The square will belong to us again,” Gibała said in a video posted to X. Emergency services respond to the attack. Getty Images



A shattered shop window after the shooting. Getty Images Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. It was not immediately clear whether the firearm used in Saturday’s attack, or the guns found in the perpetrator’s car, were legal. Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising. Images from the scene showed police officers and ambulances covering the area, which is in the centre of Krakow. A Polish Medical Air Rescue helicopter also landed in the square. Krakow is the second-largest city in Poland and roughly 250 kilometres from the capital, Warsaw. Around 15 million tourists visit Krakow annually, the majority passing through the Main Square.

World.title: Victoria Barracks sale abandoned following backlash
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalDefence Victoria Barracks sale abandoned following backlash Eryk Bagshaw November 8, 2026 — 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Albanese government has bowed to public pressure and abandoned the sale of Victoria Barracks, removing its most high-profile defence asset from its attempt to claw back $3 billion in taxpayer money. The decision, announced on Sunday, means the 186-year-old Victoria Barracks in Paddington will remain in government hands. The main building at Victoria Barracks was designed to accommodate hundreds of soldiers. Wolter Peeters The colonial-era sandstone headquarters will not be sold, but it will also no longer be used as an active Australian Defence Force facility. Instead, it will be opened to the public.



“Victoria Barracks Sydney has a special place in our nation’s history – and we will be keeping it in public hands,” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement. “This program creates opportunities to open Defence’s historic sites and buildings to the public, and to commemorate our nation’s history.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, alongside Defence Minister Richard Marles with Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen. Alex Ellinghausen Defence Minister Richard Marles had until September maintained that Victoria Barracks would be sold, describing it as “the oldest wine cellar in Sydney,” used by only a section of the military elite. The comments provoked a backlash from supporters of the site and galvanised the Save Victoria Barracks Alliance. An unlikely coalition of veterans’ groups, former prime ministers Paul Keating, John Howard and Tony Abbott, Premier Chris Minns and federal, state and local politicians all spoke out against the sale of the site.



The Daily Telegraph, which first reported the Albanese government’s backflip on Sunday morning, also campaigned heavily against the sale. “By moving personnel off these sites, and working to open them up for the public, we are ensuring that the history of Victoria Barracks is one that can be protected and returned to all Australians,” Marles said in a statement. “Given the strategic landscape we face, we cannot afford to be wasting money. We need to look at how we best use defence money for defence capability.” Loading The government estimated maintaining the site as a defence facility would cost $200 million over the next 10 years.



The decision to keep Victoria Barracks in public hands will punch a hole worth hundreds of millions of dollars in the government’s attempt to recoup $3 billion from ailing defence assets. Related Article Opinion

Planning The price of Victoria Barracks is much higher than $200 million Nadia Teong Clinical psychologist Three other sites, including Victoria Barracks and Point Cook in Melbourne and Fort Queenscliff near Geelong, will also remain publicly owned and opened up for community access. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the government was working to ensure defence has the capabilities it needs, and that the land was put to good use, including through public access. The Australian War Memorial will advise the government on showcasing the history of the sites.



The decision to stop the sale of Sydney’s Victoria Barracks will likely scupper the proposals of developers and architects, who had begun producing concept plans for the rare inner-city site, including mixed commercial, residential and public spaces. It is also set to reduce the amount of land available for housing, which the federal and state governments have labelled a priority to deal with chronic supply shortages in inner suburbs. Various politicians, including Allegra Spender, Alex Greenwich, John Howard and Tony Abbott joined the Victoria Barracks protest. Oscar Colman City of Sydney councillor Zann Maxwell said earlier this year that Victoria Barracks had to be considered as part of the solution. “We are in a housing crisis, and this is a very important site close to jobs and public transport,” he said. “It’s in the heart of one of the densest and most vibrant parts of the city. If there can be housing outcomes done sensitively and appropriately, we should absolutely be looking at them.”

World.title: Israeli president asks Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot to try to form government
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastWorld elections Israeli president asks Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot to try to form government November 8, 2026 — 7:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Israel’s president on Saturday chose Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s strongest rival, to try to form a new government following a deadlocked election that left neither man with a clear path to power. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, is fighting to stay in office after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an October 27 election but still emerged as the largest bloc in parliament. Former Israeli army chief and Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot greets supporters in Tel Aviv on election night. Getty Eisenkot, a former military chief, has declined to join forces with Arab parties, with whose support he would have a majority of seats in parliament. But Arab leaders, incensed by what they view as the racist policies of Netanyahu and his far-right allies, still nominated Eisenkot to try to form a government first — giving him the most endorsements. “President Herzog has invited Gadi Eisenkot to the President’s Residence, where he will be tasked with forming the government tomorrow,” said the spokesperson of President Isaac Herzog, whose largely ceremonial role involves nominating a candidate to form a coalition after elections.



Weeks of protracted negotiations are expected to follow Eisenkot’s nomination. He has 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension. Related Article World elections ‘Time to face reality’: Israel’s president takes first steps on building new government His potential pathways to power include trying to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside; forming a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties that he and his allies have shunned in the past; or forging a unity government with Netanyahu. Analysts say that all three options are unlikely to take shape. If Eisenkot fails, another candidate can try to form a government and if that candidate fails, parliament can nominate another. There is a deadline for the process of around 100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is ​held. Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but Netanyahu’s wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total, short of a 61-seat majority.



Eisenkot’s Yashar party emerged as the second-largest party with 21 seats, while his coalition, spanning four centre-left to right-wing Jewish-led parties, won just 48 seats. Two parties representing Israel’s Arab minority won an unprecedented 19 seats. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on election night. Getty Images A son of Moroccan immigrants, Eisenkot, 66, would be the country’s first prime minister from Israel’s Mizrahi community, Jews who trace their roots to the Middle East and North Africa. Reserved and media-shy, Eisenkot only entered politics in 2022. He briefly served in Netanyahu’s wartime cabinet following Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack on Israel before returning to the opposition. From opposition, he publicly rebuked Netanyahu over his leadership, including his management of the military campaign in Gaza, and has sworn that he would not serve in government with him.



Eisenkot’s public standing is also bound up with the personal price his family has paid since 2023: a son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza. Eisenkot highlighted his security credentials on the campaign trail, citing his “Dahiyeh doctrine” of responding to attacks with disproportionate force, which he deployed as a commander during Israel’s 2006 war with Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon. Eisenkot has criticised settler violence against Palestinians, which has surged since 2023, raising tensions in Israel’s ties with Western states, and he opposes Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who have both faced sanctions by some Western countries for inciting violence against Palestinians. World.title: Trump publicly offers UFC boss Dana White job as White House press secretary
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump publicly offers UFC boss Dana White job as White House press secretary Michael Koziol Updated November 8, 2026 — 6:59am ,first published 5:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Washington: Donald Trump said he had offered Ultimate Fighting Championship boss Dana White the job of White House press secretary, in what appeared to be a joke that underscores the US president’s desire to fight Democrats for the next two years. Trump said White was “a violent fighter and warrior”, and that he should bring mixed martial arts fighters from around the world – including Russians Islam Makhacev and Khabib Nurmagomedov – as “assistants” for the press secretary job. US President Donald Trump and UFC president and CEO Dana White arrive for the UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House in June. AP “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” The president’s offer appeared to be tongue in cheek given the UFC president’s business commitments. His post included a mock-up of White in a suit behind a podium, and pictures of various MMA fighters.



The two men are friends, and Trump hosted a UFC fight at the White House in June as part of official celebrations for America’s 250th anniversary. Trump has a long history of using social media to troll Democrats, progressives and political enemies. Even so, the post suggests the White House is leaning into the perception that it is in “fight” mode after Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate at last week’s midterm elections. Donald Trump posted a collage of images alongside the Truth Social post calling on Dana White to take up the job. Truth Social It comes a day after Trump replaced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with hardline lieutenant Stephen Miller, widely seen as the start of an aggressive staff restructure as Democrats prepare to investigate the administration in Congress. Also on Saturday (US time), the president said he was ordering the Department of Justice to investigate what he termed “Weaponisation and Lawfare” by Democrats who were threatening to impeach or investigate senior administration officials.



Trump claimed Democrats were threatening Republican donors with imprisonment – potentially a reference to Democrats’ intention to probe corporate donations to the president’s new White House ballroom. “This is extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable for this,” Trump claimed, without evidence, on social media. “These SLEAZEBAGS should go to jail for what they are doing.” Miller was homeland security adviser and the deputy chief of staff for policy at the White House. AP Typically, the Department of Justice operates at arm’s length from the president, but Trump has involved himself directly in the department’s operations, including publicly pressuring his former attorney-general Pam Bondi to hasten investigations into his political enemies. As chief of staff, Wiles urged against some of these endeavours – particularly whether to force journalists to divulge their sources in leak investigations. Miller is reportedly in favour of using stronger tactics, potentially including arrests.

From the outset, they’d had Olivia Colman in mind as the Fisherwoman, a stoic and lusty outsider who dares to ask for what she wants, and gets it. But, says Fischer, “we were told she probably won’t read this, she’s probably not going to do it, just go to somebody who’s more likely.” “But we just gave it a shot anyway,” says Wilson, “and we’re very lucky that she happens to be the kind of person who reads scripts and follows her heart…”

World.title: Six killed after gunman opens fire on tourist hotspot in Krakow
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropePoland Six killed after gunman opens fire on tourist hotspot in Krakow Updated November 8, 2026 — 8:28am ,first published 3:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Polish man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow on Saturday and opened fire, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him, authorities said. The attack, which Poland’s defence minister described as an “act of terror,” happened in Main Square, which is in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town and is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city. Emergency workers at the scene of the deadly shooting. Getty Images The 25-year-old attacker drove to multiple spots in the square and opened fire at each stop with an automatic weapon, authorities said. Although they didn’t release his name, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the man holds “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views. “Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” Kierwiński said at a news conference.



Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said drone footage appeared to show three bodies inside the home of the man behind the mass shooting. He said the two women and one man appear to be close members of the gunman’s family. Sixteen people were injured in the attack, including the suspect, two police officers and five foreign nationals. It’s unclear how many of the injured were shot. Two of them were treated and released within hours of the mass shooting. Police lock down market square in Krakow. AP The attacker wore military-style fatigues and a bulletproof vest, and used a military-type long gun, Krakow police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said. Police found many other weapons and ammunition in his car. He kept firing at the police even after being shot himself, she said.



The attacker engaged in a “wild ride” around Main Square, which is why people were wounded at several locations, Cisło said. Cisło added that the gunman acted alone and that the public is safe. Krakow mayor Łukasz Gibała said the city will be in official mourning until Wednesday. He vowed that Krakow will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy. “The square will belong to us again,” Gibała said in a video posted to X. Emergency services respond to the attack. Getty Images



A shattered shop window after the shooting. Getty Images Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. It was not immediately clear whether the firearm used in Saturday’s attack, or the guns found in the perpetrator’s car, were legal. Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising. Images from the scene showed police officers and ambulances covering the area, which is in the centre of Krakow. A Polish Medical Air Rescue helicopter also landed in the square. Krakow is the second-largest city in Poland and roughly 250 kilometres from the capital, Warsaw. Around 15 million tourists visit Krakow annually, the majority passing through the Main Square.
