World.title: Victoria Barracks sale abandoned following backlash
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalDefence Victoria Barracks sale abandoned following backlash Eryk Bagshaw November 8, 2026 — 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Albanese government has bowed to public pressure and abandoned the sale of Victoria Barracks, removing its most high-profile defence asset from its attempt to claw back $3 billion in taxpayer money. The decision, announced on Sunday, means the 186-year-old Victoria Barracks in Paddington will remain in government hands. The main building at Victoria Barracks was designed to accommodate hundreds of soldiers. Wolter Peeters The colonial-era sandstone headquarters will not be sold, but it will also no longer be used as an active Australian Defence Force facility. Instead, it will be opened to the public.



“Victoria Barracks Sydney has a special place in our nation’s history – and we will be keeping it in public hands,” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement. “This program creates opportunities to open Defence’s historic sites and buildings to the public, and to commemorate our nation’s history.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, alongside Defence Minister Richard Marles with Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen. Alex Ellinghausen Defence Minister Richard Marles had until September maintained that Victoria Barracks would be sold, describing it as “the oldest wine cellar in Sydney,” used by only a section of the military elite. The comments provoked a backlash from supporters of the site and galvanised the Save Victoria Barracks Alliance. An unlikely coalition of veterans’ groups, former prime ministers Paul Keating, John Howard and Tony Abbott, Premier Chris Minns and federal, state and local politicians all spoke out against the sale of the site.



The Daily Telegraph, which first reported the Albanese government’s backflip on Sunday morning, also campaigned heavily against the sale. “By moving personnel off these sites, and working to open them up for the public, we are ensuring that the history of Victoria Barracks is one that can be protected and returned to all Australians,” Marles said in a statement. “Given the strategic landscape we face, we cannot afford to be wasting money. We need to look at how we best use defence money for defence capability.” Loading The government estimated maintaining the site as a defence facility would cost $200 million over the next 10 years.



The decision to keep Victoria Barracks in public hands will punch a hole worth hundreds of millions of dollars in the government’s attempt to recoup $3 billion from ailing defence assets. Related Article Opinion

Planning The price of Victoria Barracks is much higher than $200 million Nadia Teong Clinical psychologist Three other sites, including Victoria Barracks and Point Cook in Melbourne and Fort Queenscliff near Geelong, will also remain publicly owned and opened up for community access. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the government was working to ensure defence has the capabilities it needs, and that the land was put to good use, including through public access. The Australian War Memorial will advise the government on showcasing the history of the sites.



The decision to stop the sale of Sydney’s Victoria Barracks will likely scupper the proposals of developers and architects, who had begun producing concept plans for the rare inner-city site, including mixed commercial, residential and public spaces. It is also set to reduce the amount of land available for housing, which the federal and state governments have labelled a priority to deal with chronic supply shortages in inner suburbs. Various politicians, including Allegra Spender, Alex Greenwich, John Howard and Tony Abbott joined the Victoria Barracks protest. Oscar Colman City of Sydney councillor Zann Maxwell said earlier this year that Victoria Barracks had to be considered as part of the solution. “We are in a housing crisis, and this is a very important site close to jobs and public transport,” he said. “It’s in the heart of one of the densest and most vibrant parts of the city. If there can be housing outcomes done sensitively and appropriately, we should absolutely be looking at them.”

World.title: Israeli president asks Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot to try to form government
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastWorld elections Israeli president asks Netanyahu rival Gadi Eisenkot to try to form government November 8, 2026 — 7:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Israel’s president on Saturday chose Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s strongest rival, to try to form a new government following a deadlocked election that left neither man with a clear path to power. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, is fighting to stay in office after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an October 27 election but still emerged as the largest bloc in parliament. Former Israeli army chief and Yashar Party leader Gadi Eisenkot greets supporters in Tel Aviv on election night. Getty Eisenkot, a former military chief, has declined to join forces with Arab parties, with whose support he would have a majority of seats in parliament. But Arab leaders, incensed by what they view as the racist policies of Netanyahu and his far-right allies, still nominated Eisenkot to try to form a government first — giving him the most endorsements. “President Herzog has invited Gadi Eisenkot to the President’s Residence, where he will be tasked with forming the government tomorrow,” said the spokesperson of President Isaac Herzog, whose largely ceremonial role involves nominating a candidate to form a coalition after elections.



Weeks of protracted negotiations are expected to follow Eisenkot’s nomination. He has 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension. Related Article World elections ‘Time to face reality’: Israel’s president takes first steps on building new government His potential pathways to power include trying to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside; forming a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties that he and his allies have shunned in the past; or forging a unity government with Netanyahu. Analysts say that all three options are unlikely to take shape. If Eisenkot fails, another candidate can try to form a government and if that candidate fails, parliament can nominate another. There is a deadline for the process of around 100 days. If no one succeeds, another election is ​held. Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but Netanyahu’s wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total, short of a 61-seat majority.



Eisenkot’s Yashar party emerged as the second-largest party with 21 seats, while his coalition, spanning four centre-left to right-wing Jewish-led parties, won just 48 seats. Two parties representing Israel’s Arab minority won an unprecedented 19 seats. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on election night. Getty Images A son of Moroccan immigrants, Eisenkot, 66, would be the country’s first prime minister from Israel’s Mizrahi community, Jews who trace their roots to the Middle East and North Africa. Reserved and media-shy, Eisenkot only entered politics in 2022. He briefly served in Netanyahu’s wartime cabinet following Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack on Israel before returning to the opposition. From opposition, he publicly rebuked Netanyahu over his leadership, including his management of the military campaign in Gaza, and has sworn that he would not serve in government with him.



Eisenkot’s public standing is also bound up with the personal price his family has paid since 2023: a son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza. Eisenkot highlighted his security credentials on the campaign trail, citing his “Dahiyeh doctrine” of responding to attacks with disproportionate force, which he deployed as a commander during Israel’s 2006 war with Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon. Eisenkot has criticised settler violence against Palestinians, which has surged since 2023, raising tensions in Israel’s ties with Western states, and he opposes Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who have both faced sanctions by some Western countries for inciting violence against Palestinians. Reuters

World.title: Police arrest man, 45, after fire sprinkler parts stolen across Auckland
World.content:
A 45-year-old man has been arrested following a series of burglaries targeting fire sprinkler connections at commercial buildings across Auckland.

Counties Manukau West Area Commander Inspector Dave Christoffersen said at least nine reports have been made of metal couplings being stolen from fire sprinkler inlets.

"So far this offending is localised to the Counties Manukau West and Auckland East area, however police are working to establish if this offending is occurring in other communities."

Acting Detective Sergeant Simon Kirby said police recovered several items from the man's property, including metal couplings allegedly stolen from these areas.

The couplings allow firefighters to boost the water supply to sprinkler systems during a fire. If they are stolen or damaged, it can limit firefighters' ability to control a fire and carry out rescues.

Police are now advising building owners to check areas around important service access points and make sure they are properly secured.

Christoffersen said the burglaries mostly happened after business hours and on weekends.

"Police intelligence suggests offending is likely to occur between 7pm and 5am," he said.

Police and the Fire Protection Association New Zealand said the thefts could put the public and firefighters at risk.

World.title: Analysis: Election night comes with a devastating cost for National
World.content:
This story was corrected on 8 November - it originally said National had five new MPs.

Seven fresh new National Party MPs head to Parliament on Tuesday, but at what cost?

While the party won the most seats - collecting 42 electorates on the night - there were more commiserations than celebrations because of what that success has cost.

With not one single list seat won after only pulling in 29 percent of the party vote, National is about to endure a procession of political funerals for some of its most senior colleagues.

Nicola Willis, Chris Bishop, Paul Goldsmith, and Gerry Brownlee are all gone.

It's a devastating outcome for a party that is still looking in a position to form the next government.

Proving that you don't need to be popular to be Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon is still in the hunt to keep his job.

With two confidence votes in his leadership and dire net approval ratings the entire term, Luxon's leadership lives on.

The question is for how long, once the caucus and wider party reach the anger stage of the grief process.

At this point Luxon has done enough - special votes allowing - to cobble a coalition together.

But he's looking set to be doing a deal with a combined Act and New Zealand First vote of 20 percent.

That's an incredible amount of power and influence for the two parties, which negotiated some significant coalition wins three years ago with just 14 percent between them.

It's not all bad news for National, but with so much loss it certainly took the shine off the wins for first-time MPs Mahesh Muralidhar, Blair Cameron, Matthew Paul, Lloyd Budd, Jess Rowe, Emma Chatterton and Katie Milne.

Luxon and his team will have to work out how to redeploy ministerial portfolios once ousted MPs have their warrants expire in 28 days.

With special votes due back in 20 days, it's near impossible a new coalition and ministers will be sorted in time.

While some of the behind-the-scenes talks might get underway with Act and New Zealand First, it's not a given at this point the three parties would get across the line without Opportunity.

Act and New Zealand First had a good night on Saturday with both parties increasing their party vote by roughly three percent.

But it was Opportunity, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori who defied the odds.

As noted after the first wave of results rolled in on Saturday by New Zealand First's deputy Shane Jones, it's no easy feat breaking through the five percent threshold.

Opportunity has done what many said it couldn't and may still decide the next government depending on how the special votes fall.

The Greens have had an historic victory collecting the party's most successful result ever despite a parliamentary term defined by mayhem and loss.

And while Te Pāti Māori came as close as it could to self-imploding and wiping itself out of Parliament, its strategy to focus only on electorates saw it win five of the seven seats on the night.

Labour MPs will be scratching their head as to how those three parties, who all campaigned on a change of government in one form or another, capitalised and it didn't.

The party collected just two extra seats on its 2023 result, which is looked back on by the party as an election to forget.

There's a small window still for Labour to stitch together a government if they pick up enough seats on the centre-left through special votes.

On current numbers, however, the maths doesn't add up in Chris Hipkins' favour.

World.title: Turnout for 2026 election on track to be the second lowest in New Zealand history
World.content:
The turnout for the 2026 election is on track to be the second lowest in New Zealand history.

The Electoral Commission said 74.6 percent of eligible voters cast a vote.

It included more than 2.4 million ordinary votes and the just under 400,000 special votes that are yet to be counted.

The 2.8 million votes compares to more than 3.6 million at the last election.

Just under 3.7 million people were enrolled to vote, 93.6 percent of the population and short of the 94.7 of the last election, though that was a record rate.

Chief Electoral office, Karl Le Quesne said the turnout was slightly under 2023's turnout.

He estimated there were about 400,000 special votes to be counted - and 96,000 of them are from overseas - so they have to allow 10 days for them to be returned.

The preliminary results are based on the 2,432,403 ordinary votes counted on election night, including informal votes. They are indicative only and will change after special votes have been checked and counted.

World.title: NZ First deputy leader Shane Jones rules out working with Labour
World.content:
New Zealand First deputy leader Shane Jones has ruled out working with the Labour Party.

"There are no exchanges of love letters at all between our party and the Labour Party," Jones said on Sunday morning.

"We have nailed our colours to the outcome of restoring the three of us to power, i.e. the ACT Party, the National Party and ourselves. But, as our leader Winston said, the full facts have not been revealed..."

Asked whether there was a chance New Zealand First would pick up the phone to Labour, Jones said "in this sunny Bay of Islands environment" there was a snowball's chance.

"No, no, that won't be happening," he said.

"We campaigned to maintain the three elements that comprise our government, and that is the stance we're going forward with."

Speaking on the loss of National's key ministers, Jones said the party had "retreated to a rump of constituency MPs".

But he said "the show goes on" and that there would be others in Parliament who would "equip themselves" and step up.

"The waka that I was asked to paddle around the country was New Zealand First, and it's up to National to determine why they've ended up where they've ended up. And although the Mowbrays may be their most powerful backers and the richest family in New Zealand, the jury's out for whether that actually did them any favours."

Jones said New Zealand First would do a "deep dive" of Saturday night's results, which saw the party increase its share from 2023.

Speaking to media outside the Duke of Marlborough in Russell, Jones said last night's party "wasn't as boisterous" as previous elections, as the country waits for the special votes.

"As you know, from time to time, I've come across as quite combative as a senior member of Parliament. But the dynamic and the vibe is that there's a genuine thirst for, and I don't want to sound trite, but hope and optimism and confidence, and people want speedy delivery in relation to a solution to their household woes."

Jones would not reveal any of New Zealand First's negotiation strategies, but he said if New Zealand First was in a position to negotiate after the specials are counted "that will be leveraged, that will not be squandered."

National's Simeon Brown says election night 'bittersweet'

National's campaign chairperson Simeon Brown said last night was "bittersweet".

"Clearly our party vote has gone backwards. We've lost some key ministers."

He said it was looking like National can from a government with its coalition partners.

"Going into this election, we always knew it would be challenging."

National would need to lose Hamilton East and Wairarapa, Brown said, and then National leader Christopher Luxon would need to make a call about whether to contact the Opportunity party.

'NZ deserves better than NZ First' - Green co-leader Marama Davidson

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson. (File photo) RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said there was still a pathway to power for a left-leaning government.

So far, the Greens have won 13.3 percent of the vote and 16 seats, the best result for any minor party since the first MMP election in 1996.

"Really proud of our campaign. We just consistently focus on putting the solutions out there for affordable lives and protecting nature, and we stayed focused despite a whole lot of things that were thrown at us. So, really proud of our campaign…

"[Voters] have given us the most historic support that we have ever seen. The Maori vote is quite phenomenal in terms of its increase even just from 2020, almost doubled. That may go up with specials. That is historic."

Davdison said she's proud of their campaign, particularly their success in getting party votes in Māori seats.

As for potentially working with NZ First, should that coalition partner entertain the idea of working with the left as they have in the past, Davidson said no.

World.title: Fire engulfs winery in Marlborough
World.content:
Firefighters have been battling a large blaze at a commercial winery in Marlborough.

Crews were called to a building in Riverlands just after 3am on Sunday, Fire and Emergency said.

Southern shift manager Amanda Taylor said the building, a commercial winery processing facility, was well alight on arrival.

Thirteen fire trucks were sent to the fire, which escalated to what firefighters call a third alarm.

World.title: Ah Kiong hat-trick helps Samoa beat Zimbabwe
World.content:
Manu Samoa winger Lattrell Ah Kiong scored a hat-trick as Samoa beat Zimbabwe 43-7 in their World Rugby Nations Cup clash at the DIY Kitchens Stadium, in Wakefield, in England on Sunday morning (NZT).

Ah Kiong scored in the seventh, 19th and 45th minutes.

His tally contributed to Manu Samoa's total haul of seven tries in the match, with others coming from Peter Umaga-Jensen (22nd), Ben Nee-Nee (42nd), Miracle Faiilagi (54th), AJ Lam (78th).

Fired up after their sivitau pre-match challenged, led by captain Theo McFarland, the islanders did not wait too long before Ah Kiong struck for his first try, following a Umaga-Jensen break down the right flank.

Flyhalves Jacob Umaga, who kicked three conversions, and his replacement Josh Ioane, managed eight points between themselves.

Ioane was one of two former All Blacks who made their debuts for Manu Samoa, alongside fullback Shaun Stevenson.

Manu Samoa's Miracle Faiilagi dives across the Zimbabwe tryline to score his try in Wakefield. World Rugby / Nathan Stirk

Samoa's win was their second in the competition and in front of a lively crowd it was the men in blue who largely dominated proceedings during a formidable display of skill and strength.

Yet the Sables' spirits never sagged and the scored a late consolation try through Dale Lemon.

Zimbabwe captain Hilton Mudariki said they needed to keep working hard and learn from the match.

"Credit to Samoa because they showed their class today," he said post-match.

"It shows we've got a lot to work on, but our fans were amazing so we'll just keep building."

Samoa led 19-0 at half-time and captain McFarland said it was good to kick off their second round with a win.

He said they will keep learning.

"Been some months before we played together again, and it was good to welcome the new boys and also get back our core players," he said.

"Zimbabwe was great and they came at us hard. Was good to have that win.

"We will take our learnings and keep moving forward."

Umaga-Jensen's combination with crack centre Lalomilo Lalomilo and AJ Lam would have made the team coaches happy as the trio turned the magic on with ball in hand.

Former Chiefs fullback Stevenson was also devastating with his counter-attacking runs from the back.

Samoa's front row of Scott Sio, Richie Asiata and veteran Michael Alalatoa held their own against the Zimbabwe scrums while locks Benjamin Petia Nee-nee and McFarland dominated in the lineout battles.

World.title: Fireworks blamed for extensive fire in public toilets and changing rooms in Hamilton
World.content:
Police investigating a suspicious fire in Hamilton's Discovery Park are appealing to the public for information.

Detective Andrew Murphy said at about 11pm last Thursday , emergency services responded to reports of a fire in the park's public toilets and changing rooms.

"Before the fire was extinguished it caused extensive damage to the building and to sports equipment.

"Witnesses reported seeing people firing fireworks at each other in the carpark shortly before the fire. The people were believed to have arrived in vehicles and reportedly left the area shortly before the fire was discovered."

Officers want to speak to anyone who was in the area between 10.30pm and 11.15pm that day, and who might have seen any suspicious activity.

"We are particularly interested to hear from anyone with photos, video or information regarding the vehicles seen leaving the area around the time of the fire."

Information can be provided online or by calling 105 using the file number 261106/5591.

World.title: Wilson backs Wallabies to overpower mutinous England
World.content:
Harry Wilson believes the Wallabies are ready to test England's reported lack of unity at Twickenham while looking to unleash a key 'X-factor' strike weapon from their bench.

The build-up to Sunday's Nations Championship Test has been dominated by stories about unrest within the England camp at their Pennyhill Park base, leaving Australia's captain Wilson to suggest his team will be out to discover whether there's any truth in the supposed disunity.

Asked on the eve of the match whether any unrest in the opposition camp might galvanise or disrupt the hosts, Wilson said: "It could go one or two ways for them, and I guess it's on us to put them under pressure to see how close they are as a team."

But the skipper was also keen to make the point of just what a united outfit his own team has become.

"We know how close we are, how much we care for each other, and how much we love playing for our coach and coaching staff," Wilson said.

"So I'm really only worried about us, and I just want us to keep keep caring for this jersey, keep caring for every person in our group."

A report had claimed England players wanted showdown talks with coach Steve Borthwick during the July tour because of a toxic environment.

But leading England players responded with indignation this week, with Jamie George declaring they would demonstrate their loyalty to Borthwick with a stirring performance.

Yet Wilson believes his men are primed for "an epic battle in the forwards" as they seek to make amends for being outplayed at Twickenham last year.

The Queenslander is particularly enthused by the new impact role for one of their best, usual back-row starter Rob Valetini.

Last November, Australia suffered when the England second-half reinforcements came on — but now, led by Valetini, he's backing the likes of Taniela Tupou and Carlo Tizzano to fight fire with fire against the so-called 'Pom Squad'.

"It's different for Bobby, and it's just a genuine X factor coming off the bench," Wilson said.

"It's rugby now, a lot of teams have some really strong players coming off the bench, and we've got one of the best players in his position in the world coming off the bench. So he can be some genuine X factor if it's close when he comes on.

"Having a player like him coming on gives the boys a lot of confidence, and that's what England did to us last year. Hopefully, Bobby can really spark us on the bench again this year."

Harry Wilson led Australia to a famous victory at Twickenham two years ago. (Getty Images: CameraSport/Andrew Kearns)

The Wallabies' last-gasp win at Twickenham in 2024 was a breakthrough moment for Wilson himself in the early days of his captaincy, as he scored a try and had an inspirational game.

Now "comfortable" in the leadership role, he's overseeing a team which has "a lot to be excited about" and is ready to rebound from the two recent chastening defeats by a rampant New Zealand.

"We definitely want to be us. We want to play our own game," said Wilson.

"We've seen this year when we do play our style of footy how much we can hurt teams.

"In the South Africa win, when we really backed our skills and kept attacking, we really played some really good footy, and we learned some valuable lessons in those New Zealand games. We really need to take them forward."

AAP

World.title: Coach says Bancroft will 'let bat do the talking' after Khawaja bombshell
World.content:
Cameron Bancroft is being backed to let his "bat do the talking" in the wake of Usman Khawaja's bombshell revelations about the sandpaper ball-tampering scandal from 2018.

Khawaja sent the cricket world into a spin on Saturday when he said the entire Test XI knew about the use of sandpaper to alter the state of the ball on the tour of South Africa.

The comments were in stark contrast to the findings from the official investigation, which determined only David Warner, Steve Smith and Bancroft knew about the plot.

Bancroft, who was caught on camera during the Cape Town Test trying to hide the sandpaper in his pants, received a nine-month suspension, while senior figures Warner and Smith were banned for a year.

Khawaja said he had urged the entire team at the time to take collective responsibility rather than scapegoating Warner, Smith and Bancroft.

"Obviously, it didn't work that way and those three guys got crucified," Khawaja told Nine Newspapers.

Bancroft played only two more Tests once he served his ban, and recently said he was no longer as motivated to return to the Test arena as he once was.

Cameron Bancroft has been backed to let his bat do the talking. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

The 33-year-old put aside the distraction of Khawaja's comments on Saturday to score 32 off 40 balls in Western Australia's 92-run one-day loss to England at the WACA.

After the match, WA coach Beau Casson praised Bancroft's maturity in the face of renewed interest in the ball-tampering scandal.

"He's a grown man and a very mature guy," Casson said.

"I think he's handled himself with distinction in that space. I don't see it changing anytime soon."

Bancroft wasn't made available to media on Saturday to talk about Khawaja's comments, and it remains to be seen whether he will eventually address the latest revelations.

"The situation was a long time ago," Casson said.

"He's keen to move on and let his bat do the talking, and that's what we promote him to do."

Cameron Bancroft scored a colossal 186 against South Australia in the most recent Sheffield Shield match. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

Cricket Australia says it remains comfortable with the past investigation of the incident, but left the door open for new information to be considered.

Bancroft will be back in action when WA takes on Victoria in a Sheffield Shield match at the MCG, starting on Wednesday.

"We're just rapt to be able to have Cameron scoring runs for us," Casson said.

"Last week was a really good example of that [when he scored 186 in a Shield win against South Australia].

"He leaves nothing to chance. He trains hard, not only technically but physically. If he's not running miles, he's thinking about cricket.

"He's a senior player within this group, and he certainly sets the example of how to go about it to be a professional cricketer."

AAP

World.title: After taming Tonga, the World Cup is New Zealand's to lose
World.content:
In fitting fashion for a sport where big is often beautiful, the Rugby League World Cup trophy is a hefty old thing.

It is officially named the Paul Barrier trophy after a pioneering French rugby league official and it weighs in at north of 20 kilograms.

That means Kalyn Ponga might have a bit of trouble lifting it over his head should New Zealand get up in next week's final given he's three weeks back from a broken arm and it could be a bit tender.

Rugby League World Cup live Kalyn Ponga has returned from a broken arm to lead New Zealand to the Rugby League World Cup final after a tense and weather-affected semifinal against Tonga. Follow live.

But he'll have to give it his best shot, because after a 34-10 win over Tonga in the first semifinal, the title of world champion is New Zealand's to lose.

In appalling conditions in Newcastle, the city's favourite son led the way as the Kiwis silenced Tonga's sea of red, drowning the Mate Ma'a under the weight of pressure and poise.

Ponga's bravery was the highlight, even though he wasn't the only one to show plenty of ticker.

Everybody in the 29,712-strong crowd had their mettle tested by a howling gale that shook the goalposts, made kicking near impossible and cut to the bone.

Tonga fans once again dominated the crowd in Newcastle. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

You could have been forgiven for thinking that wind that roared came from the Tongan fans, the mightiest red army the world has seen since the fall of the Soviet Union, who made the Hunter feel like a little piece of the kingdom all day.

Their heroes responded with a first half that had all the brutality and brilliance Tonga has been known for, only for Ponga to rise above it.

First he threw the final pass for Briton Nikora's opening score in the final five minutes, proving that the arm he broke against Australia in the tournament opener just 22 days ago was ready for action.

Ponga showed no ill-effects from the broken arm he suffered three weeks ago. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

It copped a serious test in the next stages as Tonga enjoyed its best period of the match.

First Tyson Frizell levelled Ponga on a kick return and it wasn't long before Salesi Foketi did the same in a powerful display of Tongan hospitality.

Shortly thereafter Demetric Vaimauga, who moves like someone taught a block of flats how to run, threw two dummies and got into the clear, with his eyes on the corner and Ponga in his sights.

Despite Vaimauga's best effort to leave a Ponga-shaped hole in the ground, the New Zealand fullback brought him down.

Tonga scored a few plays later regardless, but it was a sign of Ponga's willingness to push his battered body to the limit that made the difference in the most important play of the match just a few minutes later.

In the shadows of halftime, Ponga chased a Jahrome Hughes kick hard to force an error from Lehi Hopoate error and present Dane Gagai a try.

It ensured New Zealand, which was running into the hurricane for the first half, went into the break 12-10 up and they'll ride the wind all the way to Lang Park, where they'll face either Samoa or Australia.

The way they did it is why they should be favourites regardless of who they play.

Their forward pack, led this time by Erin Clark and Joseph Tapine but on any given night they can also rely on James Fisher-Harris, Naufahu Whyte or Moses Leota to do the job, is the best and deepest in the world.

New Zealand put the clamps on Tonga's powerful forwards. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

There is nobody they cannot bring to heel, even a pack of roughnecks like Tonga, and when they get the rest of it right you end up with a side that sure looks like the best in the world.

In their loss to Australia a few weeks back Jahrome Hughes, a halfback of some quality and experience, pulled the wrong rein but this time he had all the right ones in hand.

His kicking game and on-field command of the Kiwi attack was well above Isaiya Katoa's and it made a greater difference as the game went on.

Casey McLean was just as prominent throughout as one of the most incredible beginnings to a Test career in rugby league history continued. Bullets have left guns and gotten off to slower starts.

His second half score, where he carved up opposite number and Penrith teammate Paul Alamoti like a Sunday roast, was his 16th in Test football, giving him a share of fifth place on the Kiwis all-time try-scoring list in just his eighth Test, all of which has happened before his 21st birthday.

Add Ponga's attacking class and stout defensive work — he finished with three try assists and at least two try-saving tackles — as a little bit of heaven on top and it proved too much for Tonga to bear.

They stayed game as long as they could, but gradually they lost the war of attrition and the World Cup final remains the final frontier for them amidst rugby league's international revolution.

Tonga has fallen short of its first World Cup semifinal. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The hangover from last week's epic win over Samoa caught up with them as Tonga ran out of gas late, with the fires that have burned so brightly finally sputtering out in the wind.

There were little moments they can point to where things turned.

If Vaimauga had managed to trample Ponga, if Hopoate had gathered in that Hughes kick or, on an unhappy night for the Manly youngster, if he'd managed to find an unmarked Katoa after a break the set before McLean's try or if he'd been a little better under the high ball.

The margins get fine as the games get bigger and moments like that are the edge of the cliff, where steady feet can make all the difference and New Zealand's feet are dug deep, like the roots of a mountain.

Regardless of what the bookies say once the dust settles at the Sydney Football Stadium on Sunday night, New Zealand should be favourites for next week.

Samoa can shoot to kill, but they have never beaten New Zealand and their last meeting, in the 2025 Pacific Championship final, played out much like this semi-final.

Tonga and Samoa can be Origin for the new century The scale and spectacle of Tonga's Rugby League World Cup win over Samoa was not just an instant classic, it proved a demand for this clash that rugby league must find a way to supply.

The Australians are the all-conquering, perennial favourites who have lost just one game this decade and they beat New Zealand just a few weeks ago but they have not looked anything like that since.

Even then their win relied on two length-of-the-field intercept tries and Ponga missing much of the final quarter with the broken arm that threatened to end his World Cup.

Now he has returned and ultimate glory is in reach for him and the Kiwis.

The trophy they're looking to carry is heavy with silver but together, with Ponga's arm included, they're strong enough to lift it.

World.title: For queer people, community sport can be life-saving
World.content:
Stuart Bonner sits in the change rooms at a local community sporting centre with tears in his eyes.

The 31-year-old from Glasgow has a fresh buzz cut, "a skinhead", as he calls it, and knows he can come off "as an angry Scottish man" with his thick accent.

But any facade of that kind melts away as his voice cracks while talking about his soccer club, of which he is now president.

"I don't think I would still be here if it wasn't for football. I have a history of suicidal ideation, self-harm thoughts, and suicide attempts," he tells ABC Sport.

"Without the support and the friends that I've made at Melbourne Rovers specifically, God knows what could be different."

Bonner is one of many gay men across the globe who've felt disconnected from sport growing up, but he has since found a sense of belonging in adult years through a queer sporting club.

Stuart Bonner grew up in Glasglow, where, he says, playing football is tough as a queer person. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Growing up, he was "relentlessly bullied" after a friend outed at him at high school.

"Being a kid was so tough, and being in school was so tough," he says, adding that for many players like himself, football is "a really hard place to be gay".

He found the sport "just really masculine", where trying to fit in, often as a form of self-protection, was exhausting.

"It takes so much effort to mask who you are," he says.

"The only way that I can maybe try and relate it, if you're in a bad mood and you have to go to work, you know that you have to put on a smile and put on a face.

"Imagine doing that all the time, trying to hide the fact that you were gay or trying to be more masculine or trying to walk a certain way, or deepen your voice.

"Even now, when I meet new people, I deepen my voice. But then when you walk into the Rovers, you're like, 'Oh, I don't really need to do that anymore.'

" Or you do it and you're immediately met by someone who's super flamboyant and effeminate, and you're like, 'What the f*** am I doing? I do not need to pretend anymore.' "

Melbourne Rovers is a LGBTQIA+ all inclusive football (soccer) club. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

In Scotland, LGBTQ+ individuals feel more than twice as excluded from football than other sports, and in Australia, over half (53 per cent) of young LGBTQIA+ people have witnessed discrimination in community sport, and 40 per cent have personally experienced it.

Ryan Storr, adjunct fellow at Victoria University and cofounder of Proud2Play, says a lot of queer men avoid mainstream sporting clubs due to high levels of homophobia and discrimination, which can be verbal and sometimes physical.

"With football in particular, because of the historical roots, and because it's been played for such a long time, they've got that ingrained sexism, homophobia, discrimination generally into the very core of the sport," Dr Storr tells ABC Sport.

"It's particularly a sport that kind of encapsulates, let's say, masculinity in how it's performed in terms of being an aggressive sport, physical sport, [and] especially the fandom in particular."

Ryan Storr says a lot of queer men avoid mainstream sporting clubs. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

Storr gave the example of historical homophobic chants in the Premier League.

The Football Association has fined Tottenham Hotspur, West Ham, Luton Town and Leeds United in recent years for homophobic chanting and LGBT+ supporter groups have been advised not to attend World Cup matches in Russia and Qatar due to safety concerns.

This differs largely from women's sports, which often have roots in queer communities, and a large number of openly LGBTQ+ players, both at the community and elite or national level.

While facing their own unique challenges, "[queer] women generally have been in safe places in women's sport, and so didn't necessarily need to be in separate spaces", Storr says, noting that types of queerphobia, and transphobia in particular, can still deter people from community sports.

Stuart Bonner says the community he found playing at the Rovers helped saved his life. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

'I get to be free and physical'

The Rovers have two men's teams in Football Victoria's Metro leagues: one in Metro 7 and one in Metro 9.

After hearing feedback that many women's teams across the state feel unsupported by their mainstream clubs, the Rovers are adding a women's team in 2027.

Aisling Haugh is one of the players in the metro 9, a team made up of people newer to the sport.

She moved to Melbourne from Auckland hoping to join a community sports team to make friends and build a new community.

Aisling Haugh was daunted to join a women's team but wanted to find a community through sport. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

As a transwoman, she was apprehensive about joining a sports team.

"I'd obviously figured out a few things about myself that I hadn't figured out in high school … that poses some interesting problems and invites a bit of risk regarding what teams I want to join," she says.

"Plus, there's also the whole sort of thing about transwomen and women's sports."

Haugh was 26 when she started seeing a doctor and going down the pathway of transitioning. When asks what terminology she uses, she says: "I consider myself a woman, and transgender is just a part of that identity."

However, without a women's team this year, Haugh joined the men's team after being assured about the trans-inclusive nature. Plus, she says, the idea of joining a woman's team was "a little bit too much", as she was already nervous about getting back into sports as a queer person.

"Queer people, especially if they don't have community, they minimise themselves and they make themselves small and it kind of reflects in their body as well," she says.

"Like you tense up and you tuck yourself in and community sport is just an awesome way to inhabit your body again.

"I get to be free and physical and run around, just kind of act a bit like a kid again with people who I feel safe and seen with … it's so incredible. I was training with a big smile on my face."

Stuart Bonner and Aisling Haugh are starting a women's team at the Rovers in 2027. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Haugh says she is hyperaware of what her face looks like, her voice sounds like and the way she carries herself as to what impressions she gives off when in public. But when she plays, she's able to just focus on the game, the ball and her friends.

"I don't feel dysphoria when I play, and that's crazy because even playing on a men's team as well, it's just me and my body."

A sense of belonging

It's not lost on Bonner that the sport that made him feel so disconnected as a queer person growing up is now what brings him and his teammates a great sense of community.

This really came home to him when he saw the Home is Football: Belonging in Australian Soccer exhibit at the Immigration Museum in Melbourne, where he is featured alongside Ange Postecoglou, Lydia Williams, and players from diverse teams, including refugees and asylum seekers, across the country.

"The quote on the wall when you first walk in is, 'Football is the reason we came, the friendships we make is the reason that we stay', and I think … that's what we all do it for."

Research shows young LGBTQIA+ Australians are turning away from community sport due to discrimination. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

'We train to win'

One of the biggest battles Bonner has now is people not taking the club seriously enough as a competitive force.

"One thing we've tried to really reinforce to people is we are the exact same team with the same ambitions as you are in terms of on the pitch. We want to win. We train to win," he says.

"We do accept everyone … but that doesn't mean there's no competitive spirit because there absolutely is."

The club's Metro 7 side finished third this season, winning 11 out of its 18 games and scoring 87 goals.

Stuart Bonner and Aisling Haugh say the Melbourne Rovers allow them to feel a sense of belonging in community sport. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The Rovers recently travelled to Perth as part of a Pride Football Australia tournament and lost their game.

"It was heartbreaking. It was crushing … and that's a purely sporting thing. So we still take it as seriously as everyone else," Bonner says.

Part of why this gets under his skin so much is that the success of the club is personal.

"We genuinely change people's lives," he says.

"We have 68 members this year and we do surveys and stuff like that and people rate the sense of belonging as the highest out of all the metrics that we try and track.

"I just wish that people would give a bit more credit for that … I do take it really seriously, and I think for me that's because I'm trying to punch above our weight."

Bonner is aware this can translate into people walking into the club and perceiving a tough exterior.

But once anyone is around long enough to know him, the realisation is quick: "People know I'm quite soft and quite squidgy."

World.title: Cross-code star scores hat-trick as Kiwi Ferns make another final
World.content:
New Zealand cross-code superstar Stacey Waaka has led her country to another women's Rugby League World Cup final, scoring three tries in a dominant win over Fetu Samoa.

The Kiwi Ferns had made the final in all six previous editions of the women's world championship, but faced a stern early test from Fetu Samoa in their maiden semifinal.

But three tries to Waaka, and poor execution from the Samoans, ensured New Zealand would make it to a seventh consecutive decider.

Waaka, who won two Olympic gold medals in rugby 7s and two women's Rugby Union World Cups with New Zealand, continued her brilliant tournament where she has already scored six tries.

"A really close first half, but the team who was going to win was the one who played right to the end, then I think we done that," Waaka told the 7 Network post-match

"I love playing games with these young guns. It's fun learning off them too, because they've been in the game a little bit longer, but I'm just enjoying the whole experience.

"I can't wait for this next week and bring on whoever is in the final with us."

New Zealand will face either Australia or Fiji, who play the second semifinal in Sydney on Sunday.

In their maiden semifinal, Fetu Samoa suffered a horrible start with hooker Mary-Jane Taito throwing a forward pass in the first set of the match.

The Kiwi Ferns punished them immediately, with winger Mackenzie Wiki crossing in the right corner to claim an early lead after two minutes.

Fetus Samoa got themselves back into the contest with firm defence, as handling errors cruelled both sides. The Kiwi Ferns had nine errors and Samoa had seven, highlighting the tension of a semifinal.

Samoa's best chance of the first half came midway through the 35 minutes when they had four consecutive sets at the Kiwi Ferns' goal-line. But the first-time semifinalists failed to score, and would not come close again before half-time.

As the wind picked up and dark clouds closed in on Hunter Stadium, New Zealand scored a second try when Stacey Waaka charged onto a kick that was allowed to bounce by the Samoans to ensure her nation had an 8-0 lead.

Otesa Pule of New Zealand is tackled during the 2026 Women's Rugby League World Cup Semi Final match between New Zealand Kiwi Ferns and Samoa at Hunters Stadium on November 07, 2026 in Newcastle, Australia. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

As Fetu Samoa's errors continued, the Kiwi Ferns were able to punish them and take away any confidence the Pacific Island nation had.

Another kick to the in-goal was caught by a flying Waaka in the 44th minute for her second try, extending the lead to 14 points.

The Kiwis continued to press and iced the match with a three-try burst in six minutes to Mele Hufanga (58th minute), Kaiyah Atai (60th minute) and Waaka (64th minute).

Kiwi Ferns captain Raecene McGregor scored three minutes from time to cap off a well-earned win.

World.title: Ponga leads Kiwis to final after pre-match stare down lights up World Cup
World.content:
Kalyn Ponga has returned to the field 23 days after breaking his arm to lead New Zealand to its first Rugby League World Cup final since 2013.

Ponga, who suffered the broken arm in the tournament's opening match against Australia, had three try assists and a try-saving tackle to inspire the Kiwis to a 34-10 win.

But the highlight of the contest came before the opening whistle, when both sets of players engaged in one of the great moments in rugby league.

After New Zealand performed its Haka, in reply to the Sipi Tau from Tonga, the two sides stared each other down as time stood still.

A packed house at Hunter Stadium in Newcastle got louder as the stare-down lengthened, a precursor to the historic semifinal that was to come.

Kiwi centre Casey McLean, who scored a crucial second-half try for his country, told ABC Sport the pre-match stare-down was a special moment that had him ready to give everything for his teammates on Saturday.

"We have such mana boys in our team that are leaders," he said.

"We've just got to follow them, especially myself.

New Zealand defeat Fetu Samoa New Zealand cross-code superstar Stacey Waaka leads her country to another women's Rugby League World Cup final, scoring three tries in a dominant win over Fetu Samoa.

"I can learn so much off them, not just about being a player, but [also] my culture. They're front runners for Māori boys and Kiwi boys."

Ponga's impact on the match was immediate, setting up back-rower Briton Nikora for the opening try in the third minute.

New Zealand dominated the opening quarter, before Tonga winger Jojo Fifita made a line break from his own goal-line, setting up a break down the left wing by Tolutau Koula, who then threw it back to Fifita for the length-of-the-field try.

The belief in the Tongan camp grew, and they looked destined to score again when forward Demitric Vaimauga was clear and only had the much smaller Ponga to beat.

But Ponga produced a stunning try-saving tackle, one-on-one, to stop the much larger man.

"It just shows how much this Kiwi jersey means to him," McLean said.

"To be able to put on a performance like that, it just shows how much of an amazing person he is."

Just one minute later, Fifita was in for a second to give Tonga the lead off a perfectly executed scrum play.

But a mistake from fullback Lehi Hopoate allowed Kiwi Dane Gagai to score and give the Kiwis a 12-10 half-time lead.

Down by just two points, Tonga had every reason to believe they could advance to the World Cup final for the first time.

But a significant change in weather at half-time meant they played into a howling headwind for the second 40 minutes.

Hopoate was peppered with high kicks he could not reach as the wind made predicting the landing near impossible, while halfback Isaiya Katoa struggled to kick the ball much further than 30 metres at the end of sets.

It meant the Kiwis were able to camp themselves in the Tongan half of the field for the entire second half, wearing them down and scoring four tries to seal a 24-point win.

"No excuses, you've got to take your hats off to the Kiwis," Katoa said.

"The way they played footy tonight is the way you play in these conditions."

New Zealand will face either Australia or Samoa in next Sunday's final at Lang Park in Brisbane.

Relive all the action from Saturday's Rugby League World Cup semifinals in the blog below.

World.title: Demons rally and Kangaroos cruise into AFLW prelims
World.content:
Melbourne has stormed home with the last five goals of the game to beat Geelong by four points in their AFLW qualifying final.

After Demons star Paxy Paxman put them in front with a snapped goal, Chloe Scheer marked and had a shot at goal for Geelong with 20 seconds left.

But the Geelong forward missed and the Demons won 8.8 (56) to 8.4 (52) on Saturday at Princes Park.

In the later game, North Melbourne booked its prelim ticket with a commanding 7.7 (49) to 1.7 (13) win over Carlton.

Melbourne kicked the only three goals of the last quarter after looking well out of the game in the third term.

Geelong onballer Georgia Prespakis was easily best afield in the first half, but Melbourne midfielder Liv Purcell helped spark the comeback and they had 34 possessions apiece.

It was the first time Geelong's Mick Stinear has gone up against his old club since the 2022 premiership coach left Melbourne at the end of last season.

Melbourne now has the week off, while Geelong's semi-final opponent will be the winner of Sunday's Sydney-Western Bulldogs elimination final.

The threat of lightning delayed the start of the game on Saturday by 10 minutes, but Melbourne's changeable spring weather meant much of the game was played in sunshine.

The Cats kicked clear in the second term, with four goals to one and led by 22 points at the main break. They twice led by 28 in the third quarter, before the Demons hit back.

With Purcell and 100-gamer Tyla Hanks leading the way, the Demons kicked four goals to three and cut the margin to 12 points at the last change.

Alyssa Bannan's accurate snap in the first 30 seconds of the final quarter brought the Demons to within a goal. Prespakis kicked a behind, then Bannan kicked her second.

Paxman put Melbourne in front for the first time since the first quarter with her goal at 17 minutes.

Injury concern in big Roos win

Two-time North Melbourne premiership player Alice O'Loughlin is a significant casualty out of the Kangaroos' comprehensive AFLW qualifying final win.

O'Loughlin was emotional on the bench after she hurt her knee in the last quarter of Saturday's 36-point win over Carlton at Ikon Park.

She was in agony and needed two trainers to help her off the field after Gab Pound caught her in a tackle.

It was the one negative for the two-time defending premiers, who withstood a game challenge from the Blues in the first quarter.

The usual suspects starred for the Kangaroos — Jasmine Garner racked up 31 possessions, and fellow midfielder Ash Riddell had a game-high 33.

Key defender Harriet Cordner was mighty for Carlton, especially early, but eventually there was little she could do when the dam wall broke.

Carlton will next host the winner of Sunday's elimination final between Gold Coast and Hawthorn.

World.title: Lehmann says 'everyone' was ball tampering globally, denies Khawaja's sandpaper claims
World.content:
Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann claims ball tampering was once ever-present in international cricket, but denies Usman Khawaja's claim of widespread knowledge of the 2018 sandpaper plot.

Lehmann was the coach of the Test team during the Cape Town controversy, in which Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball during the match.

Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner were all suspended in the wake of the incident, while Lehmann stood down from his post.

Khawaja's explosive Sandpapergate claim Usman Khawaja claims all staff and players knew that the Australian team was using sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa.

In an interview with Nine newspapers on the eve of the release of his new book, Sabr, Khawaja claimed Cape Town was not the first time the Australian side had used sandpaper to tamper with the ball and that the plan had been known by "all of us".

"Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," Khawaja told Nine newspapers.

Speaking to ABC Sport's Summer Grandstand, Lehmann denied personal knowledge of the use of sandpaper and said he does not think all members of the Australian camp would have known about it either.

Lehmann did claim though that up until that day, "everyone around the world" was ball tampering.

Loading...

"I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann said.

"It's just how it's being done, and how you would know to that extent? That's an individual case by case, to be fair.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Khawaja said he had suggested to the entire playing group after Bancroft had been caught that they take collective responsibility.

Lehmann, who is part of the ABC's cricket commentary team and has recently joined the ABC Cricket Podcast as a co-host, said he could not confirm or deny that discussion took place, as he was not present.

Darren Lehmann stood down as Australian coach after Cape Town. (AP: Halden Krog)

"I don't remember that. There were two change rooms obviously, and there were meetings going on everywhere. To be perfectly honest I was in meetings with Cricket Australia a lot," Lehmann said.

"That could have been the case, I don't know. I'm not saying yes or no to that one. There will be different points of view everywhere on this whole matter."

Lehmann also said he was not aware of an alleged conversation between Bancroft and a member of the coaching team, which Khawaja said was important in the formation of the sandpaper plan.

Earlier on Saturday, a Cricket Australia (CA) spokesperson said they remained comfortable with the initial findings of their investigation.

"There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.

"All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

Lehmann said the 2018 incident left him in a "really dark place" and said the release of Khawaja's book and its explosive accusations has brought up "bad memories" for him, the players and their families.

"End of the day, Cricket Australia had their findings. It was a really tough week, two weeks, at that time going through the process and talking to all the relevant parties," he said.

"I was in a really dark place for a period of time where for four months I didn't leave my house.

"Eight years after the fact and trying to sell a book is a bit different. That's Usman's choice and that's the way he wants to go.

"For the families and the people involved, I feel for them right now because it's taking them back to a really bad place. It's been eight years. You get to a place where you move on, and I've moved on with my life."

Darren Lehmann said the Cape Town affair left him "in a dark place". (AP: Halden Krog)

Lehmann said Khawaja had not reached out to him in advance of these claims going public.

"For me it's a really touchy one mentally, more than anything else, and I know the boys will be feeling that as well.

"Could he have said this at the time? I suppose that's one of the things in the book. I mean, books are there to sell.

"He's spoken to Pat Cummins apparently and the players. I haven't spoken to Usman, he hasn't texted me or rang me. That's just the way it is."

In 2021, Australia's Test bowling quartet of Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon released a statement denying any knowledge of the ball-tampering plan.

Speaking to SA Grandstand on Saturday morning, former Australian fast bowler and current South Australia coach Ryan Harris said he thought it was "a bit disappointing" that it had taken Khawaja "eight years to say that".

"That's probably all I want to say on that. Like most people, I've been interested to hear what the book is going to say."

Jason Gillespie, another former Australian fast bowler, said he had always "found it a challenge to believe" only three players knew of the plan, but would not suggest everybody was across it and backed the testimony of the bowling group.

"This is what was interesting, the umpires at the time studied the ball and said they couldn't see any evidence of ball tampering. That's what I find fascinating.

"And that's what the bowlers have come out and said, the actual umpires looked at the ball and found no evidence … of ball tampering."

Tech.title: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance
Tech.content:
With temperatures rising to the 90s in Los Angeles, avoiding the heat wasn’t exactly an option while I was at a relative’s outdoor party in August. So I sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan nearby, figuring I was protected from the sun and heat. Half an hour later, I felt exhausted, dizzy, nauseous, and generally unwell, symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.

Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem, from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. It turns out UV radiation wasn’t repelled by this patio umbrella, and it’s hard to ever be fully protected because radiation can be reflected or scattered by objects in the environment. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both.

This led to a discovery: One of my medications increases my sensitivity to heat, which helped to explain similar episodes I’d experienced over the years. The Gem didn’t diagnose anything, but it prompted me to investigate something I might otherwise have dismissed. Since then, I’ve been more mindful about limiting time outdoors during hours of peak heat and UV, staying hydrated, and paying closer attention to how I’m feeling outside.

I’ll admit my initial interest in tracking UV was largely vanity-driven. As much as I try to challenge harmful beauty standards, I’m hardly immune to them. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others.

The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. Thankfully, getting these metrics doesn’t come at the cost of wearing a bulky device. The circular pendant comes with a cute, thin necklace I’d happily wear even if it didn’t track anything. Its titanium, gold- or silver-colored chain pairs well with a variety of outfits. Battery life lasted almost exactly a week (the advertised lifespan), and the Gem recharges using an included charging dock. The90 plans to release a hat clip and bag tag early next year, which seem ideal for those who prefer not to wear it around their neck.

The90 Gem’s modular design lets you detach the pendant from its necklace chain. Image: The90

The mobile app is central to the experience. It has easy-to-read graphs and jargon-light explanations. I enjoyed using it. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight.

There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. It also provides a personalized sunburn countdown, sunscreen reminders, and a daily Sun Score.

The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. I appreciated the context, but the individual estimated measurements proved more revealing than the Sun Score.

Previous Next

1 / 2

The UV readings in the app responded quickly as I moved between sunlight, shade, and indoors, even registering changes near windows. I couldn’t independently verify the sensor’s accuracy, but the readings behaved as expected as I shifted between environments. However, there were times when I noticed the Gem sometimes failed to register that I had been outside. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking.

My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too.

The vitamin D countdown wasn’t as helpful as I had hoped. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. I noticed similar fluctuations in the app’s estimated time to sunburn. With both countdowns changing so dramatically, I stopped paying much attention to the exact times and focused instead on the broader picture: whether it felt like I was getting too much or too little sun.

I appreciated how the Gem encouraged me to think more about my health than simply preventing wrinkles. Photo: Sheena Vasani / The Verge

That was perhaps the biggest surprise of testing the Gem. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade.

I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary.

At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it.

Photography by Sheena Vasani / The Verge

Tech.title: Costco members can get $5 off the reimagined Ocarina of Time

While some retailers were offering preorder discounts on the remastered Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time, it’s not too late to save if you missed out. Costco members can currently get $5 off the digital version online, bringing the price down to $54.99. Considering an annual Costco membership runs $65, that discount almost offsets one month of your plan — a prime example of “gamer math.”

My colleague Andrew Webster recently shared his thoughts on Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive, noting how impressed he was with how much impact a few modern quality-of-life changes had on what is otherwise a classic experience.
